question: (a) Define congenital heart disease and classify it with examples. (4 marks) (b) Explain the causes and the common clinical features of congenital heart disease in infants. (4 marks) (c) Describe the nursing management of an infant with congenital heart disease, including care before and after cardiac surgery. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Classification of congenital heart disease
labels: congenital heart disease – acyanotic (left-to-right shunt: ASD
AV canal; obstructive: coarctation of aorta
pulmonary stenosis) – cyanotic (decreased pulmonary blood flow: tetralogy of Fallot
tricuspid atresia; mixed blood flow: TGA

answer_html:
(a) Definition and classification (4 marks)

Definition Congenital heart disease (CHD) is a structural abnormality of the heart or the great vessels that is present at birth. It results from faulty development of the heart between the 3rd and 8th weeks of embryonic life, when the heart tube folds and the chambers, septa and valves are formed.

  • It is the commonest group of birth defects – about 8–10 per 1,000 live births. In India more than 2 lakh babies are born with CHD every year.
  • Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the commonest lesion; tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is the commonest cyanotic lesion after the newborn period.

Classification

1. Acyanotic CHD – no cyanosis because blood is not shunted from the right to the left side.

  • (i) With left-to-right shunt (increased pulmonary blood flow) – atrial septal defect (ASD), ventricular septal defect (VSD), patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), atrioventricular (AV) canal defect. Oxygenated blood returns to the lungs, causing pulmonary overcirculation, breathlessness and heart failure.
  • (ii) Obstructive lesions (no shunt) – coarctation of the aorta, aortic stenosis, pulmonary stenosis. The ventricle pumps against an obstruction.

2. Cyanotic CHD – deoxygenated blood reaches the systemic circulation.

  • (i) With decreased pulmonary blood flow – tetralogy of Fallot, tricuspid atresia, pulmonary atresia. Blood shunts from right to left because flow to the lungs is obstructed.
  • (ii) With mixed blood flow (admixture lesions) – transposition of the great arteries (TGA), truncus arteriosus, total anomalous pulmonary venous connection (TAPVC), hypoplastic left heart syndrome.
  • The cyanotic lesions are remembered as the "5 Ts" – Tetralogy of Fallot, Transposition, Truncus arteriosus, Tricuspid atresia and TAPVC.

Haemodynamic classification (used in many nursing texts) – (1) increased pulmonary blood flow (ASD, VSD, PDA, AV canal); (2) obstruction to blood flow out of the heart (coarctation, aortic and pulmonary stenosis); (3) decreased pulmonary blood flow (TOF, tricuspid atresia); (4) mixed blood flow (TGA, truncus, TAPVC, hypoplastic left heart).

Duct-dependent lesions – in some critical lesions (pulmonary atresia, severe coarctation, hypoplastic left heart, TGA) the baby survives only while the ductus arteriosus is open; when it closes in the first days of life the baby collapses or becomes deeply cyanosed.

(b) Causes and clinical features (4 marks)

Causes (risk factors) – in most children the cause is unknown; CHD is multifactorial (genetic tendency plus environmental factors acting in early pregnancy).

  1. Genetic and chromosomal – Down syndrome (AV canal defect, VSD), Turner syndrome (coarctation), trisomy 13 and 18, 22q11 deletion (TOF, truncus), Marfan and Noonan syndromes; a sibling or parent with CHD raises the risk.
  2. Maternal infections – rubella in the first trimester (PDA, pulmonary artery stenosis), cytomegalovirus, Coxsackie virus.
  3. Maternal illness – diabetes mellitus (TGA, VSD, cardiomyopathy), phenylketonuria, systemic lupus (congenital heart block), obesity.
  4. Drugs and toxins in pregnancy – alcohol (fetal alcohol syndrome), smoking, lithium (Ebstein's anomaly), phenytoin, valproate, warfarin, isotretinoin, thalidomide; radiation.
  5. Other – maternal age above 40 years, prematurity (PDA), birth at high altitude (PDA), consanguinity.

Common clinical features in infants

  • Feeding difficulty – the baby tires during feeds, takes a long time, stops to breathe and sweats on the forehead while feeding.
  • Poor weight gain and failure to thrive.
  • Fast breathing, chest retractions and recurrent chest infections (left-to-right shunts).
  • Central cyanosis of lips and tongue, worse on crying; clubbing after 6–12 months; polycythaemia.
  • Hypercyanotic (tet) spells in TOF and squatting in older children.
  • Heart murmur or thrill, abnormal heart sounds; weak or absent femoral pulses in coarctation.
  • Signs of heart failure – tachycardia, enlarged liver, gallop rhythm, puffy eyelids, excessive sweating.
  • Exercise intolerance and delayed motor milestones.
  • Screening – pulse oximetry after 24 hours of age detects critical CHD: SpO2 below 90%, or a difference of more than 3% between the right hand and a foot, needs echocardiography.

(c) Nursing management (7 marks)

Medical and surgical management (background for the nurse)

  • Drugs – diuretics (furosemide), ACE inhibitors and digoxin for heart failure; prostaglandin E1 infusion to keep the ductus open in duct-dependent lesions; ibuprofen, indomethacin or paracetamol to close a PDA in preterm babies; propranolol to prevent tet spells.
  • Catheter interventions – device closure of ASD, PDA and some VSDs; balloon dilatation of stenotic valves.
  • Surgery – palliative (Blalock–Taussig shunt, pulmonary artery banding) or corrective (patch closure of VSD, total correction of TOF, arterial switch for TGA).
  • Children identified under the Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) are referred to District Early Intervention Centres and can receive free cardiac surgery under state schemes and PM-JAY.

General nursing care of the infant with CHD

  1. Maintaining cardiac output and oxygenation
    • Monitor heart rate (apex for a full minute), respiratory rate, SpO2, colour, capillary refill, BP and temperature.
    • Keep the infant in a semi-upright position (infant seat or propped up).
    • Give oxygen as prescribed – but remember that oxygen can promote closure of the ductus in duct-dependent lesions, so it is given only as ordered.
    • Digoxin – count the apical pulse before each dose and withhold and report if it is below the ordered limit (commonly below 90–110 per minute in infants); watch for vomiting, poor feeding and bradycardia (toxicity).
  2. Reducing the work of the heart
    • Cluster nursing care to allow long rest periods; prevent prolonged crying (cuddling, pacifier); keep the baby warm (cold increases oxygen demand).
  3. Nutrition
    • Small, frequent feeds; a soft nipple with a slightly larger hole; feed in an upright position and burp often; limit each feed to about 20–30 minutes.
    • High-calorie feeds (fortified breast milk) as advised; nasogastric feeding if the baby tires; daily weight and growth chart.
  4. Fluid balance (heart failure) – strict intake and output, daily weight, diuretics, serum potassium monitoring, fluid restriction as ordered.
  5. Preventing infection – hand hygiene, keep away from people with colds, complete immunisation (including pneumococcal and influenza vaccines as advised), good oral and dental hygiene; antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis before dental procedures in high-risk children as advised by the cardiologist.
  6. Special care of the cyanotic child – maintain good hydration (dehydration increases blood viscosity and the risk of cerebral thrombosis), recognise and manage tet spells, treat iron deficiency, and watch for signs of brain abscess (fever, headache, vomiting, seizures).
  7. Supporting the family – explain the defect with simple drawings, involve parents in care, relieve guilt ("nothing you did caused this"), and link them with RBSK and financial schemes.

Care before cardiac surgery (pre-operative)

  • Baseline weight, height, vital signs and SpO2 in all four limbs; investigations – complete blood count, coagulation profile, blood grouping and cross-matching, electrolytes, renal function, chest X-ray, ECG and echocardiography.
  • Treat any chest infection or dental sepsis before surgery; continue or stop drugs (digoxin, diuretics, aspirin) as ordered.
  • Preparation of the child – age-appropriate explanation and therapeutic play with dolls, showing the dressing, chest tubes and monitors; a visit to the PICU where possible.
  • Preparation of parents – explain the operation, the PICU stay, tubes and wires they will see; informed consent.
  • Fasting as per anaesthesia instructions (for example, breast milk up to 4 hours and formula up to 6 hours before), skin preparation, identification band, pre-medication.

Care after cardiac surgery (post-operative, in the PICU)

  1. Airway and breathing – ventilator care, endotracheal suction, ABG monitoring; after extubation, humidified oxygen, chest physiotherapy, deep breathing through play (blowing bubbles, windmills).
  2. Cardiovascular monitoring – continuous ECG for arrhythmias and heart block (temporary pacing wires), arterial BP, central venous pressure, heart rate, peripheral pulses, warmth and capillary refill.
  3. Bleeding and cardiac tamponade – measure chest drain output hourly; report drainage of more than 3 ml/kg/hour for 3 hours; a sudden stop of drainage with rising CVP, falling BP and muffled heart sounds suggests tamponade – an emergency.
  4. Fluids and electrolytes – restricted IV fluids as ordered, hourly urine output (at least 1 ml/kg/hour), potassium, calcium and blood glucose.
  5. Pain relief – morphine or fentanyl infusion and paracetamol; assess pain with the FLACC scale; comfort measures.
  6. Prevention of infection – aseptic care of the sternotomy wound, central lines and drains; temperature monitoring.
  7. Neurological checks – level of consciousness, pupils, movement of limbs, seizures.
  8. Psychological care – allow parents to visit and touch the child; favourite toy; explain each procedure.

Discharge teaching

  • Wound care and signs of infection; medicines (how to give digoxin and count the pulse, diuretics); nutrition; gradual return to normal activity and school.
  • Regular follow-up and echocardiography; continue routine immunisation; dental care.
  • Seek help at once for breathlessness, poor feeding, increasing cyanosis, fever, sweating or swelling of eyelids.

Nursing importance The paediatric nurse is often the first to notice a baby who tires while feeding, sweats or looks blue. Early identification through newborn examination and pulse oximetry screening, careful feeding and fluid management, and skilled pre- and post-operative care decide the outcome for children with CHD.

Conclusion Congenital heart disease is a structural heart defect present at birth, classified as acyanotic (left-to-right shunts and obstructive lesions) and cyanotic (decreased pulmonary flow and admixture lesions). Its causes are multifactorial. Infants present with feeding difficulty, sweating, poor weight gain, breathlessness and cyanosis. Nursing management focuses on oxygenation, rest, nutrition, prevention of infection and family support, along with careful preparation and intensive monitoring around cardiac surgery.

question: Master Rohan, aged 2½ years, is brought with bluish lips that become darker when he cries, breathlessness while playing and a habit of squatting after walking a short distance. He is diagnosed with tetralogy of Fallot. (a) List the four defects in tetralogy of Fallot and explain its pathophysiology. (4 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features, investigations and complications. (4 marks) (c) Describe the management of a hypercyanotic (tet) spell and the nursing care of Rohan. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Heart in tetralogy of Fallot
labels: arrow showing right-to-left shunt of blue blood into the aorta
reduced blood flow to the pulmonary artery

answer_html:
(a) The four defects and pathophysiology (4 marks)

Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is the commonest cyanotic congenital heart disease after the newborn period (about 10% of all CHD). It consists of four defects:

  1. Ventricular septal defect (VSD) – a large defect just below the aortic valve.
  2. Pulmonary stenosis – right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (RVOTO), mainly narrowing of the infundibulum below the pulmonary valve, sometimes of the valve as well.
  3. Overriding (dextroposed) aorta – the aorta sits over the VSD and receives blood from both ventricles.
  4. Right ventricular hypertrophy – a consequence of the right ventricle pumping against the obstruction.

Pathophysiology

  • Because of the RVOT obstruction, the pressure in the right ventricle rises to equal the left ventricle.
  • Deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle passes through the VSD into the overriding aorta (right-to-left shunt) and enters the systemic circulation → cyanosis.
  • Pulmonary blood flow is reduced, so less blood is oxygenated → chronic hypoxaemia.
  • The body compensates by producing more red cells (polycythaemia) and by growth of capillaries in the fingertips (clubbing).
  • The severity of cyanosis depends on the degree of RVOT obstruction – mild obstruction gives an acyanotic or "pink" TOF; severe obstruction gives deep cyanosis.
  • Spasm of the infundibulum (with crying, feeding or straining) suddenly increases the obstruction and the right-to-left shunt → hypercyanotic (tet) spell.
  • Why squatting helps – squatting kinks the femoral arteries and raises systemic vascular resistance, so less blood shunts from right to left and more goes to the lungs; it also reduces the return of very desaturated blood from the legs.

(b) Clinical features, investigations and complications (4 marks)

Clinical features

  • Cyanosis – often not obvious at birth; it appears in the first months of life as the RVOT narrowing increases and the ductus closes; it worsens on crying or exertion.
  • Hypercyanotic spells – most common between 2 months and 2 years, usually in the morning after waking, crying, feeding or passing stool: the child becomes restless, breathes fast and deep (hyperpnoea), turns deeply blue, may become limp, unconscious or have a seizure.
  • Dyspnoea on exertion and squatting after walking or playing.
  • Clubbing of fingers and toes after about 6 months; poor growth.
  • Ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border (due to pulmonary stenosis) – the murmur becomes softer or disappears during a spell; single second heart sound.
  • Heart failure is unusual (the VSD is "protected" by the pulmonary stenosis).

Investigations

  • Pulse oximetry – low SpO2.
  • Complete blood count – raised haemoglobin and haematocrit (polycythaemia); relative iron deficiency (low MCV).
  • Chest X-ray – "boot-shaped heart" (coeur en sabot) with an upturned apex, concave pulmonary bay and oligaemic (dark) lung fields.
  • ECG – right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy.
  • Echocardiography – confirms the diagnosis and shows the anatomy.
  • CT angiography or cardiac catheterisation before surgery when needed.

Complications

  • Hypercyanotic spells, which can cause brain damage or death.
  • Cerebral thrombosis (stroke), especially with dehydration and polycythaemia.
  • Brain abscess (usually after 2 years of age), paradoxical embolism.
  • Infective endocarditis.
  • Relative iron-deficiency anaemia, poor growth and delayed development.
  • After surgery – arrhythmias, residual defects, pulmonary regurgitation.

(c) Management of a tet spell and nursing care of Rohan (7 marks)

Management of a hypercyanotic (tet) spell – stay calm and act quickly:

  1. Calm the child – let the mother hold him; avoid painful procedures during the spell.
  2. Knee-chest position – hold the child over the shoulder with the knees bent up to the chest (the infant equivalent of squatting) to raise systemic vascular resistance.
  3. Oxygen by face mask.
  4. Morphine 0.1–0.2 mg/kg subcutaneously, IM or IV, as prescribed – relieves the infundibular spasm and the hyperpnoea.
  5. IV fluid bolus (normal saline 10–20 ml/kg) to improve right ventricular filling.
  6. Sodium bicarbonate to correct metabolic acidosis.
  7. IV propranolol (or esmolol) slowly – relaxes the infundibulum and slows the heart.
  8. Phenylephrine (a vasoconstrictor) to raise systemic resistance if the spell continues; ketamine sedation; in refractory spells, general anaesthesia and an emergency shunt operation. - Prevention of spells – oral propranolol as prescribed, avoiding dehydration, treating iron deficiency and early surgery.

Definitive treatment

  • Total correction (patch closure of the VSD and relief of the RVOT obstruction) – usually done between 3 and 12 months of age, or at diagnosis in an older child like Rohan.
  • Palliative modified Blalock–Taussig (BT) shunt (subclavian artery to pulmonary artery) in small or very sick infants, to increase pulmonary blood flow until correction.

Nursing care of Rohan

1. Impaired gas exchange and risk of hypercyanotic spells

  • Monitor colour, SpO2, respiratory rate and heart rate; observe for restlessness and deepening cyanosis.
  • Prevent prolonged crying – cuddle, distract with play, plan procedures together, give a familiar toy.
  • Keep oxygen, suction and emergency drugs (morphine, propranolol, sodium bicarbonate) ready; teach the mother the knee-chest position and what to do during a spell at home.

2. Risk of cerebral thrombosis due to polycythaemia

  • Ensure adequate fluid intake, especially during fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and hot weather; keep pre-operative fasting as short as allowed.
  • Observe for weakness of a limb, facial deviation, seizures or altered consciousness and report at once.

3. Activity intolerance

  • Allow activity as tolerated with rest periods; let him squat – never pull him up from squatting; choose quiet play (puzzles, picture books).

4. Imbalanced nutrition: less than body requirements

  • Small, frequent, energy-dense meals; iron supplements if prescribed; weekly weight and growth chart.

5. Risk of infection and infective endocarditis

  • Hand hygiene, complete immunisation, good oral and dental hygiene with regular dental check-ups; antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures as advised by the cardiologist; report unexplained fever.

6. Delayed growth and development

  • Encourage age-appropriate play and toilet training; involve parents; refer for developmental assessment if needed.

7. Anxiety of parents and preparation for surgery

  • Explain the defect and the operation in simple words; tell them about free surgery under RBSK/state schemes; prepare Rohan with therapeutic play; provide pre- and post-operative care as for open-heart surgery.

Health education to parents

  • Recognise and manage spells; give fluids generously; give propranolol regularly and never stop it suddenly.
  • Report fever, headache, vomiting, weakness or seizures (stroke or brain abscess).
  • Maintain dental hygiene and immunisation; keep follow-up appointments.

Nursing importance Tet spells are frightening and can be fatal. A nurse who recognises a spell early, places the child in the knee-chest position, gives oxygen and morphine as ordered, and teaches parents to prevent dehydration and to manage spells at home protects the child until definitive surgery.

Conclusion Tetralogy of Fallot combines VSD, pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy, producing a right-to-left shunt and cyanosis. Children like Rohan present with cyanosis, clubbing, squatting and hypercyanotic spells; the X-ray shows a boot-shaped heart. Spells are managed with the knee-chest position, oxygen, morphine, fluids and propranolol, and the defect is cured by total surgical correction, supported by skilled nursing care and parent education.

question: (a) Define rheumatic fever and explain its aetiology and pathogenesis. (4 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and the diagnosis of rheumatic fever using the revised Jones criteria. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management, including secondary prophylaxis, and the nursing care of a child with rheumatic fever. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Revised Jones criteria (2015) for diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever
labels: evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection – major criteria: carditis (clinical or subclinical)
arthritis (polyarthritis; monoarthritis or polyarthralgia in moderate/high-risk populations)
prolonged PR interval – initial attack: 2 major or 1 major + 2 minor; recurrence: also 3 minor

answer_html:
(a) Definition, aetiology and pathogenesis (4 marks)

Definition Rheumatic fever (acute rheumatic fever, ARF) is a delayed, non-suppurative, inflammatory (autoimmune) complication of a throat infection with group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus, occurring about 2–4 weeks after a sore throat. It affects the heart, joints, brain (basal ganglia), skin and subcutaneous tissues.

  • Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) is the chronic damage to the heart valves (mitral valve most often, then aortic) left behind by one or repeated attacks of rheumatic fever. It remains an important cause of acquired heart disease in Indian children and young adults.
  • Rheumatic fever mainly affects children of 5–15 years; it is rare below 3 years.

Aetiology

  • Causative organism – group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) infection of the throat (pharyngitis, tonsillitis). Skin infection with the same organism causes glomerulonephritis but not rheumatic fever.
  • Only about 0.3–3% of untreated streptococcal sore throats lead to rheumatic fever, so host factors matter.
  • Predisposing factors – poverty, overcrowding, poor housing and ventilation, malnutrition, lack of treatment of sore throat, genetic susceptibility, and previous attacks (recurrences are common).

Pathogenesis

  • Molecular mimicry – antibodies and T cells produced against the streptococcal M protein and cell-wall carbohydrate cross-react with similar proteins in the heart muscle and valves, synovium, skin and basal ganglia neurons.
  • This produces inflammation of all three layers of the heart (pancarditis), arthritis and chorea.
  • Aschoff bodies (nodules of fibrinoid necrosis with Anitschkow and Aschoff cells) in the myocardium are characteristic.
  • Valvulitis produces small vegetations along the lines of closure; healing with fibrosis, thickening and fusion of commissures leads to stenosis or regurgitation – rheumatic heart disease.

(b) Clinical features and diagnosis (5 marks)

Major manifestations

  1. Carditis (50–70%) – the most serious feature: tachycardia out of proportion to fever (raised sleeping pulse), new murmurs (apical pansystolic murmur of mitral regurgitation, mid-diastolic Carey Coombs murmur, early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation), pericardial rub, cardiomegaly and heart failure. Carditis seen only on echocardiography is called subclinical carditis.
  2. Arthritis – migratory (flitting) polyarthritis of large joints (knees, ankles, elbows, wrists); joints are very painful, hot, red and swollen; each joint settles in a few days as another is involved; dramatic response to aspirin; no permanent joint damage.
  3. Sydenham's chorea – weeks to months after the infection, more in girls: involuntary, jerky, purposeless movements, clumsiness, deterioration of handwriting, emotional lability, "milkmaid's grip"; disappears during sleep.
  4. Erythema marginatum – pink, non-itchy rings with clear centres on the trunk and limbs; rare.
  5. Subcutaneous nodules – painless, firm, pea-sized nodules over bony prominences and tendons (elbows, knees, spine); usually with severe carditis.

Minor manifestations

  • Fever (38 °C or more in moderate/high-risk populations).
  • Arthralgia (joint pain without swelling).
  • Raised ESR (30 mm in the first hour or more) and/or CRP (3 mg/dl or more) in moderate/high-risk populations.
  • Prolonged PR interval on ECG (when carditis is not counted as a major criterion).

Revised Jones criteria (American Heart Association, 2015)

  • Essential – evidence of a preceding group A streptococcal infection: raised or rising antistreptolysin O (ASO) or anti-DNase B titre, positive throat culture or rapid antigen test.
  • Initial attack – 2 major criteria, or 1 major + 2 minor criteria.
  • Recurrent attack – 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor, or 3 minor criteria.
  • India is a moderate/high-risk population, so monoarthritis or polyarthralgia can count as a major criterion, monoarthralgia as minor, and lower cut-offs are used for fever and ESR.
  • Chorea alone (after excluding other causes) or indolent carditis may be enough for diagnosis.

Investigations – ASO titre, throat swab, ESR, CRP, complete blood count, ECG (prolonged PR), chest X-ray (cardiomegaly) and echocardiography (valvulitis, regurgitation, pericardial effusion).

(c) Management and nursing care (6 marks)

Medical management

  1. Bed rest – until fever and joint inflammation subside; with carditis, longer bed rest and gradual return to activity over weeks to months according to severity.
  2. Eradication of streptococci – a single deep IM injection of benzathine penicillin G (6 lakh units for children under 27 kg, 12 lakh units for 27 kg and above, after a test dose as per hospital policy), or oral penicillin V or amoxicillin for 10 days; azithromycin or erythromycin if allergic to penicillin.
  3. Anti-inflammatory treatment
    • Aspirin (high dose, divided doses after food, for several weeks and then tapered) for arthritis and mild carditis; naproxen is an alternative.
    • Prednisolone for moderate to severe carditis with heart failure, tapered over weeks, as prescribed.
  4. Heart failure – diuretics, ACE inhibitors, salt and fluid restriction, oxygen; digoxin is used cautiously because the inflamed myocardium is sensitive to it.
  5. Chorea – a quiet environment; haloperidol, sodium valproate or carbamazepine if severe.
  6. Surgery later for severe valve disease – balloon mitral valvotomy, valve repair or replacement.

Secondary prophylaxis (the most important step)

  • Purpose – to prevent recurrent streptococcal infection and recurrent attacks, which worsen valve damage.
  • Benzathine penicillin G 12 lakh units deep IM every 3 weeks (6 lakh units if weight is below 27 kg); alternatives – oral penicillin V twice daily, or erythromycin if allergic.
  • Duration (WHO/AHA):
    • Rheumatic fever without carditis – 5 years after the last attack or until 21 years of age, whichever is longer.
    • Carditis without residual valve disease – 10 years or until 21 years, whichever is longer.
    • Carditis with residual valve disease – 10 years or until 40 years of age, whichever is longer; sometimes lifelong.
  • Primary prevention – prompt treatment of every streptococcal sore throat with penicillin for 10 days, better housing and less overcrowding.

Nursing care of the child with rheumatic fever

  1. Assessment – temperature, pulse (sleeping pulse rate is a sensitive indicator of active carditis), respiration, BP, heart sounds, signs of heart failure (breathlessness, liver enlargement, oedema), joint pain and swelling, chorea.
  2. Pain in joints – handle joints gently; position them comfortably supported on pillows; use a bed cradle to keep bedclothes off painful joints; give aspirin as prescribed and record the relief.
  3. Decreased cardiac output / activity intolerance – maintain bed rest during the acute stage with all needs met by the nurse; semi-Fowler's position; oxygen if breathless; intake and output, daily weight; gradual ambulation as advised.
  4. Drug safety
    • Give aspirin after food; watch for salicylate toxicity – tinnitus, nausea, vomiting, rapid deep breathing, drowsiness, bleeding.
    • With steroids, monitor BP, blood glucose and weight, and watch for infection and mood changes.
  5. Safety in chorea – padded side rails, help with feeding (spoon and cup with a lid, soft foods), protect from falls, avoid criticising the child for clumsiness; explain to parents that the movements are part of the illness and will settle.
  6. Nutrition – nutritious, easily digestible diet; salt restriction if there is heart failure; adequate fluids.
  7. Diversion and education – quiet play, books, drawing; arrange for studies to continue so that the child does not fall behind.
  8. Adherence to prophylaxis – a penicillin card with dates of injections, reminder system, painless technique, and follow-up linked to the nearest health centre.
  9. Health education – the meaning of secondary prophylaxis and the danger of stopping it; early treatment of sore throat in all family members; dental hygiene and antibiotic cover before dental procedures in RHD; regular follow-up with echocardiography; avoid overcrowding and improve ventilation of the home.

Nursing importance Most children recover from the acute attack, but recurrences destroy the valves. The nurse's most valuable contribution is to ensure regular three-weekly benzathine penicillin injections for many years, along with early treatment of sore throat in the community.

Conclusion Rheumatic fever is an autoimmune complication of group A streptococcal pharyngitis that causes carditis, migratory polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules. Diagnosis rests on the revised Jones criteria with evidence of a preceding streptococcal infection. Treatment includes rest, eradication of streptococci, aspirin or steroids and treatment of heart failure, while long-term secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin and good nursing care prevent rheumatic heart disease.

question: Master Arjun, aged 3 years, is admitted with severe pallor, a protuberant abdomen and poor growth and is diagnosed with beta-thalassaemia major. (a) Define thalassaemia and explain its inheritance and pathophysiology. (4 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and investigations. (4 marks) (c) Describe the management, with special reference to blood transfusion and iron chelation, and the nursing care of Arjun and his family. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Inheritance of beta-thalassaemia when both parents are carriers
labels: carrier father and carrier mother – each pregnancy: 25% normal

answer_html:
(a) Definition, inheritance and pathophysiology (4 marks)

Definition Thalassaemia is an inherited disorder of haemoglobin synthesis in which the production of one type of globin chain (alpha or beta) is reduced or absent, resulting in ineffective red cell production, haemolysis and anaemia.

  • Beta-thalassaemia (defect in beta-chain production) is the commonest type in India; beta-thalassaemia major is the severe, transfusion-dependent form.
  • About 3–4% of Indians carry the beta-thalassaemia gene, with higher rates in some communities, and an estimated 10,000–15,000 children with thalassaemia major are born in India every year.

Inheritance

  • It is inherited as an autosomal recessive condition.
  • A person with one abnormal gene is a carrier (thalassaemia minor or trait) – usually healthy with mild microcytic anaemia.
  • When both parents are carriers, in each pregnancy there is a 25% chance of thalassaemia major, 50% chance of a carrier child and 25% chance of a normal child.

Pathophysiology

  1. Absent or reduced beta-chains → the normal adult haemoglobin (HbA: two alpha + two beta chains) cannot be formed.
  2. Excess alpha-chains precipitate inside developing red cells → the cells are destroyed in the bone marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis) and the spleen (haemolysis) → severe anaemia.
  3. Anaemia stimulates erythropoietin → massive expansion of the bone marrow → thinning and widening of bones, typical facial changes and "hair-on-end" skull X-ray, fractures.
  4. Extramedullary haematopoiesis in the liver and spleen → hepatosplenomegaly.
  5. Iron overload (haemosiderosis) – from repeated transfusions and increased iron absorption from the gut – iron deposits in the heart (cardiomyopathy, heart failure – the main cause of death), liver (fibrosis, cirrhosis), pancreas (diabetes), pituitary, thyroid and gonads (delayed puberty, short stature) and skin (bronze pigmentation).

(b) Clinical features and investigations (4 marks)

Clinical features – symptoms begin at 6 months to 2 years, when foetal haemoglobin (HbF) is normally replaced by HbA:

  • Progressive pallor, irritability, weakness, poor feeding and failure to thrive.
  • Hepatosplenomegaly causing a protuberant abdomen; mild jaundice.
  • Thalassaemic (chipmunk) facies – frontal and parietal bossing, prominent cheek bones and upper jaw, depressed nasal bridge, protruding upper teeth – in children who are not adequately transfused.
  • Recurrent infections, growth retardation; later delayed puberty and features of iron overload.

Investigations

  • Complete blood count – haemoglobin often 3–7 g/dl; microcytic hypochromic anaemia with target cells, nucleated red cells and fragmented cells; raised reticulocytes.
  • Haemoglobin HPLC or electrophoresis – markedly raised HbF and absent or reduced HbA in the child; HbA2 above 3.5% in the carrier parents.
  • Serum ferritin – baseline and regular monitoring of iron overload.
  • Liver function, serum bilirubin, blood sugar, thyroid and calcium profile; screening for HBV, HCV and HIV; extended red cell antigen typing before the first transfusion.
  • X-ray of skull and long bones; echocardiography and cardiac T2* MRI (for cardiac iron) in older children; DNA mutation analysis for prenatal diagnosis in future pregnancies.

(c) Management and nursing care (7 marks)

1. Regular blood transfusion (hypertransfusion)

  • Started when haemoglobin is persistently below 7 g/dl or there is growth failure or bone deformity.
  • Aim – keep the pre-transfusion haemoglobin at about 9–10.5 g/dl, which suppresses the overactive marrow and allows normal growth.
  • Leucoreduced packed red cells, ABO/Rh and extended-antigen matched, 10–15 ml/kg over 3–4 hours every 2–4 weeks, preferably at a thalassaemia day-care centre.
  • Hepatitis B vaccination before transfusions start.

2. Iron chelation therapy

  • Begun after about 10–20 transfusions or when serum ferritin exceeds 1,000 ng/ml.
  • Desferrioxamine (DFO) – slow subcutaneous infusion over 8–12 hours with a portable pump, 5–7 nights a week; side effects – local pain and swelling, hearing and visual problems, growth retardation, Yersinia infection; vitamin C is given only with DFO.
  • Deferiprone – oral, three times a day; risk of agranulocytosis (weekly neutrophil count), joint pain, red-brown urine.
  • Deferasirox – oral, once daily; monitor kidney and liver function.
  • Monitor serum ferritin every 3 months, yearly hearing and eye checks, and cardiac MRI in older children.

3. Other measures

  • Folic acid as prescribed; avoid iron tablets and iron-containing tonics.
  • Splenectomy when transfusion needs rise sharply (hypersplenism), preferably after 5 years of age, with pneumococcal, Hib and meningococcal vaccines before surgery and penicillin prophylaxis after.
  • Treatment of complications – cardiac, endocrine (diabetes, hypothyroidism, delayed puberty), bone (calcium, vitamin D) and liver.
  • Curative treatment – haematopoietic stem cell (bone marrow) transplantation from an HLA-matched sibling, best done early before iron overload; financial help is available, for example under the Thalassaemia Bal Sewa Yojana. Gene therapy is a newer option abroad.

Nursing care of Arjun

1. Safe blood transfusion

  • Check the prescription, consent, patient identity and the blood bag (group, compatibility, expiry) with a second nurse at the bedside.
  • Record baseline temperature, pulse, respiration and BP; use a blood administration set with filter; start slowly and stay with the child for the first 15 minutes.
  • Watch for transfusion reactions – fever, chills, rash, itching, breathlessness, back pain, dark urine; if they occur, stop the transfusion, keep the line open with normal saline, inform the doctor and send the bag and samples to the blood bank.
  • Watch for circulatory overload (cough, breathlessness, raised pulse); record the transfusion.

2. Iron chelation at home

  • Teach parents to prepare desferrioxamine, set up the pump, choose and rotate subcutaneous sites (abdomen, thighs) and care for local reactions.
  • Give oral chelators exactly as prescribed; report fever or sore throat (deferiprone – agranulocytosis).

3. Prevention of infection

  • Hand hygiene; immunisation including hepatitis B and pneumococcal vaccine; after splenectomy, any fever is an emergency; periodic screening for transfusion-transmitted infections.

4. Nutrition, growth and development

  • Balanced diet with adequate calcium and vitamin D; avoid iron supplements; tea with meals reduces iron absorption.
  • Plot height and weight on growth charts; assess puberty in adolescence.
  • Schedule transfusions to reduce missed school days.

5. Psychosocial support

  • Chronic illness, repeated needles and hospital visits are stressful – use local anaesthetic cream and therapeutic play, praise cooperation.
  • Support parents who may feel guilty or burdened; inform them of free transfusion and chelation services, financial schemes and thalassaemia support groups.

6. Genetic counselling and prevention

  • Explain the inheritance; test siblings and extended family members.
  • Prenatal diagnosis in future pregnancies by chorionic villus sampling at 10–12 weeks.
  • Promote carrier screening (HbA2 by HPLC) before marriage and in early pregnancy, especially in high-risk communities; avoid marriage between two carriers or plan pregnancy with prenatal testing.

Nursing importance With regular safe transfusions, effective chelation and good nursing support, children with thalassaemia major can live into adulthood, study and work. Carrier screening and genetic counselling, in which nurses play a key role, can prevent new births of affected children.

Conclusion Beta-thalassaemia major is an autosomal recessive disorder of beta-globin synthesis causing ineffective erythropoiesis, severe anaemia, bone changes, hepatosplenomegaly and iron overload. Diagnosis is confirmed by HPLC showing high HbF. Management rests on regular transfusion to keep haemoglobin around 9–10.5 g/dl, lifelong iron chelation, management of complications and, where possible, bone marrow transplantation, together with skilled transfusion nursing, family support and genetic counselling.

question: Baby Sneha, aged 4 years, is admitted with fever for two weeks, pallor, bleeding gums, bone pain and enlarged lymph nodes, and is diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL). (a) Define leukaemia, classify it and list the clinical features of ALL in children. (4 marks) (b) Explain the investigations and the phases of treatment of ALL. (4 marks) (c) Describe the nursing care of Sneha during chemotherapy, including the prevention of infection and support of the family. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Phases of treatment of childhood ALL
labels: intrathecal methotrexate; aim remission) – consolidation and CNS-directed therapy – interim maintenance and delayed intensification – maintenance (daily 6-mercaptopurine and weekly methotrexate) – total about 2–2½ years

answer_html:
(a) Definition, classification and clinical features (4 marks)

Definition Leukaemia is a malignant proliferation of immature white blood cell precursors (blasts) in the bone marrow, which replace normal blood-forming cells, spill into the blood and infiltrate other organs (lymph nodes, liver, spleen, brain, testes).

Classification

  • According to course – acute (rapid onset, immature blasts) and chronic (slow, more mature cells).
  • According to cell type – lymphoid and myeloid.
  • Thus: acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) and chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL – almost never seen in children).
  • ALL is the commonest cancer of childhood – leukaemias form about one-third of childhood cancers and about 75–80% of childhood leukaemias are ALL, with a peak at 2–5 years. Most are of B-cell type; T-cell ALL is commoner in older boys.
  • Risk factors – Down syndrome, exposure to radiation, some genetic syndromes and previous chemotherapy; in most children the cause is unknown.

Clinical features of ALL (due to marrow failure and infiltration)

  • Anaemia – pallor, tiredness, irritability.
  • Neutropenia – fever and repeated infections.
  • Thrombocytopenia – petechiae, bruises, bleeding gums, nosebleeds.
  • Bone and joint pain – limping or refusal to walk (may be mistaken for arthritis).
  • Lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly and splenomegaly.
  • CNS involvement – headache, vomiting, cranial nerve palsy; testicular enlargement in boys.
  • Mediastinal mass (T-cell ALL) – cough, breathlessness, facial swelling.
  • Loss of appetite and weight.

(b) Investigations and phases of treatment (4 marks)

Investigations

  • Complete blood count and peripheral smear – anaemia, thrombocytopenia, low, normal or high WBC count with blasts.
  • Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy – 20% or more lymphoblasts confirms the diagnosis.
  • Immunophenotyping (flow cytometry) – B-cell or T-cell type; cytogenetics and molecular tests for prognosis (for example, the Philadelphia chromosome is unfavourable).
  • Lumbar puncture and CSF examination for CNS leukaemia.
  • Chest X-ray (mediastinal mass), renal function, serum uric acid, potassium, phosphate, calcium and LDH (risk of tumour lysis), liver function, coagulation profile, blood grouping, viral serology, and echocardiography before anthracyclines.
  • Risk grouping – age 1–10 years and WBC below 50,000/mm³ are favourable (standard risk); response to induction (minimal residual disease) guides further treatment.

Phases of treatment (total therapy about 2–2½ years in standard protocols)

  1. Induction (4–6 weeks) – steroids (prednisolone or dexamethasone), vincristine, L-asparaginase with or without daunorubicin, and intrathecal methotrexate; aim – remission (less than 5% blasts in the marrow).
  2. Consolidation and CNS-directed therapy – drugs such as cyclophosphamide, cytarabine and 6-mercaptopurine; repeated intrathecal methotrexate; high-dose methotrexate with leucovorin rescue; cranial radiation only in selected high-risk cases.
  3. Interim maintenance and delayed intensification (re-induction) – to eliminate residual leukaemic cells.
  4. Maintenance – daily oral 6-mercaptopurine and weekly oral methotrexate, with periodic vincristine–steroid pulses and intrathecal therapy, mostly given at home with regular blood counts. - Supportive care – hydration and allopurinol to prevent tumour lysis, blood and platelet transfusions, antibiotics and antifungals, cotrimoxazole prophylaxis against Pneumocystis pneumonia, nutrition, and a central venous line. - Relapsed or very high-risk ALL – stem cell transplantation and newer treatments such as CAR-T cell therapy. - With modern protocols most children with standard-risk ALL can be cured.

(c) Nursing care of Sneha during chemotherapy (7 marks)

1. Prevention of infection (risk of infection due to neutropenia)

  • Single room where possible; strict hand hygiene by staff and family; limit visitors and keep away anyone with fever, cough or chickenpox; no fresh flowers or potted plants in the room.
  • Daily bath, oral care with a soft toothbrush and saline or chlorhexidine mouthwash after meals, and perineal hygiene.
  • Avoid rectal temperatures, suppositories, enemas and IM injections.
  • Safe food – freshly cooked, hot food and safe drinking water; avoid raw salads and unpasteurised milk products during neutropenia.
  • Aseptic care of the central line (dressing, flushing, hub cleaning).
  • Monitor temperature 4-hourly. Febrile neutropenia (fever of 38 °C or more with a neutrophil count below 500/mm³) is an emergency – take blood cultures and give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within one hour as per protocol.
  • No live vaccines during therapy; report exposure to measles or chickenpox.

2. Prevention of bleeding (thrombocytopenia)

  • Soft toothbrush, no nose picking; avoid injections and aspirin/NSAIDs; apply firm pressure for 5–10 minutes after needle pricks.
  • Prevent constipation and straining; padded cot sides to prevent falls.
  • Observe for petechiae, bleeding gums, blood in urine or stool and headache (intracranial bleed); give platelet transfusion as ordered.

3. Anaemia and fatigue – plan rest periods; transfuse packed red cells as ordered; encourage gradual activity.

4. Safe administration of chemotherapy and management of side effects

  • Check the drug, dose (calculated on body surface area), route and timing against the protocol with a second nurse; follow cytotoxic precautions (gloves, gown, closed systems, cytotoxic waste disposal).
  • Vincristine is given only intravenously – it is fatal if given intrathecally; it is a vesicant, so ensure a patent line and watch for extravasation; it causes constipation, jaw pain and nerve weakness.
  • Nausea and vomiting – antiemetics (ondansetron) before chemotherapy; small bland meals.
  • Mucositis – mouth care, pain relief, soft cool foods, avoid spicy and hot foods.
  • Steroids – increased appetite, mood changes, raised blood sugar and BP.
  • L-asparaginase – keep adrenaline and resuscitation equipment ready for allergic reactions; watch for abdominal pain (pancreatitis) and clotting problems.
  • Methotrexate – mouth ulcers, liver toxicity; high doses need hydration, urine alkalinisation, drug levels and leucovorin rescue.
  • Tumour lysis syndrome in early induction – generous IV fluids, strict intake and output, monitoring of potassium, phosphate, calcium, uric acid and creatinine, and allopurinol.
  • Hair loss – prepare Sneha and her parents in advance; a cap or scarf; reassure that hair will grow back.

5. Procedures – prepare Sneha for bone marrow aspiration and lumbar puncture with simple explanation, therapeutic play, local anaesthetic cream and sedation; position and observe her after intrathecal therapy as per protocol.

6. Nutrition – high-calorie, high-protein small frequent meals of her favourite foods; weekly weight; nasogastric feeds if intake is poor.

7. Pain relief – analgesics for bone pain and mucositis; distraction, music and comfort measures.

8. Psychosocial support of Sneha and her family

  • Honest, simple, age-appropriate explanations; encourage play, drawing and the hospital school.
  • Allow the parents to express shock, fear and guilt; give information step by step; involve them in care; remember the needs of siblings.
  • Inform them of financial support (PM-JAY, state schemes, Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi, childhood cancer NGOs) and parent support groups.
  • Home care during maintenance – give oral drugs exactly as prescribed, keep appointments for blood counts, avoid crowds, maintain hygiene; return immediately for fever, bleeding, increasing pallor, persistent vomiting or a child who looks unwell.
  • Long-term follow-up for late effects (growth, heart, learning, fertility); palliative care if the disease does not respond.

Nursing importance Most deaths during treatment of childhood leukaemia are due to infection and bleeding, not the leukaemia itself. Meticulous infection prevention, rapid response to febrile neutropenia, safe handling of chemotherapy and continuous emotional support of the child and family by the nurse greatly improve survival.

Conclusion ALL is the commonest childhood cancer, presenting with pallor, fever, bleeding, bone pain, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. It is diagnosed by bone marrow examination and treated over about two years in phases – induction, consolidation with CNS prophylaxis, intensification and maintenance. Nursing care centres on preventing infection and bleeding, safe chemotherapy, managing side effects, nutrition and supporting Sneha and her family through a long treatment.

question: Explain ventricular septal defect (VSD) and its management.

diagram.caption: Ventricular septal defect
labels: arrow showing left-to-right shunt of oxygenated blood from left ventricle to right ventricle
dilated left atrium and left ventricle

answer_html:
Definition A ventricular septal defect (VSD) is an abnormal opening in the interventricular septum allowing blood to pass between the two ventricles. It is the commonest congenital heart defect (about 25–30% of all CHD) and may occur alone or with other defects (as in tetralogy of Fallot).

Types (by site)

  • Perimembranous (70–80%) – in the membranous part below the aortic valve.
  • Muscular – in the muscular septum; often multiple ("Swiss-cheese"); many close spontaneously.
  • Inlet and outlet (subarterial) defects.

Pathophysiology

  • Pressure in the left ventricle is higher, so blood shunts from left to right → extra blood goes to the lungs and returns to the left heart → pulmonary overcirculation and volume overload of the left atrium and ventricle.
  • A large defect causes heart failure at 6–8 weeks of age, when pulmonary vascular resistance falls.
  • If not repaired, high pulmonary blood flow damages the pulmonary vessels → pulmonary hypertension → reversal of the shunt (right to left) and cyanosis – Eisenmenger syndrome, after which surgery is no longer possible.

Clinical features

  • Small VSD – usually no symptoms; a loud harsh pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border ("much ado about nothing" – maladie de Roger).
  • Moderate to large VSD – fast breathing, difficulty in feeding, sweating, poor weight gain, recurrent chest infections, signs of heart failure (tachycardia, enlarged liver); pansystolic murmur with a thrill; mid-diastolic murmur at the apex.

Investigations – chest X-ray (cardiomegaly, increased pulmonary markings), ECG, and echocardiography (site, size, direction of shunt, pulmonary pressure).

Management

  • Small defects – observation; 30–50% close spontaneously, especially muscular VSDs, in the first 1–2 years; good dental hygiene.
  • Heart failure – diuretics, ACE inhibitors, digoxin and high-calorie feeds.
  • Surgical patch closure under cardiopulmonary bypass for large defects, failure to thrive or rising pulmonary pressure – ideally within the first year, before pulmonary vascular disease; device closure by catheterisation for suitable muscular and some perimembranous defects.

Nursing care

  • Small, frequent feeds with rest; upright position; daily weight and growth monitoring.
  • Monitor respiratory rate, heart rate, SpO2 and signs of failure; give drugs safely (count the apex before digoxin).
  • Prevent chest infections; complete immunisation; dental hygiene.
  • Prepare the child and family for surgery and provide post-operative care; teach parents about follow-up.

Conclusion VSD is the commonest congenital heart defect, producing a left-to-right shunt with a pansystolic murmur. Small defects often close by themselves, while large defects cause heart failure and pulmonary hypertension and need timely closure, supported by careful feeding and nursing care.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: Explain patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and its management.
answer_html:
Definition Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is the failure of the ductus arteriosus to close after birth. The ductus connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta in foetal life; normally it closes functionally within 24–72 hours and anatomically by 2–3 weeks under the influence of rising oxygen and falling prostaglandins.

Risk factors – prematurity (very common in babies below 30 weeks), respiratory distress syndrome, maternal rubella, birth at high altitude, female sex.

Pathophysiology

  • After birth the aortic pressure exceeds the pulmonary pressure, so blood flows from the aorta to the pulmonary artery (left-to-right shunt).
  • Lungs and left heart are overloaded → heart failure, pulmonary hypertension and, rarely, Eisenmenger syndrome.
  • "Diastolic run-off" into the pulmonary artery lowers diastolic pressure → wide pulse pressure; in preterm babies it reduces blood flow to the gut and kidneys (risk of NEC and renal impairment).

Clinical features

  • Small PDA – no symptoms.
  • Large PDA – fast breathing, poor feeding, poor weight gain, recurrent chest infections, heart failure; in preterm babies – difficulty in weaning from the ventilator, apnoea.
  • Continuous "machinery" murmur below the left clavicle (in preterm babies often only systolic).
  • Bounding peripheral pulses and wide pulse pressure; active precordium.

Diagnosis – echocardiography (confirms and measures the duct); chest X-ray and ECG.

Management

  • Preterm infants – fluid restriction and respiratory support; drug closure with ibuprofen, indomethacin or paracetamol (they block prostaglandin synthesis); surgical ligation if drugs fail or are contraindicated.
  • Term infants and children – drugs are not effective; transcatheter device (coil or occluder) closure or surgical ligation, usually in infancy or early childhood, to prevent heart failure, pulmonary hypertension and infective endarteritis.
  • Note – in duct-dependent lesions (pulmonary atresia, TGA, severe coarctation), the ductus must be kept open with a prostaglandin E1 infusion until surgery (watch for apnoea, fever and flushing).

Nursing care

  • Monitor heart rate, respiration, SpO2, BP (pulse pressure), perfusion and urine output.
  • During drug therapy – check renal function and urine output (oliguria), platelets and bleeding, feeding tolerance and abdominal distension (NEC risk); give the drug at the correct time and dose.
  • Fluid restriction and careful intake–output recording; daily weight; small, frequent or tube feeds.
  • After device closure – check the puncture site for bleeding and the pulses of the leg; after ligation – chest care and pain relief.
  • Teach parents about follow-up and signs of heart failure.

Conclusion PDA is persistence of the foetal ductus after birth, causing a left-to-right shunt with a continuous murmur and bounding pulses. In preterm babies it is closed with ibuprofen, indomethacin or paracetamol; in older children device closure or ligation is done, with careful monitoring of fluids, kidneys and feeding by the nurse.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: Explain congestive cardiac failure in infants and children and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Congestive cardiac failure (CCF) in children is a condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the metabolic needs of the body, or can do so only with high filling pressures, leading to congestion of the lungs and systemic veins.

Causes (vary with age)

  • First week of life – hypoplastic left heart, critical aortic stenosis, severe coarctation, TGA, arrhythmias, birth asphyxia.
  • Infancy (6–8 weeks onwards) – large left-to-right shunts (VSD, PDA, AV canal) – the commonest cause.
  • Older children – rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease, viral myocarditis, cardiomyopathy, severe anaemia, hypertension (acute glomerulonephritis), infective endocarditis, arrhythmias, fluid overload.

Clinical features in infants

  • Feeding difficulty – tires, takes long, stops frequently; sweating on the forehead during feeds.
  • Poor weight gain, irritability.
  • Tachypnoea, chest retractions, grunting, cough, wheeze, crepitations.
  • Tachycardia, gallop rhythm, cardiomegaly, weak pulses, cool extremities.
  • Hepatomegaly (the most reliable sign of right-sided failure in infants); puffy eyelids; ankle oedema is uncommon in infants.
  • Older children – breathlessness on exertion, orthopnoea, fatigue, raised jugular venous pressure, oedema.

Management

  • Treat the cause – correct the heart defect, treat anaemia, rheumatic carditis, myocarditis or hypertension.
  • General – propped-up position, oxygen, rest, treatment of infection and fever.
  • Diuretics – furosemide (with potassium monitoring) and spironolactone.
  • ACE inhibitors – captopril or enalapril to reduce afterload.
  • Digoxin – improves contractility; narrow safety margin.
  • Nutrition – energy-dense feeds; fluid and salt restriction in older children as ordered.

Nursing management

  1. Monitoring – heart rate, respiratory rate, SpO2, BP, liver size, daily weight at the same time on the same scale, strict intake and output.
  2. Positioning and rest – semi-upright (infant seat, raised head end); cluster care; prevent crying; keep warm.
  3. Oxygen by nasal prongs or hood as ordered.
  4. Feeding – small frequent feeds, soft nipple, rest between sucks; nasogastric feeding if the infant tires.
  5. Safe digoxin administration – check the dose with another nurse; count the apical pulse for one full minute and withhold if below the prescribed limit; give at regular times, 1 hour before or 2 hours after feeds; do not repeat a dose that is vomited; watch for toxicity (vomiting, poor feeding, bradycardia, arrhythmias), which is increased by low potassium.
  6. Diuretic therapy – monitor potassium and urine output; give potassium-rich foods as allowed.
  7. Infection prevention and skin care of oedematous areas.
  8. Parent teaching – medicines, feeding, signs of worsening (fast breathing, poor feeding, sweating, swelling of eyelids, reduced urine), and follow-up.

Conclusion Heart failure in children is commonly due to large left-to-right shunts in infancy and rheumatic heart disease, myocarditis and anaemia in older children. Infants show feeding difficulty, sweating, tachypnoea, tachycardia and hepatomegaly. Treatment of the cause, diuretics, ACE inhibitors, digoxin and careful nursing of feeding, rest, fluids and drug safety are essential.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: Explain the home care and parent education for a child with haemophilia.
answer_html:
Introduction Haemophilia is an X-linked recessive bleeding disorder due to deficiency of factor VIII (haemophilia A, about 80–85%) or factor IX (haemophilia B). It affects boys; mothers are usually carriers. Severity depends on the factor level – severe below 1% (spontaneous bleeds into joints and muscles), moderate 1–5% and mild 5–40% (bleeding after injury or surgery). Because it is lifelong, most care happens at home and parents must become skilled carers.

1. Prevention of injury and bleeding

  • Safe home – pad sharp furniture corners, use carpets or mats, safety gates on stairs, soft toys; supervise the crawling and toddling child.
  • For toddlers, knee and elbow pads and a helmet while learning to walk.
  • Safe physical activity – encourage swimming, walking and cycling with a helmet to build strong muscles that protect joints; avoid contact sports (boxing, wrestling, rugby).
  • No IM injections – vaccines are given subcutaneously with a fine needle, followed by firm pressure for 5 minutes.
  • Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs – use paracetamol for pain and fever.
  • Dental care – soft toothbrush, fluoride toothpaste, regular dental visits; dental extraction only after factor replacement and with tranexamic acid as advised.

2. Recognition and first aid for bleeds

  • Early signs of a joint bleed (haemarthrosis) – tingling, warmth, stiffness, the child refuses to use the limb or limps; later swelling and pain (knee, elbow and ankle most often).
  • Act immediately – factor concentrate as early as possible (within 2 hours of the first sign) plus RICE: Rest, Ice (wrapped, 15–20 minutes), Compression and Elevation.
  • Emergency signs – head injury, severe headache, vomiting, drowsiness; bleeding in the neck or throat; abdominal pain; blood in urine or stool; large muscle bleeds (iliopsoas) – go to the hospital at once after giving factor.
  • Nosebleeds – sit up, lean forward, pinch the soft part of the nose for 10 minutes.

3. Factor replacement and home therapy

  • Teach parents (and later the child) home infusion of factor concentrate – storage, reconstitution, aseptic venepuncture, dose and record keeping.
  • Prophylaxis – regular infusions (usually 2–3 times a week) or emicizumab subcutaneously (haemophilia A) prevent joint damage; many states provide factor free at haemophilia treatment centres under the National Health Mission.
  • Keep a bleeding diary and attend the haemophilia centre regularly; watch for inhibitors (poor response to factor).

4. Joint care and physiotherapy – exercises to strengthen muscles after a bleed has settled; avoid prolonged immobility; orthopaedic review for target joints.

5. School and social life

  • Inform teachers, provide an emergency plan and contact numbers; encourage normal schooling and safe play.
  • Medical alert card or bracelet showing the diagnosis, type and severity.

6. Psychological and genetic support

  • Avoid overprotection; encourage independence; counselling for anxiety; link with the Haemophilia Federation (India) and support groups.
  • Genetic counselling – each son of a carrier mother has a 50% chance of haemophilia and each daughter a 50% chance of being a carrier; carrier testing of sisters and prenatal diagnosis are available.

Conclusion Home care of a child with haemophilia centres on preventing injury, avoiding IM injections and aspirin, recognising bleeds early, giving factor replacement promptly with RICE, regular prophylaxis, dental and joint care, school planning and genetic counselling, so that the child can lead an active and near-normal life.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: Define tetralogy of Fallot.
answer_html:
Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is a cyanotic congenital heart disease consisting of four defects:

  1. Ventricular septal defect (VSD) – large and just below the aortic valve.
  2. Pulmonary stenosis – obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract (mainly infundibular).
  3. Overriding aorta – the aorta sits over the VSD and receives blood from both ventricles.
  4. Right ventricular hypertrophy. - Because of the outflow obstruction, deoxygenated blood shunts from right to left through the VSD into the aorta, causing cyanosis, clubbing, squatting and hypercyanotic spells; the chest X-ray shows a boot-shaped heart. - It is the commonest cyanotic heart disease after the newborn period and is treated by total surgical correction in infancy.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: Why does a child with tetralogy of Fallot assume a squatting position?
answer_html:
After walking or playing, a child with TOF becomes breathless and cyanosed and squats (sits on the heels with knees drawn up to the chest) to get relief because:

  • Squatting kinks the femoral arteries and raises systemic vascular resistance; the higher pressure on the left side reduces the right-to-left shunt through the VSD, so more blood flows to the lungs for oxygenation.
  • It reduces the return of highly desaturated venous blood from the legs, so the blood reaching the aorta is better oxygenated.
  • As a result cyanosis and breathlessness decrease.
  • In infants the same effect is produced by the knee-chest position used during a tet spell. The child should never be forced to stand up from squatting.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: What is atrial septal defect (ASD)?
answer_html:
Atrial septal defect (ASD) is an abnormal opening in the interatrial septum, allowing blood to shunt from the left atrium to the right atrium (left-to-right shunt); it is an acyanotic heart defect.

  • Types – ostium secundum (commonest, in the region of the foramen ovale), ostium primum (part of AV canal defects, as in Down syndrome) and sinus venosus defects.
  • Features – most children have no symptoms; some have fatigue, breathlessness and chest infections; an ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border and a wide, fixed split second heart sound are characteristic.
  • Diagnosis – echocardiography.
  • Management – small defects may close by themselves; larger defects are closed by transcatheter device closure or surgery, usually at 3–5 years of age, to prevent heart failure, arrhythmias and pulmonary hypertension in adult life.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: What is Eisenmenger syndrome?
answer_html:
Eisenmenger syndrome is the reversal of a long-standing left-to-right shunt into a right-to-left shunt because of severe, irreversible pulmonary hypertension.

  • It develops when a large VSD, PDA or AV canal defect is not repaired in time; the high pulmonary blood flow damages the pulmonary arterioles, pulmonary resistance rises above systemic resistance and the shunt reverses.
  • Features – cyanosis appearing late (in older children or adults), clubbing, polycythaemia, breathlessness, fatigue, chest pain, syncope, haemoptysis; the murmur of the original shunt becomes softer.
  • Significance – the defect can no longer be closed surgically; treatment is supportive (pulmonary vasodilators) or heart–lung transplantation. Pregnancy is very dangerous.
  • Prevention – early detection and timely closure of large shunts in infancy.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: What is Sydenham's chorea?
answer_html:
Sydenham's chorea (St Vitus' dance) is a major manifestation of rheumatic fever caused by autoimmune inflammation of the basal ganglia after group A streptococcal infection.

  • It appears late – 1 to 6 months after the sore throat, mostly in girls of 5–15 years, and may be the only feature.
  • Features – involuntary, jerky, purposeless movements of the face, hands and feet that disappear in sleep; clumsiness, dropping things, deteriorating handwriting, slurred speech; "milkmaid's grip" (alternate squeezing and relaxing); emotional lability and outbursts of crying.
  • Management – a quiet environment, safety (padded bed sides, help with feeding), haloperidol, valproate or carbamazepine if severe, and long-term penicillin prophylaxis because carditis may follow. It usually recovers completely within weeks to months.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: Write the schedule of secondary prophylaxis for rheumatic fever.
answer_html:
Secondary prophylaxis is the regular use of antibiotics in a person who has had rheumatic fever, to prevent repeated streptococcal infections and recurrences that damage the heart valves.

  • Drug of choice – benzathine penicillin G 12 lakh units deep IM every 3 weeks (6 lakh units for children below 27 kg).
  • Alternatives – oral penicillin V 250 mg twice daily; erythromycin 250 mg twice daily if allergic to penicillin.
  • Duration:
    • Rheumatic fever without carditis – 5 years after the last attack or until 21 years, whichever is longer.
    • Carditis without residual heart disease – 10 years or until 21 years, whichever is longer.
    • Carditis with residual valve disease – 10 years or until 40 years, whichever is longer; sometimes lifelong.
  • The nurse maintains a penicillin card and reminder system to ensure regular injections.

question: What is acute immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) in children?
answer_html:
Acute immune (idiopathic) thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is an acquired autoimmune disorder in which antibodies destroy platelets, causing a low platelet count (below 1,00,000/mm³) with normal bone marrow.

  • In children it usually follows a viral infection or immunisation by 1–4 weeks, at 2–6 years of age.
  • Features – a well child with sudden petechiae, purpura and bruises, nosebleeds or gum bleeding; no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy (their presence suggests leukaemia).
  • Course – self-limiting; about 80% recover within 6 months.
  • Management – observation and bleeding precautions; IVIG or a short course of steroids for significant bleeding; avoid aspirin, NSAIDs and IM injections; restrict contact sports until the count recovers; platelet transfusion only for life-threatening bleeding.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: Name the iron chelating drugs used in thalassaemia and their important side effects.
answer_html:
Iron chelators bind excess iron from repeated transfusions so that it is excreted in urine or stool, preventing damage to the heart, liver and endocrine glands. They are started when serum ferritin exceeds 1,000 ng/ml (after about 10–20 transfusions).

  1. Desferrioxamine (DFO) – slow subcutaneous infusion over 8–12 hours, 5–7 nights a week; side effects – local pain and swelling, hearing and visual disturbances, growth retardation, Yersinia infection.
  2. Deferiprone – oral, three times a day; side effects – agranulocytosis (weekly neutrophil count), joint pain, nausea, reddish urine.
  3. Deferasirox – oral, once daily; side effects – gastrointestinal upset, rash, raised creatinine and liver enzymes (monthly monitoring). - Serum ferritin is checked every 3 months to adjust therapy.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: What is febrile neutropenia? State the nurse's immediate actions.
answer_html:
Febrile neutropenia is fever (a single temperature of 38.3 °C or more, or 38 °C or more lasting one hour) in a child whose absolute neutrophil count is below 500/mm³ (or expected to fall below 500), usually during cancer chemotherapy. It is an oncological emergency, because the child cannot localise infection and sepsis can kill within hours. Nurse's immediate actions

  • Check vital signs, perfusion and SpO2; look for signs of shock and a source (central line, mouth, perianal area).
  • Inform the doctor at once; collect blood cultures (from the central line and a peripheral vein) and other samples.
  • Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within one hour of arrival as per protocol; give fluids for shock.
  • Avoid rectal temperature and IM injections; maintain strict hand hygiene and neutropenic precautions; monitor closely.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: What is tumour lysis syndrome?
answer_html:
Tumour lysis syndrome (TLS) is a metabolic emergency caused by the rapid breakdown of large numbers of cancer cells, usually within 12–72 hours of starting chemotherapy for leukaemia or lymphoma with a high cell count.

  • The contents of the dying cells are released into the blood, causing hyperuricaemia, hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia and secondary hypocalcaemia.
  • Effects – acute kidney injury (uric acid and calcium phosphate crystals), cardiac arrhythmias, muscle cramps, tetany and seizures.
  • Prevention and management – generous IV hydration (about twice maintenance), allopurinol or rasburicase, strict intake–output and urine output monitoring, frequent electrolytes and creatinine, avoiding potassium in IV fluids, and dialysis if needed.
