question: Baby Kavya, aged 10 months and weighing 8 kg, is admitted with frequent watery stools and vomiting for two days. She is lethargic, has sunken eyes, drinks poorly and her skin pinch goes back very slowly. (a) Define acute gastroenteritis and list its causes in infants. (3 marks) (b) Explain the assessment of dehydration and the complications of acute gastroenteritis. (4 marks) (c) Describe the management (Plan C) and the nursing care of Kavya. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Assessment of dehydration in a child with diarrhoea
labels: severe dehydration – rows: general condition (well/alert; restless
skin pinch (goes back quickly; slowly; very slowly – more than 2 seconds) – treatment: Plan A

answer_html:
(a) Definition and causes (3 marks)

Definition Acute gastroenteritis (AGE) is an acute inflammation of the stomach and intestines, usually infective, presenting with diarrhoea – the passage of three or more loose or watery stools in 24 hours – with or without vomiting, fever and abdominal pain, and lasting less than 14 days.

  • Types of diarrhoea – acute watery diarrhoea (including cholera), dysentery (blood in stool) and persistent diarrhoea (lasting 14 days or more).
  • Diarrhoea remains one of the leading causes of death in children under five in India; deaths are mainly due to dehydration.
  • Infants of 6–24 months are most affected, because weaning foods may be contaminated, maternal antibodies wane and the child begins to crawl and put things in the mouth.

Causes in infants

  1. Viral (most common) – rotavirus (the commonest cause of severe dehydrating diarrhoea in infants), norovirus, adenovirus, astrovirus.
  2. Bacterial – Escherichia coli (enterotoxigenic, enteropathogenic), Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, Vibrio cholerae.
  3. Parasitic – Giardia lamblia, Entamoeba histolytica, Cryptosporidium.
  4. Parenteral (outside the gut) – otitis media, urinary tract infection, pneumonia, septicaemia.
  5. Non-infective – feeding errors (overfeeding, wrongly diluted formula, unclean bottles), cow's milk protein allergy, lactose intolerance, antibiotics. - Risk factors – not exclusively breastfed, bottle feeding, unsafe water, lack of hand washing, poor sanitation, malnutrition, vitamin A deficiency, recent measles, and missed rotavirus vaccination.

(b) Assessment of dehydration and complications (4 marks)

Assessment of dehydration (WHO/IMNCI)

Sign No dehydration Some dehydration Severe dehydration
General condition Well, alert Restless, irritable Lethargic or unconscious
Eyes Normal Sunken Sunken
Thirst / drinking Drinks normally Drinks eagerly, thirsty Drinks poorly or not able to drink
Skin pinch Goes back quickly Goes back slowly Goes back very slowly (more than 2 seconds)
Treatment Plan A Plan B Plan C
  • Two or more signs in a column decide the classification.
  • Kavya is lethargic, has sunken eyes, drinks poorly and her skin pinch goes back very slowly – she has severe dehydration (more than 10% loss of body weight) and needs Plan C.
  • Other signs – depressed anterior fontanelle, dry mouth and tongue, absent tears, reduced urine (dry nappies), rapid weak pulse, cold extremities, capillary refill longer than 3 seconds, low BP (late), loss of weight.

Investigations (in severe dehydration) – serum sodium and potassium, blood urea and creatinine, blood glucose, blood gas (metabolic acidosis), stool examination (pus cells, red cells, ova and cysts), stool culture when dysentery or cholera is suspected, rotavirus antigen test, complete blood count.

Complications

  1. Hypovolaemic shock and death.
  2. Acute kidney injury (pre-renal failure).
  3. Electrolyte disturbances
    • Hypernatraemia – irritable, very thirsty child with doughy skin and convulsions; must be corrected slowly.
    • Hyponatraemia – lethargy and seizures.
    • Hypokalaemia – weakness, abdominal distension (paralytic ileus), arrhythmias.
  4. Metabolic acidosis – deep, rapid (Kussmaul) breathing.
  5. Hypoglycaemia and convulsions.
  6. Persistent diarrhoea, secondary lactose intolerance and malnutrition (diarrhoea and malnutrition form a vicious cycle).
  7. Septicaemia; haemolytic uraemic syndrome after Shigella or some E. coli infections.

(c) Management (Plan C) and nursing care of Kavya (8 marks)

Plan C – treatment of severe dehydration

  1. Start IV fluids immediately – Ringer's lactate (or normal saline if not available), 100 ml/kg:
Age First give 30 ml/kg in Then give 70 ml/kg in
Infants (under 12 months) 1 hour 5 hours
Children (12 months–5 years) 30 minutes 2½ hours 
- The first 30 ml/kg may be **repeated once if the radial pulse is still very weak** or not detectable.
  1. For Kavya (8 kg) – total 800 ml Ringer's lactate: 240 ml in the first hour, then 560 ml over the next 5 hours (about 112 ml/hour).
  2. Reassess every 15–30 minutes until a strong radial pulse returns, then every hour; increase the rate if hydration is not improving.
  3. Give ORS (about 5 ml/kg/hour) as soon as she can drink, usually after 3–4 hours in an infant.
  4. Reassess after 6 hours (infants) – classify dehydration again and continue with Plan A, B or C.
  5. If IV access is not possible – ORS by nasogastric tube 20 ml/kg/hour for 6 hours (120 ml/kg), or refer urgently.

After rehydration

  • Low-osmolarity ORS for ongoing losses – 50–100 ml after each loose stool for a child under 2 years (100–200 ml for 2–10 years).
  • Zinc – 10 mg/day for infants below 6 months and 20 mg/day for those above 6 months, for 14 days; it shortens the illness and reduces recurrences.
  • Continue breastfeeding and restart age-appropriate feeding as soon as she is rehydrated; give one extra meal a day for two weeks after recovery.
  • Antibiotics only when indicated – dysentery, suspected cholera with severe dehydration or another infection; antidiarrhoeal drugs are not used.
  • Correct hypoglycaemia, hypokalaemia (potassium added to IV fluids only after urine is passed) and acidosis as ordered.

Nursing care of Kavya

1. Deficient fluid volume related to excessive loss through stools and vomiting

  • Secure an IV line quickly (intraosseous route if veins cannot be found); calculate and regulate the infusion carefully with an infusion pump or microdrip set and record hourly.
  • Monitor pulse, respiration, temperature, capillary refill, level of consciousness, fontanelle, eyes, skin pinch and tears hourly.
  • Urine output – weigh nappies (1 g = 1 ml); expect at least 1 ml/kg/hour.
  • Weigh the baby on admission and every 12–24 hours on the same scale.
  • Maintain an intake and output chart including the number, volume and type of stools and vomitus.
  • Watch for overhydration – puffy eyelids, oedema, breathlessness, rising pulse – and slow the infusion and report.

2. Risk of electrolyte imbalance and convulsions

  • Send blood for electrolytes as ordered and follow results; watch for abdominal distension and weakness (hypokalaemia), irritability and convulsions (sodium imbalance); keep emergency drugs and suction ready.

3. Imbalanced nutrition

  • Encourage the mother to continue breastfeeding frequently; start ORS in small sips as soon as Kavya can drink; then soft home foods (khichdi, dal-rice, curd, mashed banana) in small, frequent feeds.
  • Avoid sugary drinks, fruit juices, soft drinks and diluted feeds.
  • Give zinc daily and record.

4. Impaired skin integrity of the perianal area

  • Clean the buttocks with plain water after every stool, pat dry, apply a barrier cream (zinc oxide), change nappies frequently and expose the area to air.

5. Risk of spread of infection

  • Contact precautions – hand washing with soap before and after care, gloves when handling stools, safe disposal of nappies and stool as biomedical waste, disinfection of surfaces and toilets; keep her away from other infants.

6. Fever and discomfort – tepid sponging and paracetamol as ordered; mouth care; comfort by the mother.

7. Anxiety and knowledge deficit of the mother – health education

  • ORS preparation – dissolve one packet in one litre of clean drinking water; use within 24 hours.
  • How to give – a teaspoon every 1–2 minutes; if the child vomits, wait 10 minutes and then continue more slowly.
  • Give zinc for the full 14 days, even after diarrhoea stops.
  • Return immediately if the child is not able to drink or breastfeed, becomes sicker, develops fever or has blood in the stool.
  • Prevention – exclusive breastfeeding for six months; hand washing with soap after toilet use and before feeding or cooking; safe drinking water; food hygiene; use of a latrine and safe disposal of child faeces; rotavirus and measles vaccination; vitamin A supplementation.
  • Every year the STOP Diarrhoea Campaign distributes ORS and zinc to families of under-five children before the monsoon.

Nursing importance Almost all deaths from diarrhoea are preventable with timely rehydration. The nurse who classifies dehydration correctly, calculates and monitors IV fluids accurately, continues feeding and teaches the mother to use ORS and zinc saves lives and prevents future episodes.

Conclusion Acute gastroenteritis in infants is commonly caused by rotavirus and bacteria, and its main danger is dehydration with electrolyte disturbances. Kavya has severe dehydration and needs Plan C – Ringer's lactate 100 ml/kg (30 ml/kg in 1 hour and 70 ml/kg in 5 hours), frequent reassessment, then ORS, zinc for 14 days and continued feeding – along with careful monitoring, skin care, infection control and health education of the mother.

question: Baby Aryan, aged 3 months, is admitted with abdominal distension, vomiting and constipation since birth; he had passed meconium only on the third day of life. He is diagnosed with Hirschsprung's disease and is posted for colostomy. (a) Define Hirschsprung's disease and explain its pathophysiology. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and diagnosis. (4 marks) (c) Describe the pre-operative and post-operative nursing management of Aryan, including colostomy care and teaching of the parents. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Colon in Hirschsprung's disease
labels: narrow aganglionic distal segment (rectum and sigmoid)
dilated and hypertrophied proximal colon filled with faeces (megacolon)
level of colostomy in normally innervated bowel

answer_html:
(a) Definition and pathophysiology (3 marks)

Definition Hirschsprung's disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon) is a congenital disorder in which the parasympathetic ganglion cells of the submucosal (Meissner's) and myenteric (Auerbach's) plexuses are absent in a segment of the distal bowel, causing functional intestinal obstruction.

  • Incidence – about 1 in 5,000 live births; boys are affected four times more often; associated with Down syndrome in about 10%.
  • Types – short-segment (rectum and sigmoid colon – 75–80%), long-segment and total colonic aganglionosis.

Pathophysiology

  1. During weeks 5–12 of foetal life, neural crest cells fail to migrate down to the distal bowel.
  2. The aganglionic segment cannot relax or propagate peristalsis, and the internal anal sphincter does not relax.
  3. Stool and gas cannot pass this narrow segment → functional obstruction.
  4. The normal bowel above dilates and hypertrophies (megacolon), filled with stool and gas.
  5. Stasis leads to bacterial overgrowth and inflammation – Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis – the most dangerous complication, which can cause sepsis, perforation and death.

(b) Clinical features and diagnosis (4 marks)

In the newborn

  • Failure to pass meconium within 24–48 hours of birth (as in Aryan).
  • Abdominal distension, bile-stained vomiting, reluctance to feed.
  • Explosive passage of stool and gas after rectal examination or a rectal tube.

In infancy (Aryan's age)

  • Chronic constipation needing rectal stimulation, progressive abdominal distension, vomiting, poor feeding and failure to thrive.
  • Episodes of foul-smelling, explosive diarrhoea with fever and distension – suggest enterocolitis.

In older children

  • Long-standing constipation, ribbon-like foul-smelling stools, a large distended abdomen with visible peristalsis and palpable faecal masses, an empty rectum on rectal examination, malnutrition and anaemia (soiling is unusual, unlike functional constipation).

Diagnosis

  • Plain X-ray abdomen – dilated loops of bowel, absence of gas in the rectum.
  • Contrast (barium) enema (unprepared bowel) – a narrow distal segment, a cone-shaped transition zone and dilated proximal colon; barium retained after 24 hours.
  • Anorectal manometry – absence of the rectoanal inhibitory reflex.
  • Rectal suction biopsy – the definitive test – absence of ganglion cells with increased acetylcholinesterase-positive nerve fibres.

(c) Pre-operative and post-operative nursing management (8 marks)

Medical and surgical management (background)

  • Initial decompression with rectal washouts using warm normal saline, IV fluids and antibiotics if there is enterocolitis.
  • Definitive surgery – a "pull-through" operation (Swenson, Duhamel, Soave or transanal endorectal pull-through) which removes the aganglionic segment and brings normal bowel down to the anus.
  • In sick or malnourished infants, enterocolitis or long-segment disease, a staged approach is used: colostomy in normally innervated bowel first (as for Aryan), pull-through a few months later, then closure of the colostomy.

Pre-operative nursing care

  1. Assessment – vital signs, hydration, weight, abdominal girth daily at the level of the umbilicus (marked with a pen), vomiting, stools, bowel sounds.
  2. Decompression – nil by mouth as ordered; nasogastric tube for free drainage; record aspirate.
  3. Rectal washouts as prescribed – only with warm normal saline, never with tap water (water is absorbed from the large colon and causes water intoxication); small volumes, gentle technique, record return.
  4. IV fluids and electrolytes, blood tests; correct anaemia and malnutrition (parenteral nutrition if needed).
  5. Watch for enterocolitis – fever, increasing distension, explosive foul diarrhoea, lethargy – report at once.
  6. Bowel preparation and antibiotics as ordered; routine pre-operative preparation, consent and identification.
  7. Prepare the parents – explain what a colostomy is, show pictures of a stoma and pouch, reassure that it is usually temporary; allow questions.

Post-operative nursing care

  1. Vital signs, pain and comfort – monitor pulse, respiration, temperature, BP and SpO2; assess pain (FLACC scale) and give analgesics; comfort by parents.
  2. Fluids and nutrition – IV fluids until bowel sounds return; NG tube on free drainage; start breastfeeding when bowel function returns (usually 2–3 days); intake and output including stoma output.
  3. Position – supine or side-lying turned towards the stoma side so that stool drains away from the abdominal wound.
  4. Wound care – keep the incision dry and protected from stool; observe for redness, discharge and gaping.
  5. Stoma assessment – a healthy stoma is moist, pink to beefy red and slightly raised; report a dark red, purple or black stoma (poor blood supply), excessive bleeding, retraction, prolapse or no output after 72 hours.
  6. Colostomy and peristomal skin care
    • Clean the stoma and skin with warm water and soft gauze, pat dry; use a skin barrier (stoma paste, powder, skin wafer).
    • Use a pouch with an opening 2–3 mm larger than the stoma; empty it when one-third full; change it before it leaks.
    • Protect against excoriation; watch for dehydration if the output is very loose.
  7. Watch for complications – stoma prolapse, retraction, stenosis, skin breakdown, intestinal obstruction and enterocolitis, which can occur even after surgery.

Teaching the parents

  • Practise emptying and changing the pouch and caring for the skin under supervision until confident; give written instructions and a list of supplies.
  • Loose clothing; a nappy can be worn over the pouch; daily bathing is allowed.
  • Breastfeeding and later normal weaning foods; adequate fluids.
  • Danger signs – fever, abdominal distension, vomiting, foul explosive stools, change in stoma colour, no output – report at once.
  • Keep appointments for the pull-through and colostomy closure.
  • After the pull-through – perianal skin care for frequent stools, anal dilatation if prescribed, patience with toilet training, and long-term bowel management for constipation or soiling.
  • Provide emotional support and connect them with other parents or ostomy associations.

Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis – an emergency

  • Features – fever, increasing abdominal distension, explosive foul-smelling diarrhoea, vomiting, lethargy and signs of shock; it can occur before or after surgery.
  • Immediate nursing actions – inform the surgeon, keep nil by mouth, insert a nasogastric tube, start IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics as ordered, give rectal washouts with warm normal saline to decompress the colon, and monitor vital signs, abdominal girth and urine output closely.

Difference from functional (habitual) constipation

Feature Hirschsprung's disease Functional constipation
Onset From birth; delayed meconium After infancy, often at toilet training
Soiling Rare Common
Rectum on examination Empty, tight Full of hard stool
Growth Poor, malnourished Normal
Enterocolitis Risk present Absent

Recognising these differences helps the nurse refer the right child early for biopsy.

Nursing importance The nurse often first suspects Hirschsprung's disease in a newborn who has not passed meconium by 48 hours. Careful decompression with saline washouts, early recognition of enterocolitis and confident teaching of colostomy care to parents are central to a good outcome.

Conclusion Hirschsprung's disease is the congenital absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel, causing functional obstruction, delayed passage of meconium, constipation, distension and the risk of enterocolitis. It is diagnosed by contrast enema and confirmed by rectal biopsy, and treated by a pull-through operation, often after a temporary colostomy. Good pre- and post-operative care, stoma care and parent teaching enable children like Aryan to grow normally.

question: Explain cleft lip and cleft palate with their nursing management.

diagram.caption: Types of cleft lip and palate
labels: unilateral complete cleft lip and palate
bilateral complete cleft lip and palate
isolated cleft of soft and hard palate

answer_html:
Definition Cleft lip is a congenital split of the upper lip, and cleft palate is a split in the roof of the mouth, resulting from failure of fusion of the facial processes during embryonic life. They may occur separately or together and are among the commonest birth defects (about 1 in 700 live births).

Embryology and causes

  • Cleft lip – failure of fusion of the maxillary and medial nasal processes (5–8 weeks).
  • Cleft palate – failure of fusion of the palatal shelves (8–12 weeks).
  • Causes – multifactorial: family history, syndromes; maternal smoking and alcohol, folic acid deficiency, anticonvulsants (phenytoin), steroids, retinoids, maternal diabetes and obesity.

Types

  • Cleft lip – unilateral (more often on the left) or bilateral; incomplete (notch) or complete (extending into the nostril), often with a cleft of the alveolus.
  • Cleft palate (Veau classification) – I: soft palate only; II: soft and hard palate; III: complete unilateral cleft of lip, alveolus and palate; IV: complete bilateral cleft.

Problems

  • Feeding difficulty – poor suction, milk escaping through the nose (nasal regurgitation), swallowing air, choking and aspiration, poor weight gain.
  • Recurrent otitis media and hearing loss (Eustachian tube dysfunction in cleft palate).
  • Speech defects – nasal speech; dental and orthodontic problems; facial appearance and psychosocial distress for the family.

Management (team approach) – plastic surgeon, paediatrician, nurse, speech therapist, orthodontist, ENT surgeon and counsellor.

  • Pre-surgical nasoalveolar moulding in wide clefts.
  • Cleft lip repair (cheiloplasty) at about 3 months ("rule of 10s": about 10 weeks of age, 10 lb weight, haemoglobin 10 g/dl).
  • Cleft palate repair (palatoplasty) at 9–12 months, before speech develops.
  • Later – alveolar bone grafting, orthodontics, speech therapy, grommets for ear problems, revision surgery.
  • Free surgery is available through RBSK and organisations such as Smile Train.

Nursing management

Before surgery – feeding

  • Feed in an upright position (60–90 degrees); use special nipples, squeeze bottles or Haberman-type feeders, or a paladai, cup or spoon; with cleft lip alone breastfeeding is often possible as the breast fills the gap.
  • Small, frequent feeds; burp frequently (air swallowing); give a little water after feeds to clean the mouth; weigh regularly.
  • Support the parents – show before-and-after photographs of repaired clefts, encourage bonding and explain the plan of treatment.

After cleft lip repair

  • Protect the suture line – Logan's bow or adhesive strip; elbow restraints (released one at a time regularly) to prevent the baby touching the lip; position on the back or side, never prone.
  • Prevent crying (cuddling, early feeds); clean the suture line gently as ordered; feed with a spoon, dropper or syringe from the side of the mouth initially.

After cleft palate repair

  • Position on the side to allow drainage; observe for bleeding and airway obstruction; keep suction ready.
  • Feed with a cup or spoon – no bottles, straws or hard objects in the mouth; clear fluids, then a soft diet; water after each feed.
  • Elbow restraints; analgesics; continue follow-up for hearing and speech.

Conclusion Cleft lip and palate result from failure of fusion of facial processes in early pregnancy and cause feeding, hearing, speech and emotional problems. Timely surgical repair by a team, special feeding techniques, protection of the suture line and continuous support of the family by the nurse give these children an excellent outcome.

question: Explain congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS) is hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the circular muscle of the pylorus, narrowing the pyloric canal and causing gastric outlet obstruction in early infancy.

  • Incidence about 2–3 per 1,000 live births; boys (especially first-born) are affected 4–5 times more often; onset at 2–8 weeks (peak 3–6 weeks); risk increased by erythromycin given in early infancy and by family history.

Clinical features

  • Non-bilious, projectile vomiting shortly after feeds, increasing in force and frequency; sometimes coffee-ground (gastritis).
  • The baby remains hungry and feeds eagerly after vomiting ("hungry vomiter").
  • Visible gastric peristalsis moving from left to right across the upper abdomen during a feed.
  • Palpable, olive-shaped, firm mass in the right upper abdomen, felt best during a test feed when the baby is relaxed.
  • Dehydration, weight loss, constipation, scanty urine; jaundice in a few.
  • Metabolic disturbance – loss of hydrochloric acid causes hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

Diagnosis – ultrasound (pyloric muscle thickness of 3–4 mm or more and length of 15–16 mm or more); barium meal (string sign) is rarely needed; serum electrolytes and blood gas.

Management

  • It is not an emergency operation – first correct dehydration and alkalosis with IV fluids (normal saline with dextrose and potassium after urine is passed) over 24–48 hours.
  • Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy (open or laparoscopic) – the hypertrophied muscle is split down to the mucosa; the outcome is excellent.

Nursing management

Pre-operative

  • Nil by mouth; nasogastric tube for decompression; IV fluids and electrolytes as ordered.
  • Record vomiting (time, amount, character), intake and output, daily weight, signs of dehydration, urine output and electrolyte results.
  • Mouth care; keep the baby warm and comfortable; position on the side or with the head raised to prevent aspiration.
  • Explain the operation to the parents and relieve their anxiety.

Post-operative

  • Monitor vital signs, wound and pain; continue IV fluids until feeds are established.
  • Feeding – start small amounts of clear fluid or breast milk about 4–6 hours after surgery (as per protocol) and increase gradually to full feeds within 24–48 hours.
  • Hold the baby upright during feeds, burp frequently, and place on the right side or with head raised after feeds.
  • Explain that some vomiting in the first 24–48 hours is common; report persistent vomiting.
  • Teach wound care and feeding before discharge.

Conclusion CHPS is hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle causing projectile non-bilious vomiting in a hungry infant of 2–8 weeks, with an olive-shaped mass and metabolic alkalosis. After correction of fluid and electrolyte imbalance, Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy cures the condition, and careful graduated feeding completes recovery.

question: Explain anorectal malformations and the nursing care of a newborn with imperforate anus.
answer_html:
Definition Anorectal malformations (ARM) are a spectrum of congenital defects in which the anus is absent or abnormally placed and the rectum ends blindly or opens through a fistula into the perineum, urinary tract or vagina. The common term is imperforate anus. Incidence is about 1 in 4,000–5,000 live births.

Classification

  • Low (translevator) lesions – the rectum has passed through the levator muscle; perineal fistula (opening on the perineum), covered anus.
  • High/intermediate lesions – the rectum ends above or within the levator; in boys, rectourethral (bulbar or prostatic) or rectovesical fistula; in girls, rectovestibular fistula (commonest in girls) and cloaca (rectum, vagina and urethra open into one common channel).
  • Associated anomalies (in about half) – VACTERL association: vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheo-oesophageal, renal and limb anomalies; spinal cord tethering.

Clinical features

  • No anal opening seen at the first newborn examination (or an abnormally placed opening).
  • Failure to pass meconium, progressive abdominal distension and vomiting.
  • Meconium in the urine (rectourinary fistula) or passing from the perineum or vagina.

Diagnosis

  • Careful perineal inspection, repeated after 16–24 hours when meconium may appear through a fistula.
  • Cross-table prone lateral X-ray at 18–24 hours (distance of rectal gas from the skin); ultrasound of the perineum.
  • Screening for associated anomalies – echocardiography, renal ultrasound, X-ray of spine and sacrum, spinal ultrasound, passage of a nasogastric tube (oesophageal atresia).

Management

  • Low lesions – anoplasty in the newborn period.
  • High lesions and cloaca – a colostomy in the newborn period, followed at about 3–6 months by posterior sagittal anorectoplasty (PSARP), and closure of the colostomy 6–8 weeks later.
  • Anal dilatation programme with graded dilators after anoplasty or PSARP to prevent stricture.
  • Long-term bowel management (diet, laxatives or daily enemas) for continence.

Nursing care

  • Inspect the perineum of every newborn at birth; never insert a rectal thermometer before confirming anal patency.
  • Nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids; measure abdominal girth; observe the urine and perineum for meconium.
  • Keep the baby warm; prepare for investigations and surgery; support the parents.
  • After colostomy – stoma and peristomal skin care, monitoring of output, teaching parents.
  • After PSARP – position to keep pressure off the perineum (prone or side-lying), keep the wound clean and dry, catheter care in boys with urethral fistula, pain relief.
  • Teach anal dilatation to parents (size, frequency, technique, gentle lubrication) and the long-term bowel care plan; encourage follow-up for continence and urinary problems.

Conclusion Anorectal malformations range from a simple perineal fistula to complex cloacal anomalies and are often associated with VACTERL defects. They are detected by careful examination of every newborn and treated by anoplasty or staged colostomy and PSARP, with skilled stoma care, anal dilatation and long-term bowel management.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: Explain intussusception in children and its management.
answer_html:
Definition Intussusception is the telescoping (invagination) of a proximal segment of the intestine into the adjoining distal segment, causing intestinal obstruction and compromising the blood supply of the involved bowel. The ileocolic type (ileum into colon) is the commonest. It is the commonest cause of intestinal obstruction between 6 months and 2 years (peak 5–9 months); boys are affected more often.

Causes

  • Idiopathic (90%) in infants – enlargement of lymphoid tissue (Peyer's patches) after viral infections (adenovirus, rotavirus) acting as the lead point.
  • Pathological lead points in older children – Meckel's diverticulum, polyp, lymphoma, Henoch–Schönlein purpura, cystic fibrosis.

Pathophysiology The mesentery is dragged in with the bowel → venous congestion and oedema → bleeding from the mucosa (blood and mucus in stool) → arterial obstruction → gangrene, perforation and peritonitis if untreated.

Clinical features

  • Sudden, severe, colicky abdominal pain in a previously healthy infant – he screams, draws up his legs and turns pale, with episodes every 15–20 minutes; between attacks he may be quiet or lethargic.
  • Vomiting – initially of food, later bile-stained.
  • "Red currant jelly" stools (blood and mucus) – a late sign.
  • Sausage-shaped mass in the right upper abdomen with an empty right iliac fossa (Dance's sign).
  • Later – abdominal distension, fever, dehydration, shock.
  • The classical triad of pain, mass and red currant jelly stools is seen in less than a quarter of cases, so a high index of suspicion is needed.

Diagnosis – ultrasound shows the "target" or "doughnut" sign (pseudo-kidney on longitudinal view); X-ray abdomen for obstruction or perforation.

Management

  • Resuscitation – IV fluids, nasogastric decompression, antibiotics, analgesia.
  • Non-operative reduction (if no peritonitis or perforation) – hydrostatic reduction with saline under ultrasound guidance or pneumatic (air enema) reduction under fluoroscopy; successful in most children.
  • Surgery – if reduction fails or there is perforation or peritonitis: manual reduction, or resection of gangrenous bowel with anastomosis.

Nursing care

  • Monitor vital signs, signs of shock, abdominal distension and pain; record stools and vomiting.
  • Nil by mouth, nasogastric tube, IV fluids and intake–output chart; analgesics and comfort.
  • Prepare the child and parents for reduction or surgery.
  • After reduction – watch for passage of normal brown stool and barium or contrast (sign of successful reduction) and report; observe for recurrence (about 10%, mostly in the first 24–72 hours) – return of pain, vomiting or bloody stool; start feeds gradually.
  • After surgery – routine post-operative care, wound care, return of bowel sounds before feeding.
  • Teach parents to return immediately if colicky pain recurs.

Conclusion Intussusception is telescoping of bowel, mostly ileocolic, in infants of 6 months to 2 years, presenting with paroxysmal colicky pain, vomiting, a sausage-shaped mass and red currant jelly stools. Early ultrasound diagnosis and hydrostatic or pneumatic reduction usually avoid surgery, while careful nursing observation detects complications and recurrence.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: Explain intestinal worm infestation in children, its management and prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction Intestinal helminthiasis (worm infestation) is one of the commonest infections of children in India. Soil-transmitted helminths (STH) – roundworm, hookworm and whipworm – affect large numbers of children and contribute to anaemia, undernutrition and poor school performance.

Common worms and transmission

  • Roundworm (Ascaris lumbricoides) – swallowing eggs from soil-contaminated hands, food or water.
  • Hookworm (Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus) – larvae in soil penetrate the skin of bare feet; the worms suck blood in the small intestine.
  • Whipworm (Trichuris trichiura) – faeco-oral.
  • Threadworm / pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis) – eggs laid around the anus at night are carried by fingers to the mouth (autoinfection); spreads within families.
  • Tapeworm (Taenia solium, T. saginata) – undercooked pork or beef; eggs of T. solium can cause neurocysticercosis (seizures).

Effects on the child

  • Iron-deficiency anaemia (hookworm), malnutrition, growth retardation, poor concentration and school absenteeism.
  • Abdominal pain, loss of appetite, nausea, diarrhoea; intestinal obstruction by a bolus of roundworms; biliary obstruction.
  • Perianal itching at night and disturbed sleep (threadworm); rectal prolapse (heavy whipworm infection); cough and wheeze during larval migration through lungs.

Diagnosis – stool examination for ova; cellophane (adhesive) tape test of the perianal skin early in the morning for threadworm eggs; blood count (anaemia, eosinophilia).

Management

  • Albendazole 400 mg single dose (200 mg for children of 1–2 years) or mebendazole (100 mg twice daily for 3 days or 500 mg single dose).
  • Threadworm – treat the whole family and repeat the dose after 2 weeks; cut nails short, wash hands, change underclothes and bedlinen daily.
  • Iron and folic acid and nutritional rehabilitation for anaemia and undernutrition.
  • Surgery for complications such as obstruction.

Prevention

  • Hand washing with soap before eating and after defecation; keep nails short and clean.
  • Wearing footwear to prevent hookworm.
  • Use of sanitary latrines and safe disposal of faeces; safe drinking water; washing fruits and vegetables; cooking meat well.
  • National Deworming Day (NDD) – held twice a year (10 February and 10 August), with mop-up days; albendazole is given to all children and adolescents of 1–19 years in schools and anganwadis (half tablet for 1–2 years, crushed for young children).

Role of the nurse

  • Health education on hygiene, footwear and sanitation in families, schools and anganwadis.
  • Organising and giving deworming tablets on NDD under supervision (chewed, not swallowed whole, after a meal); recording; managing mild side effects (nausea, abdominal pain).
  • Screening for anaemia and malnutrition; referral of complicated cases.

Conclusion Worm infestation is common among Indian children and causes anaemia, malnutrition and poor school performance. It is easily treated with albendazole or mebendazole and prevented by hand washing, footwear, sanitation and biannual mass deworming on National Deworming Day, with nurses playing a key educational and organisational role.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: Explain the causes of vomiting in infants and the management of gastro-oesophageal reflux.
answer_html:
Introduction Vomiting is the forceful expulsion of gastric contents through the mouth, while regurgitation (possetting) is the effortless return of small amounts of milk, common in healthy infants. Vomiting is a symptom of many disorders, both inside and outside the gut.

Causes of vomiting in infants

  • Newborn – swallowed amniotic fluid or blood, feeding errors (overfeeding, poor burping), oesophageal or duodenal atresia, malrotation with volvulus, Hirschsprung's disease, necrotising enterocolitis, sepsis and meningitis, raised intracranial pressure, metabolic disorders (galactosaemia, congenital adrenal hyperplasia).
  • Infancy – gastro-oesophageal reflux, pyloric stenosis (2–8 weeks), intussusception, gastroenteritis, infections outside the gut (UTI, otitis media, pneumonia), whooping cough (post-tussive), cow's milk protein allergy.
  • Older children – gastroenteritis, appendicitis, diabetic ketoacidosis, poisoning, migraine, raised intracranial pressure, motion sickness and psychogenic vomiting.

Red flags – bile-stained (green) vomiting (surgical emergency – malrotation or obstruction), projectile vomiting, blood in vomitus, abdominal distension, dehydration, bulging fontanelle, lethargy, fever, poor weight gain.

Gastro-oesophageal reflux (GER) in infants

  • Definition – passage of stomach contents into the oesophagus because of an immature lower oesophageal sphincter, short oesophagus and liquid diet.
  • Physiological GER affects about half of infants at 2–4 months; they gain weight well ("happy spitters") and it resolves by 12–18 months.
  • GER disease (GERD) – reflux with complications: poor weight gain, irritability, feeding refusal, back-arching (Sandifer posture), oesophagitis, aspiration pneumonia, wheeze or apnoea.

Management of GER

  • Reassurance and parent education in uncomplicated reflux.
  • Feeding measures – avoid overfeeding; small, frequent feeds; burp during and after feeds; hold the baby upright for 20–30 minutes after feeds; avoid tight nappies and pressure on the abdomen.
  • Thickened feeds or anti-regurgitation formula for formula-fed infants, as advised.
  • A trial of cow's milk protein exclusion (extensively hydrolysed formula, or removal of dairy from the breastfeeding mother's diet) if allergy is suspected.
  • Avoid exposure to tobacco smoke.
  • Safe sleep – always on the back (supine); prone or raised sleeping positions are not recommended.
  • Drugs – proton pump inhibitors or H2 blockers only for confirmed GERD, as prescribed.
  • Surgery (fundoplication) rarely, for severe complications.

Nursing care of a vomiting child

  • Position the child on the side or upright to prevent aspiration; keep suction ready.
  • Record the time, amount, colour, force and relation to feeds; report bile, blood or projectile vomiting.
  • Assess hydration and weight; give small frequent sips of ORS; IV fluids if ordered.
  • Mouth care after vomiting; clean clothes and linen; comfort the child.
  • Nasogastric decompression in intestinal obstruction as ordered.

Conclusion Vomiting in infants may be due to simple feeding errors and reflux or to serious surgical and medical conditions; bilious vomiting is always an emergency. Physiological reflux needs only reassurance and feeding measures, while GERD may need dietary changes and drugs, with careful nursing observation, positioning and hydration.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: Differentiate between omphalocele and gastroschisis.
answer_html:
Both are congenital abdominal wall defects in which bowel lies outside the abdomen.

Feature Omphalocele (exomphalos) Gastroschisis
Site At the umbilicus; cord inserted on the sac To the right of the umbilicus; cord normal
Covering Covered by a sac (peritoneum and amnion) No sac – bowel exposed, often thick and matted
Contents Bowel, often liver Usually only bowel
Associated anomalies Common – chromosomal (trisomies), cardiac, Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome Uncommon (intestinal atresia)
Maternal age Older mothers Young mothers

Immediate care – cover the bowel with sterile cling film or warm saline-soaked gauze, keep the baby warm, position on the side to prevent kinking of vessels, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids and early surgical repair (primary or staged closure with a silo).

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: What is biliary atresia?
answer_html:
Biliary atresia is a progressive inflammatory obliteration of the extrahepatic bile ducts in early infancy, blocking the flow of bile from the liver to the intestine. It is the commonest surgical cause of neonatal cholestasis.

  • Features – jaundice persisting beyond 2 weeks of age, pale (clay-coloured) stools, dark urine that stains the nappy, an enlarged firm liver; later splenomegaly, poor growth, bleeding (vitamin K deficiency).
  • Diagnosis – raised conjugated bilirubin, ultrasound, hepatobiliary scan, liver biopsy and intraoperative cholangiogram.
  • Treatment – Kasai portoenterostomy, best before 60 days of age; liver transplantation if it fails.
  • Nursing role – every infant with prolonged jaundice and pale stools must be referred early; stool colour cards help mothers recognise pale stools.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: What is coeliac disease in children?
answer_html:
Coeliac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy) is an immune-mediated damage of the small intestinal mucosa triggered by gluten (a protein in wheat, barley and rye) in genetically susceptible children, leading to malabsorption. It is common in North India, where wheat is the staple.

  • Features – begin after introduction of wheat: chronic diarrhoea with bulky, foul-smelling stools, abdominal distension, failure to thrive, wasting of buttocks, irritability, anaemia not responding to iron, short stature, delayed puberty.
  • Diagnosis – anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG) IgA antibodies; duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy.
  • Treatment – lifelong strict gluten-free diet (rice, maize, jowar, bajra, pulses, potatoes are allowed); correction of nutritional deficiencies; dietary counselling of the family.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: What is umbilical hernia in infants? How is it managed?
answer_html:
Umbilical hernia is a protrusion of abdominal contents (bowel or omentum) through an incompletely closed umbilical ring, seen as a soft swelling at the umbilicus that increases on crying or straining and is easily reducible.

  • It is common in preterm and low birth weight babies and in children with hypothyroidism or Down syndrome.
  • Management – most close spontaneously by 3–4 years of age; reassure the parents.
  • Strapping, coins or binders are not advised (they do not help and may irritate the skin).
  • Surgery if the defect is large (more than 1.5–2 cm), persists beyond 4–5 years, or rarely becomes incarcerated or strangulated (painful, tense, irreducible swelling with vomiting – an emergency).

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: Master Ayaan, aged 4 years, is admitted with puffiness of the face in the mornings, swelling of the legs and abdomen and frothy urine. His urine shows 4+ protein, serum albumin is 1.8 g/dl and serum cholesterol is raised. He is diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome. (a) Define nephrotic syndrome and explain its causes and pathophysiology. (4 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features, investigations and complications. (4 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of Ayaan, including the education of his parents. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Pathophysiology of nephrotic syndrome
labels: increased glomerular permeability – massive proteinuria – hypoalbuminaemia – fall in plasma oncotic pressure – fluid shift to tissues (oedema) and reduced blood volume – renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and ADH activation – salt and water retention – more oedema; hypoalbuminaemia – increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis – hyperlipidaemia; loss of antithrombin and immunoglobulins – thrombosis and infection

answer_html:
(a) Definition, causes and pathophysiology (4 marks)

Definition Nephrotic syndrome is a clinical syndrome characterised by:

  1. Heavy (nephrotic-range) proteinuria – urine dipstick 3+ or 4+, or spot urine protein–creatinine ratio above 2 mg/mg (more than 40 mg/m²/hour);
  2. Hypoalbuminaemia – serum albumin below 2.5–3 g/dl;
  3. Oedema; and usually
  4. Hyperlipidaemia (serum cholesterol above 200 mg/dl). - It is the commonest chronic kidney disease of childhood, mostly between 2 and 6 years, with boys affected more often in young children.

Causes

  1. Primary (idiopathic) – about 90%
    • Minimal change disease (MCD) – about 80% of young children; normal glomeruli on light microscopy, fusion of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy; usually steroid-sensitive with a good prognosis.
    • Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, membranous nephropathy – more often steroid-resistant.
  2. Secondary – post-infectious glomerulonephritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, Henoch–Schönlein purpura, hepatitis B and C, HIV, malaria, drugs (NSAIDs, penicillamine), malignancy.
  3. Congenital nephrotic syndrome – onset in the first 3 months (for example, Finnish type).

Pathophysiology

  1. Increased permeability of the glomerular filtration barrier – loss of the negative charge of the basement membrane and damage to the podocytes (foot process effacement) → massive loss of protein, mainly albumin, in the urine.
  2. Hypoalbuminaemia → fall in plasma oncotic pressure → fluid moves into the interstitial spaces → oedema.
  3. Reduced intravascular volume activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and ADH → sodium and water retention → more oedema.
  4. Low albumin stimulates the liver to produce more lipoproteins → hyperlipidaemia and lipiduria.
  5. Urinary loss of antithrombin III and increased clotting factors → hypercoagulability (thrombosis).
  6. Loss of immunoglobulins and complement factors plus steroid therapy → susceptibility to infection.
  7. Loss of binding proteins → low thyroxine and vitamin D levels.

(b) Clinical features, investigations and complications (4 marks)

Clinical features

  • Periorbital puffiness, most marked in the morning, often mistaken for an allergy.
  • Generalised pitting oedema – legs, feet, genitalia (scrotal or labial swelling), ascites, pleural effusion (breathlessness); severe cases develop anasarca.
  • Weight gain, frothy urine, reduced urine output.
  • Pallor, fatigue, irritability, loss of appetite, abdominal discomfort, diarrhoea (oedema of the bowel wall).
  • Blood pressure is usually normal and there is no gross haematuria in minimal change disease.

Investigations

  • Urine – dipstick 3+/4+ protein; spot protein–creatinine ratio or 24-hour urine protein; microscopy (no red cell casts in MCD).
  • Blood – serum albumin (low), total protein (low), serum cholesterol (high), urea and creatinine (usually normal), electrolytes, complete blood count.
  • Serum complement C3 – normal in MCD; low in post-infectious GN, lupus and MPGN.
  • Hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV tests and ANA when indicated; Mantoux test or chest X-ray to exclude tuberculosis before starting steroids.
  • Renal biopsy only in atypical cases – onset below 1 year or above 12 years, persistent haematuria, hypertension, low C3, impaired renal function or steroid resistance.

Complications

  • Infections – spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (pneumococcal), cellulitis, pneumonia, UTI, septicaemia – the major cause of death.
  • Thrombosis – renal vein, cerebral venous sinus, deep veins, pulmonary embolism.
  • Hypovolaemia and shock (especially with diuretics, vomiting or diarrhoea) → acute kidney injury.
  • Electrolyte imbalance, malnutrition, steroid side effects (Cushingoid features, hypertension, growth retardation, cataract, behaviour change), frequent relapses.

(c) Management and nursing care of Ayaan (7 marks)

Medical management (Indian Society of Pediatric Nephrology guidelines)

  1. Initial episode – oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day (maximum 60 mg) as a single morning dose for 6 weeks, followed by 1.5 mg/kg (maximum 40 mg) on alternate days for 6 weeks, then stopped.
    • Most children with MCD go into remission within 2–4 weeks – urine protein nil or trace for 3 consecutive early-morning samples.
  2. Relapse (3+/4+ proteinuria for 3 consecutive days after remission) – prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day until remission, then 1.5 mg/kg on alternate days for 4 weeks.
  3. Frequent relapses (2 or more in the first 6 months after the initial episode, or 3 or more in any 12 months) and steroid dependence – steroid-sparing drugs such as levamisole, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide, tacrolimus or rituximab.
  4. Steroid resistance (no remission after 4 weeks of daily prednisolone) – renal biopsy and calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine), ACE inhibitors and specialist care.
  5. Oedema – no-added-salt diet; furosemide for significant oedema; IV 20% albumin followed by furosemide for severe, refractory oedema; diuretics are avoided if the child is hypovolaemic.
  6. Prevention and treatment of infection – prompt antibiotics; pneumococcal, influenza and varicella vaccines (live vaccines are postponed while on high-dose steroids).
  7. Supplements – calcium and vitamin D during prolonged steroid therapy.

Nursing care of Ayaan

1. Excess fluid volume related to hypoalbuminaemia and sodium retention

  • Weigh daily at the same time, on the same scale, in similar clothing; measure abdominal girth daily at the umbilicus.
  • Maintain a strict intake and output chart; record urine output and urine dipstick daily.
  • Monitor pulse, respiration, BP and breathing; elevate oedematous limbs; provide scrotal support if the scrotum is swollen; semi-Fowler's position for ascites or pleural effusion.
  • Restrict fluids only if ordered (severe oedema or hyponatraemia).

2. Risk of infection related to loss of immunoglobulins and steroid therapy

  • Strict hand hygiene; keep away from children with infections; avoid unnecessary invasive procedures.
  • Monitor temperature; report abdominal pain, fever and tenderness (peritonitis), cough or redness of the skin immediately.
  • Avoid live vaccines during high-dose steroids; inform the doctor of chickenpox or measles exposure.

3. Risk of impaired skin integrity due to oedema

  • Turn and reposition every 2 hours; keep skin folds, groin and genitalia clean and dry; soft cotton clothing; avoid injections and BP cuffs on oedematous areas; prevent pressure injuries.

4. Imbalanced nutrition and appetite changes

  • Normal protein intake for age (protein is neither restricted nor greatly increased); no-added-salt diet during oedema – avoid pickles, papad, chips, salted snacks and processed foods.
  • Small, attractive, frequent meals when ascites reduces appetite; on steroids appetite increases – guide healthy choices to prevent excessive weight gain.

5. Risk of hypovolaemia and thrombosis

  • Watch for abdominal pain, cold extremities, fast pulse, low BP and reduced urine output, especially during diuretic therapy or diarrhoea.
  • Encourage mobility – strict bed rest is not required and increases the risk of thrombosis; adequate fluids; avoid femoral venous lines.

6. Monitoring steroid therapy

  • Give prednisolone after breakfast in a single morning dose; monitor BP, weight, blood or urine sugar, mood and behaviour; observe for Cushingoid changes and explain them to the child and parents.

7. Psychosocial care

  • Explain the illness and its usually good prognosis; reassure about the puffy face and weight gain from steroids; encourage play and schooling.

Education of the parents

  • Give steroids exactly as prescribed; keep a calendar for daily and alternate-day doses; never stop steroids suddenly.
  • Home urine testing – test the first morning urine with a dipstick (or heat and acetic acid test) daily during treatment and then regularly or during colds and fevers; keep a diary; a reading of 3+/4+ for 3 days means relapse – report.
  • Recognise relapse (puffiness, frothy urine, weight gain, reduced urine) and infection (fever, abdominal pain, cough) and seek care early.
  • Follow the no-added-salt diet during oedema and a normal balanced diet in remission.
  • Keep vaccinations up to date as advised; attend regular follow-up; allow normal activities and school during remission.

Nursing importance Nephrotic syndrome in children is usually steroid-sensitive but relapsing. Accurate daily weight, abdominal girth and urine monitoring, early detection of infection and hypovolaemia, and training parents to test urine and give steroids correctly are the nurse's main contributions to preventing complications.

Conclusion Nephrotic syndrome is characterised by heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia, most often due to minimal change disease in young children like Ayaan. It responds well to prednisolone (6 weeks daily and 6 weeks on alternate days) but tends to relapse. Complications such as infection, thrombosis and hypovolaemia are prevented by careful nursing, a no-added-salt diet, infection control and thorough education of the parents.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: Explain acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis in children and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is an immune-complex inflammation of the glomeruli following infection with nephritogenic strains of group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus. It is the commonest cause of acute nephritic syndrome in children of 5–12 years.

Aetiology and pathogenesis

  • It follows pharyngitis by 1–2 weeks or skin infection (impetigo, pyoderma, infected scabies) by 3–6 weeks.
  • Antigen–antibody complexes are deposited in the glomeruli → complement activation and inflammation → reduced glomerular filtration → retention of salt and water, and leakage of red cells and some protein into the urine.

Clinical features

  • Haematuria – smoky, tea- or cola-coloured urine.
  • Periorbital puffiness and mild oedema of the feet.
  • Oliguria.
  • Hypertension – may cause hypertensive encephalopathy (headache, vomiting, blurred vision, convulsions).
  • Circulatory overload – breathlessness, cough, pulmonary oedema, heart failure.
  • Fever, malaise, loin pain; history of a recent sore throat or skin sores.

Investigations

  • Urine – red blood cells and red cell casts, mild to moderate proteinuria.
  • Raised blood urea and creatinine; electrolytes (hyperkalaemia).
  • Low serum C3 (returns to normal within 6–8 weeks).
  • Evidence of streptococcal infection – raised ASO (after throat infection) or anti-DNase B (after skin infection), throat or skin swab.
  • Chest X-ray for congestion.

Management

  • Bed rest during the acute phase (oedema, hypertension, gross haematuria).
  • Fluid restriction – insensible loss (about 400 ml/m²/day) plus the previous day's urine output.
  • Salt restriction; restrict potassium and protein if there is oliguria and rising urea.
  • Diuretic – furosemide for oedema and hypertension.
  • Antihypertensives – amlodipine or nifedipine; emergency treatment of hypertensive encephalopathy.
  • Penicillin for 10 days to eradicate streptococci (prevents spread to contacts).
  • Dialysis for severe kidney failure, hyperkalaemia or fluid overload.
  • Prognosis – excellent; more than 95% of children recover completely; microscopic haematuria may persist for months.

Nursing management

  • Monitor BP 4-hourly (more often if high); watch for headache, vomiting, visual disturbance and seizures; keep seizure precautions.
  • Daily weight, strict intake and output, urine colour and dipstick daily.
  • Fluid restriction – explain to the child and parents, use small cups, spread fluids over the day, give mouth care.
  • Diet – salt-free or low-salt diet with adequate calories; restrict potassium-rich foods (banana, coconut water, citrus fruits) if potassium is high.
  • Observe for breathlessness and crackles (pulmonary oedema); position upright.
  • Give medicines as prescribed; skin care for oedematous areas; diversional play during bed rest.
  • Health education – early treatment of sore throat and skin infections, personal hygiene, completion of penicillin, follow-up urine tests and BP checks.

Conclusion PSGN follows streptococcal throat or skin infection and presents with cola-coloured urine, periorbital oedema, oliguria and hypertension, with low C3 and red cell casts. With fluid and salt restriction, diuretics, antihypertensives and careful nursing monitoring of BP, weight and output, nearly all children recover fully.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: Explain Wilms' tumour and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Wilms' tumour (nephroblastoma) is a malignant embryonal tumour of the kidney arising from primitive renal tissue (metanephric blastema). It is the commonest renal tumour of childhood, usually seen at 2–5 years of age.

Risk factors – usually sporadic; associated with WAGR syndrome (Wilms' tumour, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, intellectual disability), Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome, hemihypertrophy and Denys–Drash syndrome.

Clinical features

  • A painless, firm, smooth mass in one flank, often noticed by the mother while bathing or dressing the child; it usually does not cross the midline.
  • Abdominal pain or distension, haematuria, hypertension (renin secretion), fever, anaemia, weight loss.
  • Metastasis mainly to the lungs (cough, breathlessness) and liver.

Investigations

  • Ultrasound abdomen; CT or MRI of abdomen (extent, opposite kidney, renal vein and IVC involvement); CT chest for lung metastases.
  • Complete blood count, renal and liver function, urinalysis; urinary catecholamines (to exclude neuroblastoma).

Staging – stage I (confined to kidney, completely removed) to stage IV (distant metastases); stage V – bilateral tumours.

Management

  • Surgery – radical nephrectomy through a transperitoneal approach, avoiding rupture of the tumour.
  • Chemotherapy – vincristine and actinomycin D, with doxorubicin in higher stages; given before surgery (to shrink the tumour) or after, according to the protocol.
  • Radiotherapy for higher stages.
  • Prognosis – excellent; survival is about 90% for early-stage disease.

Nursing management

Pre-operative

  • "Do not palpate the abdomen" – put a notice on the bed; handle, bathe and dress the child gently, because pressure can rupture the capsule and spread tumour cells.
  • Monitor BP; prepare the child with simple explanation and therapeutic play; support the shocked parents.

Post-operative

  • Monitor vital signs, BP and urine output (the child now has one kidney); intake and output.
  • Nasogastric tube and bowel sounds – watch for abdominal distension and paralytic ileus after transperitoneal surgery.
  • Pain relief, chest physiotherapy and early mobilisation; wound care.
  • Chemotherapy care – neutropenic precautions, mouth care, antiemetics; vincristine is given IV only (watch for constipation and nerve weakness); actinomycin D is a vesicant.

Long-term care and teaching

  • Protect the remaining kidney – avoid nephrotoxic drugs, treat urinary infections promptly, maintain good hydration; regular BP and kidney function checks.
  • Attend follow-up with chest imaging and abdominal ultrasound; recognise signs of infection during chemotherapy; support return to school and normal life.

Conclusion Wilms' tumour is the commonest kidney cancer of young children, presenting as a painless flank mass, sometimes with haematuria and hypertension. With nephrectomy, chemotherapy and, if needed, radiotherapy, most children are cured. Gentle handling (no abdominal palpation), careful post-nephrectomy care and protection of the remaining kidney are key nursing responsibilities.

question: Explain hypospadias and the nursing care of a child after hypospadias repair.
answer_html:
Definition Hypospadias is a congenital anomaly in which the urethral opening (meatus) lies on the ventral (under) surface of the penis, anywhere from the glans to the perineum, due to incomplete fusion of the urethral folds. It occurs in about 1 in 200–300 male births.

Types (by position of the meatus)

  • Anterior (distal) – glanular and coronal (the commonest).
  • Middle – penile shaft.
  • Posterior (proximal) – penoscrotal, scrotal and perineal (severe).

Associated features

  • Chordee – downward (ventral) curvature of the penis, especially on erection.
  • Hooded foreskin – excess foreskin on the dorsal side with a deficient ventral foreskin.
  • Undescended testes and inguinal hernia; in severe hypospadias with undescended testes, a disorder of sex development must be excluded (karyotype).

Problems – downward or spraying urinary stream (the boy may have to sit to pass urine), difficulty with sexual function and fertility later, and psychological distress.

Management

  • Circumcision must not be done – the foreskin is needed for the repair.
  • Surgical repair at 6–18 months of age (ideally before 1 year) – straightening of the penis (orthoplasty), creation of a new urethra (urethroplasty, for example the tubularised incised plate repair), meatoplasty and glanuloplasty; severe cases need staged repair.
  • Epispadias – the meatus is on the dorsal (upper) surface, usually as part of the exstrophy–epispadias complex, often with urinary incontinence; it also needs surgical reconstruction.

Nursing care after hypospadias repair

  1. Urinary drainage – a fine urethral stent or catheter for 5–10 days, usually draining into a double nappy (inner nappy for stool, outer nappy for urine); keep it patent, unkinked and secured; never pull it.
  2. Dressing – keep the compressive dressing clean and dry; check the glans tip for colour (pink, not blue or black) and swelling; report bleeding.
  3. Prevent interference – supervise the child, keep hands away from the dressing (distraction, loose clothing, restraints only if necessary).
  4. Pain and bladder spasms – analgesics as ordered; oxybutynin for bladder spasms; comfort measures.
  5. Fluids and bowel – encourage plenty of fluids to keep urine flowing; prevent constipation and straining.
  6. Infection prevention – antibiotics as prescribed; hand hygiene and perineal care.
  7. After stent removal – observe the urinary stream; report a thin stream or straining (meatal stenosis or stricture) or urine leaking from another opening (urethrocutaneous fistula).
  8. Parent teaching – care of the stent and nappy at home, warm baths after the dressing is removed, avoid straddle toys (rocking horse, bicycle) for a few weeks, follow-up visits, and reassurance about the cosmetic and functional result.

Conclusion Hypospadias is a ventral opening of the urethra, often with chordee and hooded foreskin. The foreskin must be preserved for surgical repair, done ideally in infancy. Careful post-operative care of the stent, dressing, pain and bladder spasms, observation for fistula and stenosis, and teaching of parents ensure a good outcome.

question: Explain acute kidney injury in children and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a sudden decrease in kidney function with retention of urea and creatinine and disturbance of fluid, electrolyte and acid–base balance. It is defined by a rise in serum creatinine of 0.3 mg/dl or more within 48 hours, or 1.5 times the baseline within 7 days, or a urine output below 0.5 ml/kg/hour for 6 hours.

Causes in children

  1. Pre-renal (reduced kidney blood flow) – commonest – dehydration due to gastroenteritis, shock, septicaemia, haemorrhage, burns, hypovolaemia in nephrotic syndrome.
  2. Renal (intrinsic) – acute glomerulonephritis, haemolytic uraemic syndrome (after bloody diarrhoea), acute tubular necrosis (prolonged ischaemia, nephrotoxic drugs such as aminoglycosides and NSAIDs, contrast), snake bite, malaria, leptospirosis.
  3. Post-renal (obstruction) – posterior urethral valves, stones, blocked catheter.

Clinical features

  • Oliguria or anuria (sometimes non-oliguric).
  • Oedema, fluid overload – breathlessness, pulmonary oedema, heart failure, hypertension.
  • Hyperkalaemia – muscle weakness, arrhythmias, cardiac arrest.
  • Metabolic acidosis – deep, rapid breathing.
  • Uraemia – nausea, vomiting, lethargy, itching, bleeding, seizures, coma.
  • Hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia.

Investigations – blood urea, creatinine, electrolytes, blood gas, calcium and phosphate; complete blood count and smear (HUS); urinalysis; ultrasound of kidneys and bladder.

Management

  • Treat the cause – restore circulating volume in pre-renal AKI (fluid bolus of normal saline 10–20 ml/kg as ordered); relieve obstruction (catheter); stop nephrotoxic drugs.
  • Fluid management – once volume is restored, restrict fluids to insensible losses (about 400 ml/m²/day) plus urine output and other losses.
  • Hyperkalaemia – stop potassium intake; IV calcium gluconate (protects the heart), salbutamol nebulisation, insulin with glucose, sodium bicarbonate and potassium-binding resins, as ordered.
  • Acidosis – sodium bicarbonate; hypertension – antihypertensives and diuretics.
  • Nutrition – adequate calories, moderate protein, restricted potassium, phosphate and salt.
  • Adjust drug doses for kidney function.
  • Dialysis (peritoneal dialysis is commonly used in small children; haemodialysis or CRRT) for refractory acidosis, hyperkalaemia, fluid overload, uraemic symptoms or poisoning.

Nursing management

  • Strict intake and output with hourly urine output (urinary catheter); daily or twice-daily weight.
  • Monitor vital signs and BP; cardiac monitoring for hyperkalaemia; watch for breathlessness and oedema.
  • Give measured fluids spread over 24 hours; mouth care for thirst.
  • Follow electrolyte and creatinine results; give medicines safely (no potassium-containing fluids without orders).
  • Diet as prescribed; avoid banana, coconut water and fruit juices if potassium is high.
  • Infection prevention – aseptic catheter and line care; skin care.
  • Peritoneal dialysis care – warm the dialysate, strict asepsis, accurate recording of inflow, dwell and outflow volumes; observe the effluent – cloudy fluid suggests peritonitis; watch for leak, abdominal pain and breathlessness.
  • Neurological observation and seizure precautions; support and explain to parents.

Conclusion AKI in children is most often pre-renal from dehydration, but may result from glomerulonephritis, HUS, nephrotoxins or obstruction. Early correction of the cause, careful fluid restriction, management of hyperkalaemia and acidosis, timely dialysis and meticulous nursing monitoring of output, weight and electrolytes help most children recover.

question: What is exstrophy of the urinary bladder?
answer_html:
Exstrophy of the bladder (ectopia vesicae) is a rare congenital defect in which the anterior abdominal wall and the front wall of the bladder fail to close, so that the bladder mucosa lies open and exposed on the lower abdomen, with urine dribbling continuously from the ureteric openings.

  • It is part of the exstrophy–epispadias complex – associated with epispadias, separation of the pubic bones (pubic diastasis), a low umbilicus and inguinal hernias.
  • Immediate care – cover the exposed bladder with sterile cling film (not gauze, which sticks), irrigate with saline, keep the baby warm, prevent infection, and protect the surrounding skin from urine.
  • Treatment – staged surgical reconstruction (closure of bladder and abdominal wall, repair of epispadias, and later procedures for continence).

subject: Child Health Nursing II

question: What are posterior urethral valves?
answer_html:
Posterior urethral valves (PUV) are abnormal folds of mucosa in the posterior (prostatic) urethra of boys that obstruct the outflow of urine. They are the commonest cause of lower urinary tract obstruction (obstructive uropathy) in male infants.

  • Effects – back-pressure causes a thick-walled bladder, bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, kidney damage and urinary infections.
  • Features – often detected on antenatal ultrasound; after birth – poor, dribbling urinary stream, straining, a palpable distended bladder, urinary tract infection, poor weight gain, and in severe cases respiratory distress (lung hypoplasia) and kidney failure.
  • Diagnosis – ultrasound and micturating cystourethrogram (MCU).
  • Treatment – immediate bladder drainage with a catheter, then endoscopic valve ablation; long-term follow-up for kidney function.

question: Baby Meera, aged 5 months, is admitted with a rapidly enlarging head, a bulging anterior fontanelle, "sunset" eyes, irritability and vomiting. She is diagnosed with hydrocephalus and a ventriculoperitoneal shunt is planned. (a) Define hydrocephalus and explain its causes and types. (4 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features and diagnosis. (4 marks) (c) Describe the pre-operative and post-operative nursing care of Meera, including teaching the parents about the shunt. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt
labels: ventricular catheter in the dilated lateral ventricle
one-way valve and reservoir behind the ear
distal tubing tunnelled under the skin of neck and chest
coiled end in the peritoneal cavity (extra length for growth)

answer_html:
(a) Definition, causes and types (4 marks)

Definition Hydrocephalus is an abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) within the ventricles of the brain, due to an imbalance between its production and absorption, causing dilatation of the ventricles and raised intracranial pressure (ICP). In infants, whose sutures are not fused, it causes rapid enlargement of the head.

Normal CSF circulation (basis of the types) CSF is formed by the choroid plexus in the lateral ventricles → foramen of Monro → third ventricle → aqueduct of Sylvius → fourth ventricle → foramina of Luschka and Magendie → subarachnoid space → absorbed by the arachnoid villi into the venous sinuses. Obstruction anywhere along this path, or failure of absorption, causes hydrocephalus.

Types

  1. Non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus – CSF flow is blocked within the ventricular system.
    • Aqueductal stenosis (the commonest congenital cause).
    • Arnold–Chiari type II malformation (with myelomeningocele) and Dandy–Walker malformation.
    • Tumours (especially posterior fossa), cysts, vein of Galen malformation.
  2. Communicating hydrocephalus – CSF flows out of the ventricles but is not absorbed in the subarachnoid space.
    • After meningitis (especially tubercular meningitis in India), intraventricular haemorrhage of prematurity, subarachnoid haemorrhage.
  3. Overproduction of CSF – choroid plexus papilloma (rare). - It may also be classified as congenital (present at birth – malformations, intrauterine infections such as toxoplasmosis and CMV) or acquired (infection, haemorrhage, tumour, injury).

(b) Clinical features and diagnosis (4 marks)

In infants (like Meera)

  • Rapid increase in head circumference, crossing centile lines on the growth chart.
  • Bulging, tense anterior fontanelle; widely separated sutures.
  • Thin, shiny scalp with dilated scalp veins; frontal bossing; the face looks small compared with the head.
  • "Setting sun" sign – eyes deviated downwards with sclera visible above the iris.
  • Irritability, high-pitched cry, poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy.
  • Macewen's ("cracked-pot") sign on percussion of the skull; transillumination of the skull in severe cases.
  • Delayed head control and milestones; spasticity of the lower limbs.
  • Late signs – seizures, apnoea, Cushing's triad (bradycardia, hypertension, irregular breathing).

In older children (sutures closed) – morning headache, vomiting, papilloedema, double vision (sixth nerve palsy), ataxia, behaviour change and falling school performance.

Diagnosis

  • Serial measurement of head circumference (occipito-frontal) plotted on a growth chart.
  • Cranial ultrasound through the open anterior fontanelle – ventricular size (bedside and safe).
  • CT scan or MRI – type and cause of hydrocephalus.
  • Fundoscopy for papilloedema; antenatal ultrasound may detect it before birth.

(c) Pre-operative and post-operative nursing care (7 marks)

Treatment (background)

  • Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt – the commonest operation: a catheter drains CSF from the lateral ventricle through a one-way pressure valve under the scalp, and a tube tunnelled under the skin into the peritoneal cavity, where it is absorbed; extra tubing is left to allow for growth.
  • Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) – an opening is made in the floor of the third ventricle; useful in obstructive hydrocephalus and avoids a shunt.
  • Temporary external ventricular drainage (for example, in infection); acetazolamide and furosemide only as a temporary measure.

Pre-operative nursing care

  1. Neurological observation – level of consciousness, cry, fontanelle tension, pupils, vital signs (watch for bradycardia and irregular breathing); report increasing drowsiness or seizures.
  2. Measure head circumference daily at the same point (largest occipito-frontal diameter) with the same tape and record.
  3. Support the heavy head – lift with one hand under the head and one under the body; turn every 2 hours; use a soft pillow, gel pad or ring to prevent pressure sores on the scalp.
  4. Feeding – small, frequent feeds; hold the head well supported; place the baby on the side after feeds to prevent aspiration if she vomits; record intake and output and weight.
  5. Eye care if the eyelids do not close fully; skin care.
  6. Seizure precautions; keep suction and oxygen ready.
  7. Prepare the scalp and abdomen as ordered; explain the operation to the parents and obtain consent.

Post-operative nursing care

  1. Position – lie the baby on the side opposite the shunt valve; keep the baby flat or with the head raised only as ordered (raising the head too early can drain CSF too quickly and cause collapse of the ventricles or subdural haematoma).
  2. Neurological and vital sign monitoring – level of consciousness, fontanelle, pupils, temperature, pulse, respiration and BP; head circumference daily.
    • Sunken fontanelle suggests over-drainage; bulging fontanelle, vomiting and irritability suggest shunt blockage – report immediately.
  3. Abdominal assessment – distension, tenderness, bowel sounds; start feeds when bowel sounds return.
  4. Prevention of shunt infection – aseptic care of the head and abdominal wounds; observe for fever, redness or swelling along the shunt tract, CSF leakage and poor feeding; antibiotics as prescribed.
  5. Pain relief, fluids and nutrition – analgesics, IV fluids then oral feeds, intake and output.
  6. Do not pump the shunt unless specifically ordered by the neurosurgeon.
  7. Continue skin care and positioning; encourage parents to hold and feed the baby.

Teaching the parents

  • Signs of shunt blockage – vomiting, irritability, drowsiness, poor feeding, bulging fontanelle, enlarging head, sunset eyes, headache and seizures in older children.
  • Signs of shunt infection – fever, redness along the shunt, abdominal pain, poor feeding – most common in the first 6 months after surgery.
  • Measure the head at follow-up visits; the shunt may need revision as the child grows.
  • Allow normal handling, bathing and play; avoid contact sports later; a medical alert card.
  • Early developmental stimulation and regular follow-up for development, vision and learning.

Complications of a VP shunt (to be watched lifelong)

  • Blockage (obstruction) – the commonest problem, at the ventricular or peritoneal end; presents with signs of raised ICP.
  • Infection – usually by skin organisms (Staphylococcus epidermidis) within the first months; shunt removal and antibiotics may be needed.
  • Over-drainage – slit-like ventricles, headache on standing, subdural haematoma in infants with large heads.
  • Mechanical problems – disconnection, fracture or migration of the tubing as the child grows.
  • Abdominal complications – peritoneal pseudocyst, peritonitis, bowel perforation, inguinal hernia or hydrocele.
  • Seizures and the need for repeated revisions.

Developmental and psychosocial care

  • Encourage the parents to cuddle, talk to and play with Meera; provide visual and sound stimulation suited to her age.
  • Refer for early intervention (physiotherapy, vision and hearing checks) because many children with hydrocephalus have motor delay or learning difficulties.
  • Help the parents cope with a chronic condition and repeated hospital visits; link them with RBSK and support services.

Nursing importance Shunt malfunction and infection are common and can be fatal if missed. The nurse who measures the head accurately, recognises early signs of raised ICP, positions the baby correctly after surgery and teaches parents what to watch for protects the child's brain and life.

Conclusion Hydrocephalus is excess CSF in the ventricles due to obstruction, poor absorption or rarely overproduction. Infants like Meera present with an enlarging head, bulging fontanelle, separated sutures and sunset eyes. It is treated mainly with a VP shunt or ETV, supported by careful neurological monitoring, positioning, infection prevention and parent education about shunt problems.
