question: A newborn girl is born with a sac-like swelling over the lower back that is leaking clear fluid, and she does not move her legs. She is diagnosed with lumbosacral myelomeningocele. (a) Define spina bifida and explain its types. (4 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features, associated problems and prevention of neural tube defects. (4 marks) (c) Describe the pre-operative and post-operative nursing care of the baby and her long-term care. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Types of spina bifida
labels: intact skin with tuft of hair or dimple)

answer_html:
(a) Definition and types (4 marks)

Definition Spina bifida is a neural tube defect (NTD) in which the vertebral arches fail to fuse, so that the spinal canal remains open, with or without protrusion of the meninges and spinal cord. It results from failure of closure of the caudal end of the neural tube by about the 28th day of gestation – often before the woman knows she is pregnant.

Types

  1. Spina bifida occulta
    • Only the bony defect (usually L5–S1); skin intact; no sac.
    • Marked by a tuft of hair, dimple, lipoma, haemangioma or sinus over the lower back.
    • Usually no symptoms; occasionally a tethered cord causes leg weakness or bladder problems later.
  2. Spina bifida cystica – a visible sac:
    • Meningocele – the sac contains meninges and CSF only; the spinal cord is in its normal position; usually covered with skin; little or no neurological deficit.
    • Myelomeningocele (meningomyelocele) – the sac contains meninges, CSF and the spinal cord or nerve roots; it is the most common and most serious form (about three-quarters of spina bifida cystica), usually lumbosacral, often thin-walled or leaking CSF, with paralysis below the level of the lesion.
    • Other NTDs are anencephaly (absence of the cranial vault and brain – incompatible with life), encephalocele and craniorachischisis.

(b) Clinical features, associated problems and prevention (4 marks)

Clinical features and associated problems of myelomeningocele

  • Sac over the back – may be ruptured, leaking CSF, with risk of meningitis.
  • Motor loss – flaccid paralysis of the legs below the lesion, muscle wasting, absent reflexes.
  • Sensory loss below the lesion – risk of pressure sores and unnoticed burns or injuries.
  • Neurogenic bladder – dribbling of urine or retention, recurrent urinary tract infections, reflux and kidney damage.
  • Neurogenic bowel – patulous anus, constipation or faecal incontinence.
  • Orthopaedic deformities – club feet, dislocated hips, kyphosis, scoliosis, contractures.
  • Hydrocephalus in 80–90% due to the Arnold–Chiari type II malformation; it may appear only after the sac is closed.
  • Chiari II symptoms – stridor, apnoea, swallowing difficulty; later learning difficulties, latex allergy, tethered cord, obesity and psychosocial problems.

Diagnosis

  • Antenatal – raised maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (16–18 weeks); anomaly ultrasound at 18–20 weeks (lemon and banana signs); amniotic fluid AFP and acetylcholinesterase.
  • After birth – clinical examination, MRI of spine and brain, cranial ultrasound, X-ray of spine and hips, renal ultrasound and urodynamic studies.

Prevention

  • Folic acid 0.4 mg (400 micrograms) daily for all women planning pregnancy, from at least one month before conception until 12 weeks of pregnancy.
  • Folic acid 4 mg daily for women who have had a previous baby with an NTD, have an NTD themselves, or take antiepileptic drugs (especially valproate, which should be avoided where possible).
  • Food fortification with folic acid (for example, fortified rice and wheat flour), good control of maternal diabetes and obesity, avoiding hyperthermia in early pregnancy, and antenatal screening.

(c) Nursing care (7 marks)

Surgical treatment (background) – closure of the myelomeningocele is done within 24–72 hours of birth to prevent infection and further damage; a VP shunt is inserted if hydrocephalus develops.

Pre-operative nursing care

  1. Protect the sac
    • Place the baby prone (or side-lying) – never on the back.
    • Cover the sac with a sterile, non-adherent dressing soaked in warm normal saline, covered with cling film or a plastic sheet to prevent drying; change as ordered.
    • Handle gently; no nappy over the sac; place a plastic barrier below the sac to keep urine and stool away.
  2. Prevent infection – strict asepsis, hand hygiene, observe the sac for leakage, redness or pus; IV antibiotics as prescribed.
  3. Maintain temperature – nurse in an incubator or under a radiant warmer (the exposed sac and prone position increase heat loss).
  4. Neurological assessment – movement and sensation of legs, anal wink, urinary dribbling; head circumference and fontanelle daily.
  5. Positioning of limbs – hips slightly abducted with a rolled nappy between the legs; feet in neutral position; gentle range of motion as advised.
  6. Feeding – breast milk by cup, tube or breastfeeding in side-lying or prone position with the head turned; record intake and output.
  7. Latex-free environment from birth (gloves, catheters and equipment).
  8. Support the parents – they are shocked and grieving; allow them to see and touch the baby; explain the surgery and its expected results; obtain consent.

Post-operative nursing care

  • Keep the baby prone or side-lying until the wound heals; keep the wound clean and dry and free from urine and stool; observe for CSF leakage, swelling and infection.
  • Monitor head circumference, fontanelle and signs of raised ICP daily – hydrocephalus often develops after closure.
  • Vital signs, pain relief, IV fluids, then feeds; intake and output.
  • Bladder care – clean intermittent catheterisation (CIC) as ordered to prevent retention and infection; urine culture when needed.
  • Pressure area care – change position frequently, inspect the skin, soft padding; protect insensitive skin from heat and injury.
  • Physiotherapy – positioning and passive exercises.

Long-term care and parent teaching

  • Multidisciplinary follow-up – neurosurgeon, paediatrician, orthopaedic surgeon, urologist, physiotherapist and occupational therapist.
  • Teach CIC to parents (and later to the child) using a clean technique, usually every 3–4 hours.
  • Bowel programme – regular toilet times, high-fibre diet, fluids, laxatives or suppositories as advised.
  • Daily skin inspection, prevention of pressure sores and burns (check bath water), suitable footwear and orthoses.
  • Mobility – orthoses, calipers, walkers or wheelchair; treatment of club feet and hip problems.
  • Watch for shunt problems, urinary infection, worsening leg function or back pain (tethered cord).
  • Prevent obesity; encourage schooling, independence and social participation; disability certificate (UDID) and welfare schemes; early intervention through RBSK.
  • Genetic counselling – folic acid 4 mg before and during any future pregnancy.

Latex allergy precautions – children with spina bifida are at high risk of severe allergy to latex because of repeated exposure from birth (gloves, catheters, surgery). Use latex-free gloves, catheters, tourniquets and equipment from the first day, label the cot and records, and teach the family to avoid latex balloons and toys.

Clean intermittent catheterisation (CIC) – points to teach the parents

  1. Wash hands with soap and water; gather a clean catheter of the right size, water-soluble lubricant, clean cloth and container.
  2. Clean the genital area from front to back.
  3. Lubricate and gently insert the catheter until urine flows; let the bladder empty completely, then withdraw slowly.
  4. Wash reusable catheters with soap and water, rinse, dry and store in a clean container.
  5. Catheterise at regular times (usually every 3–4 hours) and record the amount; report cloudy, foul-smelling or blood-stained urine, fever or leakage between catheterisations. - CIC keeps the bladder empty, prevents infection and back-pressure on the kidneys and helps the child achieve social continence.

Nursing importance Protecting the sac from drying and infection, preventing hydrocephalus and kidney damage from being missed, and teaching CIC, skin care and bowel care to the family decide the long-term health and independence of a child with myelomeningocele.

Conclusion Spina bifida is a neural tube defect due to failure of fusion of the vertebral arches; myelomeningocele is its most serious form, causing paralysis, sensory loss, neurogenic bladder and bowel, orthopaedic deformities and hydrocephalus. It can largely be prevented by periconceptional folic acid. Early surgical closure with careful pre- and post-operative nursing, and lifelong multidisciplinary and family-centred care, help these children live fuller lives.

question: Baby Ishaan, aged 9 months, is admitted with high fever, irritability, vomiting and refusal of feeds. He has a high-pitched cry, a bulging anterior fontanelle and had one convulsion at home. CSF examination suggests acute bacterial meningitis. (a) Define meningitis and list the causative organisms according to age. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features, CSF findings and complications of bacterial meningitis in children. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of Ishaan. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: CSF findings in meningitis
labels: tubercular – rows: appearance (clear; turbid; clear; clear or cobweb)
protein (15–45 mg/dl; markedly raised; normal or slightly raised; markedly raised)
glucose (two-thirds of blood glucose; very low; normal; low)

answer_html:
(a) Definition and causative organisms (3 marks)

Definition Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges (pia mater and arachnoid) and the CSF in the subarachnoid space, most often due to infection. Acute bacterial (pyogenic) meningitis is a medical emergency in children; delay in treatment leads to death or permanent brain damage.

Causative organisms according to age

  • Newborn (0–2 months) – group B streptococcus, Escherichia coli and other Gram-negative bacilli, Listeria monocytogenes, Staphylococcus aureus.
  • 2 months to 5 years – Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus), Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) (much less common since Hib vaccination), Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus).
  • Above 5 years – pneumococcus and meningococcus.
  • Other causes – tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis, subacute), viruses (enteroviruses – usually mild), fungi (in immunocompromised children).
  • Routes – spread through the blood from the nasopharynx or another focus (pneumonia, otitis media), direct spread from sinusitis or mastoiditis, skull fracture, or an open neural tube defect.

(b) Clinical features, CSF findings and complications (5 marks)

Clinical features in infants (like Ishaan) – signs are non-specific:

  • Fever (or low temperature in newborns), irritability, high-pitched cry, lethargy, poor feeding, vomiting.
  • Bulging anterior fontanelle (a key sign in infants); neck stiffness is often absent below 1 year.
  • Seizures, apnoea, poor tone, shock.
  • Purpuric rash (meningococcal septicaemia).

Clinical features in older children

  • Fever, severe headache, vomiting, photophobia, drowsiness, confusion.
  • Neck stiffness, Kernig's sign and Brudzinski's sign.
  • Seizures, focal neurological deficits, cranial nerve palsies, altered consciousness.

Diagnosis – lumbar puncture and CSF examination (if there are no signs of severely raised ICP or shock)

Finding Normal Bacterial meningitis Viral meningitis Tubercular meningitis
Appearance Clear Turbid Clear Clear, cobweb on standing
Cells / mm³ 0–5 lymphocytes Hundreds to thousands, mainly neutrophils Tens to hundreds, lymphocytes 100–500, lymphocytes
Protein (mg/dl) 15–45 Markedly raised Normal or slightly raised Markedly raised
Glucose About two-thirds of blood glucose Very low Normal Low
  • Gram stain, culture and sensitivity, latex agglutination or PCR of CSF; blood culture, blood glucose (for CSF–blood ratio), complete blood count, CRP, electrolytes; CT scan if raised ICP or focal signs.

Complications

  • Acute – raised ICP and brain herniation, seizures, septic shock, SIADH (hyponatraemia), subdural effusion or empyema, cerebral oedema, brain abscess, ventriculitis.
  • Long-term – sensorineural hearing loss (the commonest sequela), hydrocephalus, intellectual disability, cerebral palsy, epilepsy, blindness and learning problems.

(c) Management and nursing care of Ishaan (7 marks)

Medical management

  1. Emergency care – airway, breathing and circulation; oxygen; treat shock with fluid boluses; control seizures (benzodiazepine, then levetiracetam or phenytoin).
  2. Antibiotics immediately (after blood culture, and LP if safe – never delay antibiotics for the LP):
    • Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day IV in one or two doses (or cefotaxime), with vancomycin where resistant pneumococcus is suspected; for neonates – ampicillin with cefotaxime or gentamicin.
    • Duration – usually 10–14 days (7–10 days for Hib, 5–7 days for meningococcus), longer in neonates; adjusted to culture results.
  3. Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg every 6 hours for 2–4 days, started before or with the first antibiotic dose in infants and children above 6 weeks, as prescribed – reduces hearing loss, especially in Hib meningitis.
  4. Fluids – maintenance isotonic fluids; watch for SIADH (restrict fluids only if hyponatraemia develops) and avoid dehydration.
  5. Raised ICP – head end raised to 30 degrees, mannitol or hypertonic saline as ordered.
  6. Fever control, nutrition, treatment of complications (drainage of subdural empyema, VP shunt for hydrocephalus).
  7. Chemoprophylaxis for close contacts in Hib and meningococcal meningitis (rifampicin, or ceftriaxone single dose) as advised.

Nursing care of Ishaan

  1. Isolation – droplet precautions for 24 hours after starting effective antibiotics (meningococcal and Hib); hand hygiene, mask for close care.
  2. Neurological observation – level of consciousness (paediatric Glasgow Coma Scale), cry, fontanelle tension, pupils, limb movements, and seizures, every 1–2 hours initially; head circumference daily (subdural effusion, hydrocephalus).
  3. Vital signs – temperature, pulse, respiration, BP and SpO2; watch for shock (cold extremities, prolonged capillary refill, weak pulse) and Cushing's response (bradycardia, hypertension, irregular breathing).
  4. Seizure precautions – padded cot sides, suction and oxygen ready, side-lying position during a fit; record the type and duration; anticonvulsants as ordered.
  5. Positioning and comfort – side-lying with head slightly raised and neck in line; dim, quiet room; minimal handling and cluster care; avoid neck flexion; analgesics.
  6. Antibiotics on time – correct dose by weight, proper dilution and rate; watch the IV site.
  7. Fluid balance – strict intake and output, daily weight, serum sodium; report reduced urine output with low sodium (SIADH).
  8. Fever – tepid sponging and paracetamol.
  9. Nutrition – continue breastfeeding when conscious and able; nasogastric feeds if drowsy; prevent aspiration.
  10. Hygiene and skin – mouth care, eye care, change of position, skin care.
  11. Lumbar puncture care – hold the infant firmly in the correct position, observe the puncture site afterwards.
  12. Support the parents – explain the illness, procedures and the need for isolation; allow them to stay and help with comfort care.

Before discharge and follow-up

  • Hearing assessment (OAE or BERA) before discharge or soon after; developmental, vision and neurological follow-up.
  • Teach parents to watch for enlarging head, vomiting, seizures or developmental delay.
  • Prevention – complete immunisation: pentavalent vaccine (includes Hib), pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) under the UIP, measles–rubella and JE vaccine in endemic districts; early treatment of ear and chest infections.

Special points – meningitis in the newborn

  • Signs are very non-specific – temperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy, apnoea, jaundice, seizures and a bulging fontanelle; meningitis must be excluded in every newborn with suspected sepsis.
  • Organisms are group B streptococcus, E. coli and Listeria; treatment is with ampicillin plus cefotaxime or gentamicin for at least 14–21 days.

Tubercular meningitis (TBM) – brief comparison

  • Subacute onset over 2–3 weeks with low-grade fever, irritability, vomiting, headache, then altered sensorium, cranial nerve palsies, seizures and hydrocephalus.
  • History of contact with an adult with tuberculosis is common; CSF shows lymphocytes, high protein and low glucose; CBNAAT of CSF and MRI help diagnosis.
  • Treatment is with antitubercular drugs for 12 months along with steroids; it is prevented by BCG vaccination, contact screening and TB preventive treatment of child contacts.

Nursing importance In infants the signs of meningitis are subtle – irritability, poor feeding and a bulging fontanelle. Early recognition, immediate antibiotics, meticulous neurological monitoring and seizure care, and arranging hearing and developmental follow-up are key nursing contributions to survival and good outcome.

Conclusion Bacterial meningitis is an emergency caused mainly by pneumococcus, Hib and meningococcus in infants and children, and by group B streptococcus and E. coli in newborns. Ishaan's fever, irritability, high-pitched cry, bulging fontanelle and seizure are typical. Diagnosis is by CSF examination, and treatment is with early ceftriaxone, dexamethasone and supportive care. Careful nursing observation, seizure care, fluid balance, isolation, follow-up for hearing loss and immunisation for prevention are essential.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: (a) Define cerebral palsy and explain its causes. (4 marks) (b) Explain the types and clinical features of cerebral palsy and its associated problems. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of a child with cerebral palsy, including the education of parents. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Types of cerebral palsy by distribution
labels: spastic diplegia (both legs more than arms)
spastic quadriplegia (all four limbs); child with scissoring of legs and toe walking

answer_html:
(a) Definition and causes (4 marks)

Definition Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of permanent disorders of the development of movement and posture, causing activity limitation, that are attributed to non-progressive disturbances that occurred in the developing foetal or infant brain. The motor disorder is often accompanied by disturbances of sensation, perception, cognition, communication and behaviour, by epilepsy and by secondary musculoskeletal problems.

  • The brain lesion does not progress, but the clinical picture changes as the child grows.
  • It is the commonest cause of physical disability in childhood, affecting about 2–3 per 1,000 live births.

Causes – in many children more than one factor is present.

  1. Prenatal (the majority)
    • Congenital infections – TORCH (toxoplasmosis, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes), Zika.
    • Placental insufficiency, pre-eclampsia, antepartum haemorrhage, maternal hypoxia, severe anaemia.
    • Brain malformations, genetic factors, multiple pregnancy, teratogens (alcohol, radiation).
  2. Perinatal
    • Prematurity and low birth weight – periventricular leukomalacia and intraventricular haemorrhage (commonly spastic diplegia).
    • Birth asphyxia (hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy), difficult or prolonged labour.
    • Kernicterus from severe neonatal jaundice (dyskinetic CP).
    • Neonatal sepsis, meningitis, hypoglycaemia.
  3. Postnatal (up to about 2–3 years)
    • Meningitis, encephalitis, cerebral malaria.
    • Head injury, near-drowning, stroke, severe dehydration, poisoning.

(b) Types, clinical features and associated problems (5 marks)

Types according to the motor disorder

  1. Spastic CP (70–80%) – damage to the motor cortex and pyramidal tracts.
    • Increased tone (stiff limbs, clasp-knife rigidity), brisk reflexes, positive Babinski sign, clonus, weakness, contractures.
    • Scissoring of the legs (crossing when held upright), toe walking, fisted hands.
    • By distribution – hemiplegia (one side, arm more than leg; early hand preference), diplegia (both legs more affected than arms; preterm babies), quadriplegia (all four limbs; the most severe, often with intellectual disability, epilepsy and feeding problems).
  2. Dyskinetic CP (athetoid/dystonic, 10–15%) – damage to the basal ganglia (kernicterus, severe asphyxia).
    • Involuntary, slow, writhing movements, fluctuating tone, abnormal postures, drooling, difficulty in speech (dysarthria); intelligence is often normal.
  3. Ataxic CP (about 5%) – cerebellar damage.
    • Poor balance, wide-based unsteady gait, intention tremor, low tone.
  4. Mixed CP – features of more than one type. - Severity is graded by the Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) levels I to V.

Early signs in infancy

  • Delay in motor milestones – no head control by 4 months, not sitting by 9 months.
  • Persistence of primitive reflexes (Moro, asymmetric tonic neck reflex) beyond 6 months.
  • Abnormal tone – floppy or stiff baby; arching of the back; fisting beyond 3 months; hand preference before 1 year.
  • Feeding difficulty, excessive irritability, poor sucking and swallowing.

Associated problems

  • Intellectual disability (about half), epilepsy (about one-third), learning difficulties and behaviour problems.
  • Visual problems (squint, cortical visual impairment) and hearing loss.
  • Speech and language difficulties; feeding and swallowing problems with aspiration, malnutrition and poor growth; drooling; gastro-oesophageal reflux; constipation; dental caries.
  • Orthopaedic – contractures, hip dislocation, scoliosis, osteoporosis.
  • Sleep problems, pain and emotional stress for the family.

(c) Management and nursing care (6 marks)

Management (multidisciplinary; aim – maximum function and independence)

  • Early intervention – District Early Intervention Centres (DEIC) under RBSK provide screening, therapy and referral.
  • Physiotherapy – stretching, positioning, strengthening, balance and gait training; occupational therapy for hand function and daily activities; speech and swallowing therapy.
  • Orthoses – ankle–foot orthoses, splints, standing frames, walkers and wheelchairs.
  • Drugs for spasticity – oral baclofen, diazepam, tizanidine; botulinum toxin injections into spastic muscles; intrathecal baclofen in selected children.
  • Orthopaedic surgery – tendon lengthening (Achilles tendon), adductor release, hip and spine surgery; selective dorsal rhizotomy in selected children.
  • Anticonvulsants for epilepsy; treatment of reflux, constipation and dental problems.
  • Nutrition – high-calorie diet; gastrostomy feeding when swallowing is unsafe.
  • Special or inclusive education, communication aids, vocational training; disability certificate (UDID card) and welfare benefits such as the Niramaya health insurance scheme.

Nursing care

  1. Impaired physical mobility – passive and active range-of-motion exercises as taught by the physiotherapist; correct positioning in lying, sitting and standing (side-lying, prone lying, supported sitting with hips and knees at 90 degrees, avoiding "W" sitting); apply splints correctly and check the skin under them.
  2. Risk of injury – safe, padded environment; helmet if falls are frequent; seizure precautions and first aid.
  3. Risk of aspiration and imbalanced nutrition
    • Feed in an upright position with the head slightly forward (chin tuck); small amounts; thickened fluids if advised; allow enough time; never feed a child lying flat.
    • Energy-dense foods, regular weight monitoring; oral care and dental check-ups; manage drooling; prevent constipation with fibre and fluids.
  4. Impaired communication – talk to the child clearly and patiently; use pictures, gestures and communication boards; check hearing and vision.
  5. Self-care deficit – encourage independence in feeding, dressing and toileting with adaptive aids (spoons with thick handles, Velcro fastenings, adapted seats); praise every achievement.
  6. Delayed growth and development – early stimulation, play suited to ability, inclusive schooling.
  7. Skin integrity – change position every 2 hours in immobile children; pressure area care.

Education and support of parents

  • Explain that CP is not progressive and not contagious; it cannot be cured, but therapy greatly improves function.
  • Train parents to carry out home exercises, positioning, safe feeding and handling every day.
  • Warn against costly, unproven "cures"; encourage regular follow-up with the therapy team.
  • Counselling, respite care, support groups and information on government schemes, disability benefits and inclusive education.
  • Prevention – good antenatal and intrapartum care, prevention of preterm birth, magnesium sulphate for neuroprotection before very preterm birth, skilled neonatal resuscitation, prevention of kernicterus and hypoglycaemia, immunisation and prevention of head injuries.

Common nursing diagnoses in a child with cerebral palsy | Nursing diagnosis | Key nursing interventions | |---|---| | Impaired physical mobility related to spasticity | Range-of-motion exercises, positioning, orthoses, mobility aids | | Risk for aspiration related to impaired swallowing | Upright feeding, chin tuck, thickened fluids, suction ready | | Imbalanced nutrition: less than body requirements | Energy-dense feeds, weight monitoring, gastrostomy care if present | | Impaired verbal communication | Speech therapy, picture boards, patient communication | | Risk for injury related to seizures and poor balance | Safe environment, helmet, seizure precautions | | Interrupted family processes / caregiver role strain | Counselling, respite, support groups, information on schemes |

Community-based care – District Early Intervention Centres under RBSK, community-based rehabilitation workers, anganwadi workers and special educators help families continue therapy at home and include the child in school and community life.

Nursing importance The nurse is often the first to notice delayed milestones or abnormal tone in an infant at risk. Early referral, correct positioning and feeding, and empowering parents to continue therapy at home make a lifelong difference to the child's independence.

Conclusion Cerebral palsy is a non-progressive disorder of movement and posture due to injury to the developing brain from prenatal, perinatal or postnatal causes. Spastic CP is the commonest type, and many children have associated intellectual disability, epilepsy, feeding, vision and hearing problems. Management is multidisciplinary and lifelong; nursing focuses on mobility, safe feeding, communication, self-care, prevention of complications and supporting the family.

question: Explain febrile seizures in children and their management.
answer_html:
Definition A febrile seizure is a seizure occurring with fever (38 °C or above) in a child aged 6 months to 5 years, without infection of the central nervous system, metabolic disturbance or a history of afebrile seizures. It is the commonest type of seizure in childhood, affecting about 2–5% of children (peak 12–18 months).

Causes and risk factors

  • Usually occurs early in a viral infection – upper respiratory infection, otitis media, roseola, gastroenteritis; sometimes after vaccination.
  • Family history of febrile seizures; the immature brain has a lower seizure threshold during rising temperature.

Types | Simple febrile seizure | Complex febrile seizure | |---|---| | Generalised (tonic–clonic) | Focal onset or features | | Lasts less than 15 minutes | Lasts more than 15 minutes | | Only once in 24 hours | Recurs within 24 hours | | No neurological deficit after | May have post-ictal weakness (Todd's paresis) |

Prognosis

  • Recurrence in about one-third of children (higher if the first seizure is before 1 year or there is a family history).
  • Small risk of later epilepsy (slightly more after complex seizures); simple febrile seizures do not cause brain damage.

Management

  1. First aid – place the child on the side on a safe surface, loosen clothing, do not put anything in the mouth, do not restrain, note the time, stay with the child.
  2. If the seizure lasts more than 5 minutes – buccal or intranasal midazolam (0.2–0.3 mg/kg) or rectal diazepam (0.5 mg/kg), as prescribed; oxygen; treat as status epilepticus if it continues.
  3. After the seizure – look for the cause of fever (ear, throat, chest, urine); lumbar puncture if there are signs of meningitis, or in infants who are not fully immunised or have received antibiotics; EEG and brain imaging are not needed for simple febrile seizures.
  4. Fever control – paracetamol or ibuprofen and light clothing for comfort (they do not prevent recurrence).
  5. Prophylaxis – continuous anticonvulsants are not recommended; intermittent oral clobazam during febrile illnesses may be advised for frequent or prolonged seizures.

Nursing care and parent education

  • Observe and record the seizure (onset, type, duration, colour, post-ictal state); maintain airway; keep suction and oxygen ready; side-lying position.
  • Reassure the parents – febrile seizures are frightening but usually harmless.
  • Teach home first aid, use of rescue medicine (buccal midazolam), and fever management.
  • Seek urgent help if a seizure lasts more than 5 minutes, breathing is difficult, the child does not wake up normally, or there is neck stiffness, rash or repeated vomiting.
  • Continue routine immunisation.

Conclusion Febrile seizures are common, mostly benign seizures in children of 6 months to 5 years during a febrile illness. Simple seizures are brief and generalised. Management consists of first aid, rescue benzodiazepine for prolonged seizures, finding the cause of fever and, above all, reassuring and educating the parents.

question: Explain the emergency management of status epilepticus in children.
answer_html:
Definition Status epilepticus (SE) is a seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, or two or more seizures without full recovery of consciousness in between. (The older definition used 30 minutes; treatment is now started at 5 minutes because prolonged seizures cause brain injury and become harder to stop.) It is a medical emergency.

Causes in children

  • Prolonged febrile seizure; CNS infections – meningitis, encephalitis, cerebral malaria, neurocysticercosis.
  • Known epilepsy with missed or reduced antiepileptic drugs.
  • Metabolic – hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia.
  • Head injury, poisoning, hypertensive encephalopathy, hypoxia.

Time-based emergency management 0–5 minutes – stabilisation

  • Airway – position on the side, head tilt–chin lift, gentle suction; high-flow oxygen; monitor SpO2, heart rate, BP and temperature.
  • Check blood glucose at the bedside – if low, give 10% dextrose 2–5 ml/kg IV.
  • Secure IV access (intraosseous if not possible); send blood for glucose, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, CBC, cultures, drug levels and toxicology.

5–10 minutes – first-line drug (benzodiazepine)

  • IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg) or IV diazepam 0.2–0.3 mg/kg.
  • Without IV access – buccal or intranasal midazolam 0.2–0.3 mg/kg or IM midazolam 0.2 mg/kg.
  • Repeat once after 5 minutes if the seizure continues (not more than two doses).

10–30 minutes – second-line drug (established SE)

  • IV levetiracetam (40–60 mg/kg), or phenytoin/fosphenytoin (20 mg/kg; phenytoin diluted in normal saline, given slowly with cardiac monitoring), or sodium valproate (20–40 mg/kg), or phenobarbitone (20 mg/kg), as per protocol.

More than 30–40 minutes – refractory SE

  • Transfer to PICU; intubation and ventilation; continuous midazolam infusion (or thiopentone/propofol); EEG monitoring.

Throughout – treat the cause (antibiotics, acyclovir, antimalarials), control fever, correct electrolytes and manage raised ICP.

Nursing responsibilities

  • Stay with the child; protect from injury; never force anything into the mouth; maintain airway and oxygen; keep a bag-valve-mask and suction ready (benzodiazepines can depress breathing).
  • Note the time of onset and record the type, duration and response to each drug.
  • Calculate and give drugs accurately by weight; observe the IV site (phenytoin is irritant).
  • Monitor respiration, SpO2, heart rate, BP, temperature and blood glucose; watch for hypotension and arrhythmias.
  • Post-ictal care – recovery position, neurological observation, safety, comfort.
  • Support the parents; teach drug adherence and home rescue medication (buccal midazolam) before discharge.

Conclusion Status epilepticus is a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes and is an emergency. Management follows a strict time-based plan – stabilisation and glucose check, benzodiazepines, a second-line drug such as levetiracetam or phenytoin, and PICU care for refractory seizures – with the nurse ensuring airway safety, accurate drug administration and close monitoring.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
