question: Explain acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) in children, with special reference to Japanese encephalitis.
answer_html:
Definition Acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) is a clinical syndrome defined as acute onset of fever with a change in mental status (confusion, disorientation, inability to talk, coma) and/or new onset of seizures (excluding simple febrile seizures), in a person of any age at any time of the year. It is a major cause of childhood death and disability in parts of India such as eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Assam and West Bengal.

Causes

  • Viral – Japanese encephalitis (JE) (the most important), herpes simplex virus, enteroviruses, dengue, measles, Nipah virus, Chandipura virus.
  • Bacterial and others – scrub typhus (an important treatable cause), leptospirosis, cerebral malaria (Plasmodium falciparum), bacterial meningitis.
  • Toxic or metabolic – litchi-associated hypoglycaemic encephalopathy in undernourished children who eat litchis and miss the evening meal, Reye syndrome.

Japanese encephalitis

  • Caused by the JE virus (a flavivirus), transmitted by Culex mosquitoes (Culex tritaeniorhynchus) breeding in paddy fields; pigs are amplifying hosts and wading (ardeid) birds are reservoirs; humans are dead-end hosts.
  • Most infections are mild, but encephalitis has a high case fatality and leaves many survivors with neurological sequelae.

Clinical features

  • Fever, headache, vomiting, followed by altered sensorium, irritability, seizures, abnormal movements (tremors, rigidity), focal weakness, coma; signs of raised ICP and shock in severe cases.
  • Sequelae – paralysis, intellectual disability, epilepsy, behaviour problems, speech difficulties.

Investigations – CSF (lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein), JE IgM ELISA in CSF or serum, scrub typhus IgM, malaria tests, blood glucose, blood count, electrolytes; MRI (thalamic lesions in JE); EEG.

Management

  • No specific antiviral treatment for JE – care is supportive and must start early:
    • Airway, breathing, oxygen; control of seizures; management of raised ICP (head end raised, mannitol or hypertonic saline).
    • Correct hypoglycaemia immediately (10% dextrose) – vital in litchi-associated AES.
    • Fluids, fever control, nutrition, care of the unconscious child, PICU care.
  • Empirical treatment until the cause is known – ceftriaxone, acyclovir (herpes), doxycycline or azithromycin (scrub typhus) and artesunate (malaria), as per national guidelines.
  • Rehabilitation – physiotherapy, speech therapy and follow-up of survivors.

Prevention and control

  • JE vaccination – included in the Universal Immunization Programme in endemic districts (two doses at 9–12 months and 16–24 months), with campaigns for older children and adults.
  • Vector control – larvicides, fogging in outbreaks, mosquito nets, repellents, full-sleeved clothing; keeping pig sties away from homes.
  • Early referral of any child with fever and altered sensorium; awareness campaigns.
  • Ensure children have an evening meal and avoid eating large amounts of litchi on an empty stomach in litchi-growing areas.

Role of the nurse – early recognition and referral, care of the unconscious child (airway, positioning, eye and mouth care, pressure area care), seizure care, accurate monitoring, health education on vaccination and mosquito control, and rehabilitation support.

Conclusion AES is fever with altered mental status or seizures, caused in India mainly by Japanese encephalitis, scrub typhus, malaria and other infections and metabolic causes. JE has no specific cure, so early supportive care, empirical treatment of treatable causes, JE vaccination and vector control are essential, with nurses playing a key role in care and prevention.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: Explain the special features of head injury in children and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Introduction Head injury is a leading cause of death and disability in children. Most injuries are mild, but a small number cause serious brain damage that must be recognised quickly.

Why children are more vulnerable

  • Large, heavy head and weak neck muscles – the head is thrown about more in falls and collisions.
  • Thin, pliable skull and open sutures and fontanelles in infants.
  • The brain has more water content and is prone to diffuse swelling; infants can lose significant blood volume into the scalp or skull.

Causes

  • Falls – from beds, stairs, rooftops (while flying kites), trees, balconies – the commonest cause in young children.
  • Road traffic injuries – as pedestrians, cyclists or passengers without restraints.
  • Sports and playground injuries.
  • Abusive head trauma ("shaken baby") – suspect in infants with subdural bleeding, retinal haemorrhages and an injury not explained by the history.

Types

  • Scalp injuries – lacerations, cephalhaematoma, subgaleal haematoma.
  • Skull fractures – linear, depressed, "ping-pong" fracture in infants, basal skull fracture (raccoon eyes, Battle's sign, CSF leak from nose or ear).
  • Brain injuries – concussion, contusion, extradural haematoma (often with a lucid interval followed by rapid deterioration), subdural haematoma, diffuse axonal injury.

Assessment

  • Paediatric Glasgow Coma Scale (verbal response adapted for infants – cooing, irritable cry, cry to pain, moan, none) or AVPU.
  • Pupils (size, equality, reaction), limb movements, anterior fontanelle, vomiting, seizures.
  • Vital signs – Cushing's triad (slow pulse, rising BP, irregular breathing) is a late sign of raised ICP.
  • CT scan when indicated by clinical decision rules (low GCS, signs of skull fracture, prolonged unconsciousness, repeated vomiting, severe mechanism).

Management

  • Mild injury (GCS 13–15) – observation for 4–6 hours; discharge with written head-injury advice if well.
  • Moderate or severe injury – airway with cervical spine protection, oxygen, avoid hypoxia and low BP; head raised 30 degrees in the midline; control seizures; treat raised ICP (mannitol or hypertonic saline); neurosurgery for extradural or subdural haematoma or depressed fracture; PICU care.

Nursing management

  • Neurological observations (GCS, pupils, limb power) every 15 minutes to hourly, and report any deterioration immediately.
  • Monitor vital signs, SpO2, temperature; prevent fever.
  • Keep the airway clear, position with head raised and neck straight; seizure precautions.
  • IV isotonic fluids as ordered; intake and output; nil by mouth if vomiting or awaiting surgery; avoid nasogastric tubes through the nose in suspected basal fracture.
  • CSF leak – do not pack the nose or ear; place a sterile pad loosely; no nose blowing; watch for meningitis.
  • Pain relief (paracetamol); quiet environment; reassurance of child and parents.
  • Child-protection referral when abuse is suspected.

Head-injury advice to parents at discharge – return immediately if the child has repeated vomiting, increasing drowsiness, severe headache, convulsions, unequal pupils, weakness, clear fluid from the nose or ears, or unusual behaviour.

Prevention – supervision, window and stair guards, no play on unprotected rooftops, helmets for cyclists and two-wheeler riders, child car seats, safe playgrounds.

Conclusion Children are especially prone to head injuries because of their large heads and thin skulls; falls are the commonest cause. Careful assessment with the paediatric GCS, prompt treatment of raised ICP and haematomas, close neurological nursing observation, clear advice to parents and prevention of falls and road injuries reduce death and disability.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: List the signs of ventriculoperitoneal shunt malfunction in an infant.
answer_html:
Shunt blockage (raised intracranial pressure)

  • Vomiting, poor feeding, irritability, high-pitched cry.
  • Bulging, tense anterior fontanelle; rapidly increasing head circumference; distended scalp veins.
  • "Sunset" eyes, drowsiness, lethargy, seizures; bradycardia and irregular breathing (late).
  • In older children – headache, vomiting, blurred vision, decline in school performance.

Shunt infection

  • Fever, redness, swelling or tenderness along the shunt tract or at the wound; CSF leak; abdominal pain or distension (peritoneal end).

Over-drainage – sunken fontanelle, irritability or headache on sitting up.

  • Any of these signs needs immediate medical review.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: What are Kernig's sign and Brudzinski's sign?
answer_html:
Both are signs of meningeal irritation, seen in meningitis and subarachnoid haemorrhage (often absent in infants below one year).

  • Kernig's sign – with the child lying supine, the hip is flexed to 90 degrees and then the knee is extended; pain in the back and hamstrings and resistance to knee extension is a positive sign.
  • Brudzinski's sign (neck sign) – with the child supine, the examiner passively flexes the neck; involuntary flexion of the hips and knees is a positive sign.
  • Together with neck stiffness, they suggest meningitis and indicate the need for lumbar puncture (if safe).

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: What is the Arnold–Chiari malformation?
answer_html:
The Arnold–Chiari (Chiari type II) malformation is a congenital anomaly in which the cerebellar vermis, fourth ventricle and lower brainstem are displaced downwards through the foramen magnum into the upper cervical canal.

  • It is present in almost all children with lumbosacral myelomeningocele.
  • It blocks CSF flow and is the main cause of the hydrocephalus (80–90%) seen in these children.
  • Brainstem compression causes stridor (vocal cord palsy), apnoea, weak cry, swallowing and feeding difficulties, aspiration, neck pain and weakness of the arms.
  • Management – VP shunt for hydrocephalus; surgical decompression of the posterior fossa for severe brainstem symptoms; careful monitoring of breathing and feeding.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: What is the Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS)?
answer_html:
The Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) is a five-level system that classifies the gross motor ability of children with cerebral palsy, based on what they can do in sitting, walking and mobility in daily life.

  • Level I – walks without limitations.
  • Level II – walks with limitations (difficulty on uneven surfaces, stairs need a rail).
  • Level III – walks using a hand-held mobility device (walker, crutches).
  • Level IV – self-mobility is limited; uses powered mobility or is transported.
  • Level V – transported in a manual wheelchair; very limited head and trunk control.
  • It helps in predicting function, planning therapy and equipment, and communicating among the team and family.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Cardiovascular, Haematological, Gastrointestinal, Genitourinary and Nervous System Disorders
question: Write the first aid for a child having a seizure.
tags: do not put anything in mouth
answer_html:
During the seizure

  • Stay calm and stay with the child; note the time it starts.
  • Move away dangerous objects; place the child on a soft, flat surface; cushion the head.
  • Turn the child on the side (recovery position) to keep the airway clear and let saliva drain; loosen tight clothing.
  • Do not put anything in the mouth (no spoon, finger or water), do not restrain movements and do not give anything by mouth.
  • Give rescue medication (buccal midazolam) if prescribed and the seizure lasts more than 5 minutes.

After the seizure – keep the child in the recovery position until fully awake; check breathing; reassure; let the child rest.

  • Seek emergency help if the seizure lasts more than 5 minutes, recurs, breathing is difficult, the child is injured, or it is the first seizure.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: Master Kabir, aged 18 months and weighing 10 kg, fell from a height and sustained a fracture of the shaft of the right femur. He is placed on Gallows (Bryant's) traction. (a) Explain the special features of fractures in children and list the common types. (4 marks) (b) Explain the principle of Gallows traction and describe the nursing care of Kabir while on traction. (7 marks) (c) Describe the care of a child in a hip spica cast and the discharge teaching of the parents. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Gallows (Bryant's) traction for fracture femur in a child under two years
labels: both legs suspended vertically by skin traction from an overhead beam
hips flexed at 90 degrees with knees straight
buttocks just clear of the mattress
child's body weight acting as countertraction

answer_html:
(a) Special features of fractures in children and common types (4 marks)

Special features

  1. Bones are more flexible and porous with a thick, strong periosteum – they often bend or break incompletely (greenstick, torus and plastic bowing fractures).
  2. Rapid healing – the active periosteum forms callus quickly (a femoral shaft fracture in an infant heals in about 3–4 weeks, compared with 3 months in an adult); non-union is rare.
  3. Remarkable remodelling – mild angulation and overriding correct with growth, especially in young children and near the growth plate; femoral fractures may even overgrow by 1–2 cm, so slight overlap is accepted.
  4. Growth plate (physis) injuries – the growth plate is weaker than ligaments and bone, so children get physeal fractures (Salter–Harris) rather than sprains; these may cause growth arrest, shortening or angular deformity.
  5. Joint stiffness is uncommon after immobilisation.
  6. Assessment is difficult – a young child cannot describe pain; he may simply cry, refuse to use the limb or refuse to walk.
  7. Neurovascular complications – for example Volkmann's ischaemic contracture after supracondylar fracture of the humerus.
  8. Non-accidental injury must be considered – a fracture in a non-walking infant, spiral femoral fracture in an infant, metaphyseal "corner" fractures, posterior rib fractures, multiple fractures of different ages, delay in seeking care or an inconsistent history.

Common types

  • Incomplete – greenstick (one cortex breaks, the other bends), torus or buckle (cortex buckles under compression), plastic deformation (bending without a visible break).
  • Complete – transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted.
  • Physeal (epiphyseal) injuries – Salter–Harris types I to V.
  • Common sites – distal radius (the commonest), clavicle (including birth injury), supracondylar humerus (age 3–10 years), forearm bones, femoral shaft (toddlers after falls; older children in road accidents), tibia ("toddler's fracture").

(b) Gallows traction and nursing care of Kabir (7 marks)

Principle of Gallows (Bryant's) traction

  • A form of skin traction applied to both legs (the unaffected leg too, to keep the pelvis level and the child stable).
  • The legs are suspended vertically from an overhead beam with the hips flexed to 90 degrees and the knees straight.
  • The buttocks are lifted just clear of the mattress – enough to slide a flat hand underneath – so that the child's own body weight provides countertraction, keeping the fracture fragments aligned and relieving muscle spasm.
  • Indication – fracture of the shaft of the femur in children under 2 years of age and below about 12–15 kg; in heavier or older children it is not used because of the risk of vascular compromise.
  • It is usually maintained for 3–4 weeks until callus forms, followed by a hip spica cast if needed.

Nursing care of Kabir on Gallows traction

1. Maintaining effective traction

  • Ropes run freely in the pulley grooves; knots are secure and away from the pulleys; weights hang freely and do not touch the floor or bed.
  • Buttocks just off the bed, legs vertical and the body in straight alignment; check every hour and after every care activity.
  • Bandages are smooth, firm and not slipping; do not remove or adjust the traction without orders.

2. Neurovascular observation of both legs (every hour initially, then 2–4-hourly)

  • Colour, warmth, capillary refill, dorsalis pedis pulse, swelling, movement of toes and sensation.
  • Remember the five Ps – pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia and paralysis; report pale, cold or blue feet, absent pulses, numbness or inability to move the toes immediately (vascular compromise or compartment syndrome).
  • Watch for pressure on the common peroneal nerve at the head of the fibula (foot drop).

3. Skin care and prevention of pressure injury

  • Inspect the skin under and around the traction tapes daily for redness, blisters or allergy; check the heels, malleoli and Achilles tendon area.
  • Care of the back, shoulders, sacrum and occiput, which bear the body weight; keep the sheet wrinkle-free and dry.

4. Safety and restraint

  • A jacket restraint or harness as per hospital policy prevents the toddler from turning, sitting up or slipping; check that it does not restrict breathing.
  • Cot sides up; no loose objects in the cot.

5. Hygiene and elimination

  • Bed bath; frequent nappy changes and perineal care; keep the traction bandages dry.
  • Prevent constipation – adequate fluids, fruits and fibre; record bowel movements and urine output.

6. Nutrition and fluids

  • Feed carefully in the lying position with the head supported and turned; small amounts at a time to prevent aspiration.
  • A diet rich in protein, calcium and vitamin D for bone healing; plenty of fluids.

7. Pain relief and comfort – analgesics (paracetamol, ibuprofen) as ordered, especially in the first days; gentle handling; comfort by the mother.

8. Respiratory care – encourage play that promotes deep breathing (blowing bubbles, whistles); observe for chest infection.

9. Growth, development and play – hang colourful toys and mobiles within reach; music, picture books, talking and singing; encourage the mother to stay and care for him; maintain his usual routines to prevent regression and boredom.

10. Psychological support of the family – explain the purpose of traction; involve the parents in care; if injury does not match the history, follow the child-protection procedure sensitively.

(c) Hip spica cast care and discharge teaching (4 marks)

Care of the child in a hip spica cast

  • Drying – a plaster cast takes 24–48 hours to dry; leave it uncovered, support it on pillows with waterproof covers, turn the child every 2 hours for even drying; handle the wet cast with the palms, not fingertips (dents cause pressure sores); do not use heaters.
  • Neurovascular checks of the toes – colour, warmth, movement, swelling, sensation.
  • Edges – smooth and padded ("petalled" with tape); check for rubbing; there should be room for two fingers between the abdomen and the cast.
  • Skin – inspect the skin at the edges daily; never insert objects inside to scratch; no powders or lotions under the cast; report a foul smell, discharge, hot spots or fever.
  • Toileting – line the perineal opening with waterproof tape; tuck a small nappy under the cast edges and put a larger nappy over it; change often; keep the head end slightly raised so urine flows away from the cast.
  • Positioning – change position every 2–4 hours (back, prone, side) using pillows; never lift the child by the abduction bar.
  • Feeding – small, frequent meals (the cast compresses the abdomen); prevent constipation; watch for vomiting and abdominal distension (cast syndrome).
  • Play – prone on a wedge or bean bag to play; toys within reach; outings in an adapted pram or wagon.

Discharge teaching of the parents

  • All the points of cast care above; safe lifting and carrying; an adapted car seat or stroller.
  • Report immediately – swelling, blue or pale toes, numbness, severe pain, foul odour, discharge, cracks or softening of the cast, fever, breathing difficulty or persistent vomiting.
  • Keep follow-up appointments for X-ray and cast removal (usually about 6 weeks).
  • After removal – wash the skin gently, apply moisturiser, do not scrub off dry skin; stiffness and a slightly odd gait settle with normal play within weeks.
  • Home safety to prevent further falls (window guards, stair gates, supervision).

Nursing importance Children on traction or in spica casts depend entirely on the nurse for safety, comfort and development. Correct maintenance of traction, frequent neurovascular checks, meticulous skin and nappy care and creative play prevent complications, and thorough teaching enables parents to care for the child confidently at home.

Conclusion Fractures in children differ from those in adults because bones are flexible, heal and remodel fast, and growth plates may be injured; non-accidental injury must always be considered. Femoral shaft fractures in children under 2 years like Kabir are treated with Gallows traction using body weight as countertraction, followed by a hip spica cast. Nursing care centres on effective traction, neurovascular observation, skin and elimination care, nutrition, play and parent education.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: Explain congenital talipes equinovarus (club foot) and its management.
answer_html:
Definition Congenital talipes equinovarus (CTEV, club foot) is a congenital deformity of the foot in which the foot is turned downwards and inwards. It is one of the commonest musculoskeletal birth defects (about 1–2 per 1,000 live births); boys are affected twice as often and it is bilateral in about half.

Components (CAVE)

  • Cavus – high arch of the midfoot.
  • Adductus – forefoot turned inwards.
  • Varus – heel turned inwards.
  • Equinus – foot pointing downwards (tight Achilles tendon).

Types and causes

  • Postural (positional) – due to intrauterine position; flexible and passively correctable; responds to stretching.
  • Idiopathic (structural) – rigid; the commonest true club foot; multifactorial (genetic and environmental).
  • Syndromic or neurogenic – with spina bifida, arthrogryposis, cerebral palsy; more resistant.

Assessment – examination of every newborn's feet; severity graded by the Pirani score (0–6); look for other anomalies (spine, hips).

Management

  • Ponseti method – the treatment of choice, started in the first weeks of life:
    1. Gentle manipulation and serial long-leg plaster casts changed every week (usually 5–7 casts) to correct the deformity step by step.
    2. Percutaneous Achilles tenotomy (in most children) to correct the equinus, followed by a final cast for 3 weeks.
    3. Foot abduction brace (shoes attached to a bar, turned outwards) worn 23 hours a day for 3 months, then at night and nap times until 4–5 years of age to prevent relapse.
  • Surgery (soft-tissue release, tendon transfer) for resistant, neglected or relapsed cases.
  • Club foot is among the birth defects screened under RBSK, and free treatment is available in many government centres.

Nursing care

  • Early detection at birth and referral to start casting early.
  • Cast care – check the toes for colour, warmth, swelling and movement; keep the cast clean and dry; elevate the legs; watch for slipping of the cast (toes disappearing into the cast) and report.
  • Brace care – teach parents to put on the brace correctly, check the skin for pressure marks, use cotton socks, and never stop the brace early (the commonest cause of relapse).
  • Reassure the parents that with proper treatment most children walk normally; encourage follow-up.

Conclusion Club foot is a congenital deformity with cavus, adductus, varus and equinus. Early treatment by the Ponseti method – serial casting, Achilles tenotomy and a foot abduction brace – corrects most cases without major surgery, and the nurse's role in cast care and in ensuring brace compliance is vital.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: Explain developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) and its management.
answer_html:
Definition Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) is a spectrum of abnormal development of the hip joint, ranging from a shallow acetabulum (dysplasia) to partial displacement (subluxation) and complete dislocation of the femoral head. It was earlier called congenital dislocation of the hip.

Risk factors

  • Female sex (4–6 times more), first-born, breech presentation, family history, oligohydramnios.
  • Tight swaddling with the legs straight and pressed together.
  • Associated foot deformities and torticollis; the left hip is affected more often.

Clinical features

  • Newborn to 3 months
    • Ortolani test – a dislocated hip is reduced with a "clunk" on abduction.
    • Barlow test – an unstable hip is dislocated on adduction with gentle backward pressure.
  • After 3 months
    • Limited abduction of the hip (the most reliable sign).
    • Asymmetrical thigh and gluteal skin folds, apparent shortening of the leg (Galeazzi sign – the knee is lower on the affected side when hips and knees are flexed).
  • Walking child
    • Limp, Trendelenburg gait (waddling gait if bilateral), toe walking, increased lumbar lordosis.

Diagnosis

  • Ultrasound of the hips in infants below 4–6 months (the femoral head is still cartilage).
  • X-ray of the pelvis after 4–6 months.

Management (depends on age)

  • 0–6 months – Pavlik harness, which holds the hips flexed and abducted so the femoral head stays in the acetabulum and the socket deepens; worn full time for about 6–12 weeks with ultrasound checks.
  • 6–18 months – closed reduction under anaesthesia (with adductor tenotomy if needed) and a hip spica cast for about 3 months.
  • Above 18 months – open reduction, often with pelvic or femoral osteotomy.
  • Complications – avascular necrosis of the femoral head, re-dislocation, femoral nerve palsy (harness), early arthritis.

Nursing care

  • Screening – Ortolani and Barlow tests at the newborn examination and hip checks at immunisation visits; refer infants with risk factors for ultrasound.
  • Pavlik harness teaching – keep the harness on as instructed; do not adjust straps; check the skin under straps daily; sponge bathe; put nappies under the straps; dress clothes over the harness.
  • Spica cast care – neurovascular checks, skin and nappy care, positioning and feeding as for any spica cast.
  • "Hip-healthy" swaddling – allow the legs to bend up and out at the hips; avoid wrapping legs straight.
  • Support the parents and stress the importance of follow-up.

Conclusion DDH is abnormal development of the hip joint, commoner in first-born girls and breech babies. Early detection by Ortolani and Barlow tests and ultrasound allows simple treatment with a Pavlik harness; later cases need reduction and spica casting or surgery, with the nurse responsible for screening and teaching harness and cast care.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: Explain otitis media in children and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Otitis media is inflammation of the middle ear. It is one of the commonest infections of childhood and an important cause of preventable hearing loss in India.

Why children are more prone

  • The Eustachian tube is shorter, wider and more horizontal, so infection spreads easily from the nasopharynx.
  • Enlarged adenoids, frequent colds, immature immunity.
  • Bottle feeding in the lying position, exposure to smoke, crowded homes and day-care centres; children with cleft palate and Down syndrome are at higher risk.

Types and clinical features

  1. Acute otitis media (AOM) – sudden ear pain; infants show ear pulling or rubbing, irritability, crying and waking at night, fever, poor feeding, vomiting; a red, bulging eardrum; if it perforates, pus discharges and the pain eases.
  2. Otitis media with effusion (OME, "glue ear") – painless fluid in the middle ear after AOM or with adenoid enlargement; causes hearing loss, speech delay, inattention and poor school performance.
  3. Chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM) – persistent or recurrent ear discharge through a perforated eardrum for more than 2–6 weeks, with hearing loss; the "unsafe" type with cholesteatoma can cause serious complications.

Complications – perforation, conductive hearing loss, mastoiditis (swelling behind the ear pushing the pinna forward), facial nerve palsy, meningitis, brain abscess.

Management

  • AOM – analgesics (paracetamol or ibuprofen); amoxicillin for 5–10 days (amoxicillin–clavulanate if not improving); mild cases in older children may be observed for 48–72 hours under supervision; decongestants are not useful in young children.
  • OME – watchful waiting for about 3 months; grommets (ventilation tubes), with or without adenoidectomy, if fluid and hearing loss persist.
  • CSOM – regular aural toilet (dry mopping), topical antibiotic drops (ciprofloxacin), keeping the ear dry; tympanoplasty or mastoidectomy for persistent or unsafe disease.
  • Under IMNCI, a child with tender swelling behind the ear (mastoiditis) is referred urgently.

Nursing management

  • Pain and fever relief – analgesics, warmth over the ear, comfort.
  • Teach ear wicking – roll clean, soft cloth or tissue into a wick, insert gently into the ear, remove when wet and repeat until dry, three times a day; never use cotton buds deep in the ear, oil or home remedies.
  • Instilling ear drops – warm the bottle in the hand; for children under 3 years pull the pinna down and back, for older children up and back; keep the head tilted for a few minutes.
  • Keep the ear dry – during bathing plug the ear with cotton smeared with petroleum jelly; no swimming with a perforation.
  • Feeding – breastfeed or bottle feed in an upright position; never prop bottles.
  • Prevention – breastfeeding, avoiding smoke, prompt treatment of colds, pneumococcal and influenza vaccination.
  • Hearing assessment for children with recurrent or persistent ear problems; liaison with teachers; services under the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Deafness.

Conclusion Otitis media is common in children because of their short, horizontal Eustachian tubes. Acute infection needs pain relief and antibiotics, glue ear may need grommets, and chronic discharge needs dry mopping and drops. Nurses play a key role in teaching ear care, correct feeding position and prevention, and in identifying hearing loss early.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: Explain atopic dermatitis (infantile eczema) and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Atopic dermatitis (atopic eczema) is a chronic, relapsing, intensely itchy inflammatory skin disease that usually begins in infancy. It is part of the atopic triad (eczema, asthma, allergic rhinitis) and often runs in families; about 10–20% of children are affected at some time.

Causes and triggers

  • Defective skin barrier (filaggrin gene defects) → dry skin that loses water and lets irritants and allergens in; immune dysregulation (allergic tendency).
  • Triggers – soaps, detergents, heat and sweating, woollen and synthetic clothes, dust mites, pet dander, infections (Staphylococcus aureus), dry weather, emotional stress; food allergy in some infants.

Clinical features

  • Intense itching – the hallmark; scratching worsens the rash (itch–scratch cycle) and disturbs sleep.
  • Infantile phase (2 months–2 years) – red, oozing, crusted patches on the cheeks, forehead, scalp and extensor surfaces of limbs; the nappy area is usually spared.
  • Childhood phase (2–12 years) – dry, thickened (lichenified) patches in the flexures – elbow and knee creases, neck, wrists, ankles.
  • Dry skin all over; darkening or lightening of skin after healing.

Complications

  • Secondary bacterial infection (crusting, pus).
  • Eczema herpeticum – widespread painful punched-out blisters due to herpes simplex – an emergency.
  • Sleep loss, irritability, poor school performance, psychological stress for the family.

Management

  1. Emollients (the cornerstone) – apply liberally at least twice daily and within 3 minutes after bathing ("soak and seal"), even when the skin looks clear.
  2. Bathing – short (5–10 minutes) lukewarm baths, soap-free cleanser, pat dry gently.
  3. Topical corticosteroids for flares – low-potency (hydrocortisone) on the face and folds, moderate potency on the body, applied thinly once or twice daily for short periods (measured by the fingertip unit), then tapered.
  4. Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus) for the face and flexures in children above 2 years.
  5. Oral antihistamines (sedating type at night) to relieve itching and improve sleep; wet-wrap therapy for severe flares.
  6. Treat infection – antibiotics for bacterial infection; acyclovir for eczema herpeticum.
  7. Severe cases – phototherapy or systemic drugs under a dermatologist.

Nursing management and parent education

  • Demonstrate application of emollients and steroid creams (amount, direction of hair growth, gentle technique); clear the fears about steroid creams when used correctly.
  • Prevent scratching – keep nails short, cotton mittens for infants at night, distraction and play.
  • Avoid triggers – loose cotton clothing, mild detergents and thorough rinsing of clothes, avoid wool and overheating, reduce dust.
  • Do not restrict foods unnecessarily – only under medical advice when a food allergy is proven.
  • Observe for infection and eczema herpeticum and report early; continue routine immunisation.
  • Emotional support; explain that eczema often improves with age and that consistent skin care controls it.

Conclusion Atopic dermatitis is a chronic itchy eczema of infancy and childhood caused by a skin barrier defect and allergic tendency. Daily emollients, gentle bathing, short courses of topical steroids, avoidance of triggers and treatment of infection control it well, and the nurse's teaching of correct skin care to parents is the key to success.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: Explain squint and amblyopia in children, with the role of the nurse in vision screening.
answer_html:
Squint (strabismus)

  • Definition – misalignment of the eyes, so that both eyes do not look at the same object at the same time.
  • Types – convergent (esotropia, eye turned in), divergent (exotropia, eye turned out), vertical; concomitant (non-paralytic, usual in children) or paralytic (due to nerve palsy).
  • Pseudosquint – a broad nasal bridge or epicanthic folds make the eyes look crossed in infants; the light reflex is normal.
  • Occasional misalignment is normal up to 3–4 months; any squint persisting beyond 4–6 months needs referral.
  • Causes – refractive errors (especially hypermetropia – accommodative esotropia), unequal refraction between the two eyes, congenital, cataract, retinoblastoma, prematurity, neurological disorders.

Amblyopia ("lazy eye")

  • Definition – reduced vision in an otherwise healthy eye because the brain did not receive a clear image from it during early childhood; the brain suppresses the image from the squinting or blurred eye.
  • Causes – squint, unequal or high refractive errors, cataract or ptosis blocking vision.
  • It can be treated only in early childhood (best before 7–8 years); later the vision loss becomes permanent.

Refractive errors in children – myopia (short sight, increasing with screen use and less outdoor play), hypermetropia and astigmatism; signs – holding books close, squinting, headaches, rubbing eyes, poor school performance.

Assessment

  • Red reflex test in every newborn and infant – an absent or white reflex (leukocoria) suggests cataract or retinoblastoma (urgent referral).
  • Hirschberg corneal light reflex test and cover–uncover test for squint.
  • Age-appropriate visual acuity tests; refraction after cycloplegic eye drops.

Management

  • Correct refractive errors with spectacles, worn all the time.
  • Treat amblyopia – occlusion therapy (patching the good eye) for prescribed hours daily, or atropine eye drops in the good eye (penalisation), to force the brain to use the weaker eye.
  • Squint surgery (adjusting eye muscles) for residual squint; treat cataract or other causes.

Role of the nurse in vision screening

  • Perform the red reflex test at newborn and infant examinations; observe eye alignment and visual behaviour (fixing and following).
  • School eye screening under RBSK and the National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment, which provides free spectacles to school children with refractive errors.
  • Teach patching – patch the good eye as prescribed (never the weak eye), make it fun with stickers and play, protect the skin; encourage wearing spectacles regularly and caring for them.
  • Health education – at least 1–2 hours of outdoor play daily, limit screen time, good lighting for reading; regular follow-up.

Conclusion Squint and refractive errors in children can lead to amblyopia, a permanent loss of vision if not treated early. Red reflex testing, regular vision screening, spectacles, patching and timely surgery preserve vision, and nurses play an important role in early detection and in ensuring compliance with treatment.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: What are the Ortolani and Barlow tests?
answer_html:
Both are clinical tests for developmental dysplasia of the hip, done on a relaxed baby lying on the back, one hip at a time, up to about 3 months of age.

  • Barlow test (dislocation test) – the hip is flexed to 90 degrees and adducted, and gentle backward pressure is applied on the knee; if the femoral head slips out of the acetabulum, the hip is dislocatable (unstable).
  • Ortolani test (reduction test) – the flexed hip is gently abducted while the greater trochanter is lifted forward with the fingers; a "clunk" felt as the femoral head slips back into the acetabulum means the hip was dislocated and is reducible.
  • A positive test needs ultrasound and referral; after 3 months, limited abduction becomes the main sign.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: What is a Pavlik harness? State the nursing points.
answer_html:
A Pavlik harness is a soft fabric splint with chest and shoulder straps and stirrups that holds the infant's hips flexed (about 90–100 degrees) and abducted, keeping the femoral head in the acetabulum so that the hip can develop normally. It is used for developmental dysplasia of the hip in infants under 6 months, usually for 6–12 weeks full time. Nursing points

  • Do not remove or adjust the straps unless instructed; check the fit at every visit.
  • Inspect the skin under the straps daily, especially behind the knees and in the groin; sponge bathe.
  • Put the nappy under the straps; dress clothes over the harness.
  • Watch for inability to kick the leg (femoral nerve palsy) and report; keep follow-up ultrasound visits.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: Differentiate between greenstick and torus fractures.
answer_html: Both are incomplete fractures typical of children, because their bones are soft and flexible with a thick periosteum. | Greenstick fracture | Torus (buckle) fracture | |---|---| | The bone bends; the cortex on one side breaks while the opposite cortex is bent but intact – like bending a green twig | The cortex buckles or bulges under compression without a clear break | | Usually in the shaft of the radius, ulna or clavicle | Usually near the metaphysis, commonly the distal radius after a fall on the outstretched hand | | May need reduction to correct angulation; plaster cast for 4–6 weeks | Stable; heals quickly in a splint or short cast for about 3 weeks |

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: Write the Salter–Harris classification of growth plate injuries.
answer_html:
The Salter–Harris classification describes fractures involving the growth plate (physis) in children; the higher the type, the greater the risk of growth disturbance.

  • Type I – S (Straight across / Separated) – fracture through the growth plate only.
  • Type II – A (Above) – through the growth plate and a piece of metaphysis above it (commonest).
  • Type III – L (Lower) – through the growth plate and the epiphysis below, into the joint.
  • Type IV – T (Through) – through metaphysis, growth plate and epiphysis.
  • Type V – R (Rammed / cRush) – crushing of the growth plate; often missed on X-ray; high risk of growth arrest.
  • Types III and IV usually need accurate (often surgical) reduction; follow-up for limb-length discrepancy and deformity.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: What is Perthes disease?
answer_html:
Perthes (Legg–Calvé–Perthes) disease is avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children, usually between 4 and 10 years, and about four to five times commoner in boys; the cause is unknown.

  • Features – a limp, with pain in the hip, thigh or knee (referred pain), and limited abduction and internal rotation of the hip; X-ray shows increased density, fragmentation and flattening of the femoral head, which heals by re-ossification over 2–4 years.
  • Management – aims to keep the femoral head "contained" in the acetabulum and preserve movement: rest from strenuous activity, analgesics, physiotherapy, abduction bracing or casting, and osteotomy in older children; the outlook is better when it begins before about 6 years.
  • Nursing care – care of the brace or cast and skin, pain relief, safe mobility, schooling and emotional support.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: Baby Anaya, aged 2 years and not immunised, is admitted with high fever, cough, running nose and red watery eyes, followed by a reddish rash that began behind the ears and spread to the face and body. She is diagnosed with measles. (a) Explain the cause, mode of spread and clinical stages of measles. (5 marks) (b) List the complications of measles. (3 marks) (c) Describe the nursing care of Anaya in hospital and at home, and the prevention of measles. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Clinical course of measles
labels: Koplik's spots on buccal mucosa) – rash on day 4 starting behind the ears and hairline
trunk and limbs over 3 days – fading in the same order with brownish staining and fine scaling

answer_html:
(a) Cause, mode of spread and clinical stages (5 marks)

Cause Measles (rubeola) is an acute, highly contagious viral disease caused by the measles virus, an RNA virus of the genus Morbillivirus (family Paramyxoviridae). There is only one serotype, and one attack gives lifelong immunity. Malnourished, vitamin A-deficient and unimmunised children of 6 months to 5 years suffer the most severe disease.

Mode of spread

  • Droplet and airborne spread – the virus is present in nasal and throat secretions and remains suspended in the air of a closed room for up to 2 hours.
  • Direct contact with secretions.
  • It is one of the most contagious human diseases – about 9 out of 10 non-immune contacts become infected.
  • Incubation period – 10–14 days (7–21 days).
  • Infectious period – from 4 days before to 4 days after the appearance of the rash.

Clinical stages

  1. Incubation stage – no symptoms.
  2. Prodromal (catarrhal) stage – 3–5 days; the most infectious stage
    • High fever, malaise, irritability.
    • The "three Cs" – cough, coryza (running nose) and conjunctivitis (red, watery eyes with photophobia).
    • Koplik's spots – tiny bluish-white spots ("grains of salt") on a red base on the buccal mucosa opposite the lower molars, appearing 1–2 days before the rash – pathognomonic.
  3. Eruptive (rash) stage
    • Around the 4th day of fever, a dusky red maculopapular rash appears behind the ears and along the hairline, spreads to the face, neck, trunk and then the limbs over 3 days (cephalocaudal spread), and becomes blotchy and confluent.
    • Fever is highest when the rash appears and falls 2–3 days later; Koplik's spots disappear.
  4. Convalescent (post-measles) stage
    • The rash fades in the same order, leaving brownish staining and fine branny scaling (not on palms and soles).
    • The child is weak and loses weight; immunity is depressed for weeks to months, so infections, diarrhoea and tuberculosis are common after measles.

(b) Complications (3 marks)

  • Respiratory – pneumonia (viral or secondary bacterial – the commonest cause of death), otitis media (the commonest complication), laryngotracheobronchitis (croup), bronchiolitis.
  • Gastrointestinal – diarrhoea and dehydration, stomatitis and mouth ulcers, cancrum oris (noma) in malnourished children.
  • Nutritional – weight loss, precipitation of severe malnutrition (kwashiorkor).
  • Eye – conjunctivitis, keratitis, corneal ulcer, xerophthalmia and keratomalacia leading to blindness (vitamin A deficiency) – measles is a major cause of childhood blindness.
  • Neurological – febrile seizures, acute encephalitis (about 1 in 1,000), and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) – a rare, fatal degenerative brain disease appearing 7–10 years later.
  • Others – flare-up of tuberculosis, thrombocytopenia, myocarditis, death.

(c) Nursing care in hospital and at home, and prevention (7 marks)

Specific management

  • There is no specific antiviral drug; treatment is supportive.
  • Vitamin A – two doses 24 hours apart (50,000 IU below 6 months, 1,00,000 IU at 6–11 months, 2,00,000 IU at 12 months or more), with a third dose 2–4 weeks later if there are eye signs of vitamin A deficiency. It reduces complications and deaths.
  • Antibiotics for secondary bacterial pneumonia, otitis media or other infections; ORS and zinc for diarrhoea; paracetamol for fever.

Nursing care in hospital

  1. Isolation (airborne precautions) – a single, well-ventilated room (negative pressure if available) with the door closed, until 4 days after the onset of rash; only immune staff should care for her; N95 respirators for staff whose immunity is uncertain; keep away from other children, especially infants and immunocompromised children.
  2. Fever – tepid sponging, light cotton clothing, paracetamol; plenty of fluids; seizure precautions.
  3. Respiratory care – monitor respiratory rate, chest indrawing and SpO2; propped-up position; clear the nose with saline drops and gentle suction; oxygen and antibiotics as ordered.
  4. Eye care – clean the eyes with sterile saline or boiled cooled water, wiping from the inner to the outer canthus with a separate swab for each eye; keep the room light dim for comfort (photophobia); prevent rubbing; antibiotic eye drops if there is discharge; observe for corneal clouding.
  5. Mouth care – clean the mouth with saline after feeds; apply petroleum jelly to dry lips; soft, bland, cool foods if the mouth is sore.
  6. Skin care – daily lukewarm sponge bath; calamine lotion for itching; short nails; clean linen and loose clothes.
  7. Nutrition and hydration – continue breastfeeding; give high-calorie, high-protein soft foods in small frequent meals; extra fluids and ORS; weigh regularly.
  8. Ear care – observe for ear discharge and pain; clean discharge by dry mopping.
  9. Observation for complications – fast breathing, chest indrawing, diarrhoea, dehydration, ear discharge, convulsions, drowsiness, eye changes – report early.
  10. Rest, comfort and diversion – quiet play, the mother's presence and reassurance.
  11. Counselling against harmful beliefs – some families stop bathing, feeding or treatment during measles believing it to be a divine visitation; explain the importance of nutrition, hygiene and medical care.

Home care advice

  • Keep the child at home and away from other children, infants and pregnant women until 4 days after the rash appears; a well-ventilated room.
  • Continue breastfeeding and feeding; extra fluids; eye, mouth and skin care as above; complete the vitamin A doses.
  • Bring the child back immediately if there is fast or difficult breathing, chest indrawing, inability to drink, convulsions, drowsiness, eye clouding or pain, ear discharge, or diarrhoea with dehydration.
  • After recovery – extra food for weight gain; watch for cough and weight loss (tuberculosis) and other infections for some weeks.

Prevention of measles

  • Measles–rubella (MR) vaccine under the Universal Immunization Programme – first dose at 9–12 months and second dose at 16–24 months, with catch-up through Mission Indradhanush and campaigns; at least 95% coverage with two doses is needed to stop transmission.
  • Case-based surveillance of every child with fever and rash, notification and outbreak response.
  • Post-exposure protection – MR vaccine within 72 hours of exposure for susceptible contacts above 6 months; immunoglobulin within 6 days for infants under 6 months, immunocompromised children and pregnant contacts, as advised.
  • Vitamin A supplementation and good nutrition; health education to families.
  • India is working towards measles and rubella elimination together with other countries of the WHO South-East Asia Region.

Nursing importance Deaths from measles are largely due to pneumonia, diarrhoea and malnutrition. Isolation, vitamin A, careful eye, mouth and nutritional care, early detection of complications and, above all, ensuring two doses of MR vaccine for every child are the nurse's main contributions.

Conclusion Measles is a highly contagious viral disease spread by droplets and air, passing through incubation, prodromal (fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik's spots), eruptive (cephalocaudal maculopapular rash) and convalescent stages. Its complications – pneumonia, otitis media, diarrhoea, malnutrition, blindness and encephalitis – can be fatal. Anaya needs airborne isolation, vitamin A, supportive nursing care and good home care, while two doses of MR vaccine prevent the disease.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: (a) Explain why children are more susceptible to communicable diseases. (3 marks) (b) Prepare a table showing the incubation period, mode of spread and period of isolation of common communicable diseases of childhood. (5 marks) (c) Describe the role of the nurse in the hospital care, home care, control and prevention of communicable diseases in children. (7 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Why children are more susceptible (3 marks)

  1. Immature immune system – infants and young children have not yet built immunity through previous exposure.
  2. Loss of maternal antibodies after about 6 months of age.
  3. Incomplete or missed immunisation, and some infections occurring before the age of vaccination.
  4. Close contact in families, crèches, anganwadis and schools; children share toys, food and utensils.
  5. Hygiene habits not yet developed – hand-to-mouth behaviour, crawling and playing on the floor, poor hand washing, nose-picking.
  6. Malnutrition and micronutrient deficiency (vitamin A, zinc, iron) lower resistance; lack of breastfeeding.
  7. Environmental factors – overcrowding, poor ventilation, unsafe water, poor sanitation, open defecation, mosquito breeding.
  8. Special conditions – HIV infection, chronic illness, steroid or cancer therapy; temporary immune suppression after measles.
  9. Low awareness of parents about prevention and early care.

(b) Incubation period, mode of spread and period of isolation (5 marks)

Disease Incubation period Mode of spread Period of isolation / exclusion from school
Measles 10–14 days Droplet, airborne Until 4 days after onset of rash
Rubella (German measles) 14–21 days Droplet Until 7 days after onset of rash; keep away from pregnant women
Chickenpox 14–16 days (10–21) Airborne, droplet, contact with vesicle fluid Until all lesions are crusted (about 5–7 days after rash)
Mumps 16–18 days Droplet, saliva Until 5 days after onset of parotid swelling
Diphtheria 2–5 days Droplet, contact Until two negative throat cultures 24 hours apart after completing antibiotics
Pertussis (whooping cough) 7–10 days Droplet Until 5 days after starting antibiotics (3 weeks from onset of cough if untreated)
Poliomyelitis 7–14 days Faeco-oral, droplet Enteric precautions; virus is shed in stools for several weeks
Hepatitis A 2–6 weeks (about 4 weeks) Faeco-oral Until 1 week after onset of jaundice
Typhoid fever 10–14 days Faeco-oral (food, water) Enteric precautions until stool cultures are negative after treatment
Influenza 1–4 days Droplet About 7 days, or until 24 hours after fever subsides
Scarlet fever / streptococcal sore throat 2–5 days Droplet Until 24 hours after starting antibiotics
Pulmonary tuberculosis (adolescent, smear-positive) Weeks to years Airborne Airborne precautions until about 2 weeks of effective treatment and clinical improvement (young children are rarely infectious)

(c) Role of the nurse (7 marks)

1. Hospital care

  • Early identification and triage – a separate area for children with fever and rash, cough or diarrhoea so that others are not exposed.
  • Isolation according to the mode of spread (transmission-based precautions)
    • Airborne (measles, chickenpox, TB) – single room with negative pressure or good ventilation, door closed, N95 respirators.
    • Droplet (diphtheria, pertussis, mumps, influenza, meningococcal infection) – single room or cohort, surgical masks within 1 metre.
    • Contact / enteric (diarrhoea, hepatitis A, typhoid, polio) – gloves and gown, safe disposal of stools and nappies.
  • Standard precautions for all – hand hygiene at the five moments, safe injection practices, biomedical waste segregation, disinfection of toys, equipment and surfaces, safe handling of linen.
  • Cohorting of children with the same infection; restricting visitors; immune staff for measles and chickenpox; pregnant staff avoid caring for rubella, chickenpox and parvovirus infections.
  • Specific and supportive care – antitoxins and antibiotics as prescribed; control of fever; hydration and nutrition; care of eyes, mouth, skin and airway; monitoring for complications.
  • Play and psychological care in isolation – isolation can frighten and bore a child; allow the mother to stay, provide washable toys, books and music, explain the reason for masks and gowns.

2. Home care (teaching the family)

  • Keep the sick child in a separate, well-ventilated room with one main caregiver; keep other children, infants and pregnant women away.
  • Hand washing with soap; covering the mouth and nose while coughing; separate towels and utensils; safe disposal of secretions and stools; boiling or washing of soiled clothes.
  • Fluids, feeding, fever care and skin care; recognition of danger signs and when to return.
  • Keep the child away from school until the isolation period is over and inform the school.

3. Control of communicable diseases

  • Notification – report notifiable diseases (measles, diphtheria, pertussis, acute flaccid paralysis, AES, dengue, cholera and others) through the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme on the IHIP portal.
  • Surveillance – AFP surveillance (every child under 15 years with sudden weakness of a limb – two stool samples 24 hours apart within 14 days), case-based measles–rubella surveillance, fever surveillance by ASHAs.
  • Contact tracing and protection – identify, examine and immunise contacts; chemoprophylaxis as advised (for example, erythromycin and a vaccine booster for diphtheria contacts, azithromycin for household contacts of pertussis, rifampicin for meningococcal contacts).
  • Support outbreak investigation, sample collection and transport in the cold chain, and community mobilisation.
  • Environmental measures – safe water, chlorination, sanitation, vector control.

4. Prevention

  • Immunisation of every child according to the Universal Immunization Programme (BCG, OPV, hepatitis B, pentavalent, rotavirus, PCV, fIPV, MR, JE in endemic districts, DPT and Td boosters), tracking dropouts and recording doses digitally (U-WIN); Mission Indradhanush for left-out children.
  • Vitamin A supplementation, breastfeeding and good nutrition; biannual deworming.
  • Health education – hand washing, safe water and food, toilet use, cough etiquette, mosquito control, early care-seeking.
  • School and anganwadi health – screening, health talks, hand-washing stations and exclusion of infectious children.

Nursing diagnoses commonly used for a child with a communicable disease | Nursing diagnosis | Key interventions | |---|---| | Risk of spread of infection to others | Correct isolation, hand hygiene, PPE, safe disposal of secretions and excreta, disinfection, contact tracing | | Hyperthermia | Tepid sponging, light clothing, paracetamol, extra fluids, seizure precautions | | Risk of deficient fluid volume | Oral fluids and ORS, intake–output chart, daily weight, IV fluids as ordered | | Impaired skin and mucous membrane integrity | Skin, mouth and eye care; short nails; calamine for itching | | Imbalanced nutrition | Continue breastfeeding, small frequent energy-dense meals, vitamin A and zinc as prescribed | | Social isolation and anxiety of child and family | Mother stays with the child, play materials, simple explanations, reassurance | | Deficient knowledge of parents | Teaching about home care, danger signs, isolation period and immunisation |

Link with community health workers – the hospital nurse informs the ANM, ASHA or school health team about notifiable cases so that contacts are screened and immunised, and the child's missed vaccines are completed after recovery.

Nursing importance Nurses are the link between the sick child, the family, the hospital and the public health system. Prompt isolation, strict infection control, notification, contact tracing and, above all, complete immunisation prevent outbreaks of childhood communicable diseases.

Conclusion Children are especially susceptible to communicable diseases because of their immature immunity, close contacts, hygiene habits and nutritional problems. Knowledge of incubation and isolation periods guides isolation and school exclusion. The nurse provides safe hospital care with transmission-based precautions, teaches home care, participates in surveillance, notification and contact tracing, and promotes immunisation and hygiene for prevention.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: Explain tuberculosis in children, with special reference to diagnosis and prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction Tuberculosis (TB) in children usually results from close contact with an adult (often a family member) who has infectious pulmonary TB. Children, especially those under 5 years and malnourished or HIV-infected children, progress more often to disease and to severe forms such as TB meningitis and miliary TB. Childhood TB is often missed because its features are non-specific.

Common forms

  • Pulmonary TB – primary complex (lung focus with enlarged hilar lymph nodes), progressive primary disease, pleural effusion in older children; adult-type cavitary disease in adolescents.
  • Extrapulmonary TB – cervical lymph node TB (the commonest), TB meningitis, miliary TB, abdominal TB, bone and joint TB (spine – Pott's disease), pericardial TB.

Clinical features

  • Fever for more than 2 weeks, cough for more than 2 weeks, weight loss or failure to gain weight (growth faltering), loss of appetite, fatigue and reduced playfulness.
  • Painless matted neck glands, abdominal distension, limp or back stiffness, headache with vomiting and drowsiness (TBM).
  • History of contact with a TB patient is very important.

Diagnosis (NTEP approach)

  • Specimens – children cannot cough up sputum, so gastric aspirate (early morning, two consecutive days), induced sputum, stool samples, nasopharyngeal aspirate, lymph node aspirate or CSF are collected.
  • Rapid molecular tests (NAAT) – CBNAAT or Truenat, which also detect rifampicin resistance; smear microscopy and culture.
  • Chest X-ray; Mantoux (tuberculin skin) test – induration of 10 mm or more is positive (5 mm or more in HIV-infected or severely malnourished children) – or IGRA as supportive evidence of infection.
  • Histopathology of lymph nodes; CSF examination and imaging for TBM.

Treatment

  • Free treatment under the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP) with daily, weight-band paediatric fixed-dose combination (dispersible) tablets.
  • Drug-sensitive TB – intensive phase of 2 months with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol (HRZE), followed by a continuation phase of 4 months with HRE; the continuation phase is extended (total about 12 months) for TB meningitis and bone and joint TB; steroids are added for TBM.
  • Drug-resistant TB is treated with specialised regimens.
  • Nutritional support through the Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana (direct benefit transfer) and registration on the Ni-kshay portal.

Prevention

  • BCG vaccine at birth – protects mainly against severe forms (TBM and miliary TB).
  • Contact screening – every child in the household of a TB patient is screened.
  • TB preventive treatment (TPT) for child contacts after ruling out active disease – for example, 6 months of daily isoniazid, or weekly isoniazid–rifapentine (3HP) in children above 2 years, as per NTEP.
  • Early diagnosis and treatment of adult cases, good ventilation, nutrition and HIV prevention.

Role of the nurse

  • Suspect TB in children with prolonged fever, cough, weight faltering and a contact history; collect gastric aspirates correctly (early morning, before feeding).
  • Ensure adherence – teach parents to dissolve dispersible tablets in water and give them daily; involve a treatment supporter; record doses.
  • Observe side effects – jaundice, vomiting and abdominal pain (hepatotoxicity), joint pain, rash; explain that rifampicin turns urine orange-red; check vision in children on ethambutol.
  • Growth monitoring, nutrition, continuation of schooling, infection control around the adult source case, and follow-up.

Conclusion Childhood TB is usually acquired from an infected adult and presents with prolonged fever, cough and weight faltering. Diagnosis needs alternative specimens and rapid molecular tests, and treatment with daily paediatric FDCs under NTEP is highly effective. BCG, contact screening and TB preventive treatment, along with nursing support for adherence and nutrition, prevent disease and deaths.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: Explain diphtheria in children and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Diphtheria is an acute, toxin-mediated bacterial infection caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, affecting mainly the throat, tonsils, larynx and nose, characterised by a greyish-white pseudomembrane and by the effects of its exotoxin on the heart and nerves. It affects unimmunised or partially immunised children; outbreaks in older children and adolescents occur when booster doses are missed.

Spread – droplets and direct contact with secretions or skin lesions; incubation period 2–5 days.

Types and clinical features

  1. Faucial (pharyngotonsillar) diphtheria – the commonest
    • Low-grade fever, sore throat, malaise.
    • Greyish-white, adherent pseudomembrane on the tonsils and pharynx that bleeds when removed; foul breath.
    • "Bull neck" – marked swelling of the neck due to lymph node enlargement and oedema; toxic appearance.
  2. Laryngeal diphtheria – hoarseness, croupy cough and stridor, leading to airway obstruction.
  3. Nasal (anterior) diphtheria – blood-stained nasal discharge; mild.
  4. Cutaneous diphtheria – chronic ulcers.

Complications (due to toxin)

  • Myocarditis (in the 2nd week) – arrhythmias, heart block, heart failure, sudden death.
  • Neuritis (3rd–6th week) – palatal palsy (nasal voice, regurgitation of fluids through the nose), squint and blurred vision, limb weakness, diaphragmatic paralysis.
  • Airway obstruction, pneumonia, kidney failure.

Diagnosis – treatment must not be delayed for laboratory results; throat swab for Albert's stain (metachromatic granules) and culture on Loeffler's serum slope; toxin testing (Elek's test).

Management

  • Antidiphtheritic serum (ADS) as early as possible – neutralises circulating toxin; dose (20,000–1,00,000 units) depends on the site, extent and duration; given IV after a sensitivity test, with adrenaline ready for reactions.
  • Antibiotics – penicillin or erythromycin for 14 days to eliminate the organism.
  • Airway care – intubation or tracheostomy for obstruction.
  • Strict bed rest for 2–3 weeks because of myocarditis; ECG monitoring.
  • Immunise after recovery – the disease does not give reliable immunity.
  • Contacts – throat swabs, erythromycin prophylaxis and a booster dose of vaccine.

Nursing management

  • Droplet isolation until two negative cultures 24 hours apart after completing antibiotics.
  • Airway – observe for stridor, restlessness, chest retractions and cyanosis; keep oxygen, suction and a tracheostomy tray ready.
  • Cardiac monitoring – pulse rate and rhythm, BP, ECG; strict bed rest, avoid exertion, assist with all activities.
  • Feeding – soft or liquid diet; nasogastric feeding if there is palatal palsy (fluids coming out through the nose) to prevent aspiration.
  • ADS administration – sensitivity test, slow infusion, close watch for anaphylaxis; warn about serum sickness (fever, rash, joint pains after 7–10 days).
  • Mouth care, fluid balance, temperature monitoring and emotional support.
  • Prevention – DPT (as pentavalent) at 6, 10 and 14 weeks, DPT boosters at 16–24 months and 5–6 years, and Td at 10 and 16 years; tracing and completing immunisation of contacts.

Conclusion Diphtheria is a vaccine-preventable toxin-mediated disease with a characteristic bleeding pseudomembrane and a risk of airway obstruction, myocarditis and neuritis. Early ADS, antibiotics, airway care, strict bed rest and isolation, along with complete primary and booster immunisation, save lives.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: Explain pertussis (whooping cough) in infants and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Pertussis (whooping cough) is an acute, highly contagious respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis, characterised by paroxysms of severe coughing ending in a high-pitched inspiratory "whoop". It is most dangerous for young infants, who may have apnoea and die.

Spread – droplets; most infectious in the catarrhal stage; incubation period 7–10 days.

Clinical stages

  1. Catarrhal stage (1–2 weeks) – mild cold: running nose, sneezing, slight fever, mild cough – indistinguishable from a cold, but most infectious.
  2. Paroxysmal stage (2–6 weeks)
    • Bouts of rapid, repeated coughs in one breath, the face turns red or blue, the tongue protrudes and eyes bulge, followed by a forceful inspiration with a "whoop".
    • Vomiting after coughing; exhaustion; attacks are worse at night and may be triggered by feeding or crying.
    • Young infants often do not whoop – they present with apnoea, cyanosis, choking or seizures.
  3. Convalescent stage (weeks to months) – cough gradually decreases ("hundred-day cough").

Complications – pneumonia (the commonest cause of death), apnoea and hypoxic brain damage, seizures, encephalopathy, dehydration and malnutrition due to vomiting, subconjunctival haemorrhage, nosebleeds, ulcer under the tongue, umbilical and inguinal hernia, rectal prolapse, flare-up of TB, bronchiectasis.

Diagnosis – mainly clinical; marked lymphocytosis in the blood count; PCR or culture of a nasopharyngeal swab.

Management

  • Antibiotics – azithromycin for 5 days (or erythromycin, clarithromycin); started early it reduces severity, and at any stage it reduces spread.
  • Hospitalise infants, especially those below 6 months – oxygen, gentle suction, monitoring for apnoea, IV or nasogastric fluids and feeds.
  • Cough suppressants are not useful; avoid smoke and dust.
  • Household contacts – azithromycin prophylaxis (especially for infants) and completion of immunisation.

Nursing management

  • Droplet isolation until 5 days of antibiotic therapy.
  • During a paroxysm – stay with the child, hold the infant upright or leaning forward, clear mucus from the mouth and nose with gentle suction, give oxygen if cyanosed, and stimulate breathing if apnoea occurs; keep a bag and mask ready.
  • Record the paroxysms – number, duration, cyanosis, apnoea, vomiting; use an apnoea monitor or pulse oximeter for infants.
  • Nutrition and hydration – small, frequent feeds; refeed soon after vomiting (the child is usually calm after a bout); continue breastfeeding; IV or NG feeds if needed; daily weight.
  • Avoid triggers – quiet environment, minimal handling, no smoke, cluster nursing care, rest.
  • Mouth care after vomiting; observe for complications (pneumonia, convulsions, hernias).
  • Reassure parents that the cough will last weeks but will settle; teach home care and danger signs.

Prevention – pentavalent (DPT-containing) vaccine at 6, 10 and 14 weeks and DPT boosters at 16–24 months and 5–6 years under UIP; Tdap vaccination of pregnant women (where available) protects newborns; early treatment of cases and contacts.

Conclusion Pertussis causes paroxysmal coughing with a whoop and post-tussive vomiting, and in young infants apnoea and death. Azithromycin, isolation, careful suction, oxygen, feeding after vomiting and close monitoring are the essentials of nursing care, while timely DPT vaccination prevents the disease.
