question: Explain neonatal tetanus – its causes, clinical features, management and prevention.
answer_html:
Definition Neonatal tetanus (tetanus neonatorum) is tetanus occurring in a newborn within the first 28 days of life, caused by the toxin of Clostridium tetani entering through the umbilical stump. It is often called the "disease of the seventh day" because it usually begins 3–14 days after birth.

Causes and risk factors

  • Mother not immunised against tetanus (so the baby has no protective antibodies).
  • Unhygienic delivery and cord care – cutting the cord with an unclean blade or sickle, tying with dirty thread, and applying cow dung, ash, mud, oil or other substances to the stump.
  • Home delivery by untrained persons.

Clinical features (WHO case definition)

  • The baby sucks and cries normally for the first 2 days, and between day 3 and day 28 develops:
    • Inability to suck due to stiffness of the jaw (trismus), excessive crying.
    • Generalised stiffness, risus sardonicus (sardonic smile), clenched fists, opisthotonus (arching of the back).
    • Spasms or convulsions, triggered by touch, noise or light; the baby remains conscious.
  • Fever, apnoea during spasms, aspiration pneumonia and dehydration; mortality is very high.

Management

  • Quiet, dark room with minimal handling; care in an SNCU/NICU.
  • Airway – suction, oxygen; ventilator support if spasms cause apnoea.
  • Neutralise toxin – human tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG) 500 IU IM (or anti-tetanus serum after a test dose).
  • Antibiotic – metronidazole (or penicillin) for 7–10 days.
  • Control of spasms – diazepam (IV or by nasogastric tube in high doses), with phenobarbitone or magnesium sulphate as needed.
  • Nutrition – nasogastric feeding with expressed breast milk (oral feeding causes spasms and aspiration); IV fluids initially.
  • Cord care – clean the stump and remove applied substances.
  • Recovery does not give immunity – start routine immunisation of the baby; immunise the mother.

Nursing care

  • Observe and record spasms (frequency, duration, triggers), respiration, colour, temperature and SpO2.
  • Group all care to reduce stimulation; keep suction and oxygen ready.
  • Give drugs on time and watch for respiratory depression with sedatives.
  • Gentle NG feeding, mouth care, skin care and position changes.
  • Support and counsel the mother; teach the importance of immunisation and clean delivery for future births; notify the case (each case is investigated).

Prevention

  • Td immunisation of every pregnant woman – two doses in the first pregnancy (one booster if immunised within the last three years).
  • Clean delivery practices – institutional delivery or a skilled birth attendant, and the "five cleans" – clean hands, clean delivery surface, clean blade, clean cord tie and clean cord care (keep the stump clean and dry; apply nothing).
  • Health education against harmful cord practices.
  • India was validated for maternal and neonatal tetanus elimination in 2015, and these measures must continue to sustain it.

Conclusion Neonatal tetanus results from infection of the umbilical stump in babies of unimmunised mothers, causing inability to suck, stiffness and spasms from the third day of life, with high mortality. Treatment includes TIG, metronidazole, sedation, NG feeding and minimal stimulation, but the disease is fully preventable through Td immunisation in pregnancy and clean delivery and cord care.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: Explain poliomyelitis – the nursing care of a child with paralytic polio and the measures to keep India polio-free.
answer_html:
Definition Poliomyelitis is an acute viral infection caused by poliovirus types 1, 2 and 3 (enteroviruses) that may damage the motor neurons of the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord and brainstem, causing acute flaccid paralysis (AFP).

Spread – mainly faeco-oral, also by droplets; incubation period 7–14 days.

Clinical types

  • Inapparent infection (90–95%), abortive polio (minor illness), non-paralytic polio (aseptic meningitis).
  • Paralytic polio (less than 1%) – fever and muscle pain followed by sudden, asymmetrical flaccid paralysis, usually of the legs, without sensory loss; reflexes are lost; bulbar polio affects swallowing and breathing.
  • IM injections, strenuous exercise and tonsillectomy during the illness can precipitate paralysis (provocation paralysis).

Present status – India was certified polio-free in March 2014; the last case occurred on 13 January 2011 in Howrah, West Bengal. Wild poliovirus still circulates in Pakistan and Afghanistan, and vaccine-derived poliovirus can emerge where immunity is low, so vigilance must continue.

Nursing care of a child with paralytic polio

  1. Acute stage
    • Complete bed rest; avoid IM injections and exertion.
    • Positioning to prevent deformities – firm mattress, footboard to prevent foot drop, limbs in neutral position with pillows and sandbags, splints as advised; change position every 2 hours.
    • Moist hot packs and analgesics for muscle pain and spasm.
  2. Respiratory care – watch for difficulty in breathing, weak cough, nasal voice, difficulty swallowing; keep suction and oxygen ready; ventilator support for respiratory paralysis; nasogastric feeding in bulbar polio.
  3. Elimination – bladder and bowel care; prevent constipation and urinary retention.
  4. Skin care – prevention of pressure sores.
  5. Enteric precautions – safe disposal of stools; hand washing.
  6. Convalescent stage and rehabilitation – passive and then active exercises once pain subsides; physiotherapy; calipers, crutches and corrective surgery; schooling and vocational support; emotional support for child and family.

Measures to keep India polio-free

  • Routine immunisation – OPV at birth, 6, 10 and 14 weeks with a booster at 16–24 months, and fractional IPV (fIPV) intradermally at 6 and 14 weeks, with a third dose at 9–12 months (introduced from January 2023) along with MR vaccine.
  • Pulse polio and sub-national immunisation days in high-risk areas and for migrant and mobile populations; vaccination at border and transit points.
  • AFP surveillance – every child under 15 years with sudden weakness or floppiness of any limb is reported immediately, two stool samples are collected 24 hours apart within 14 days of onset and sent in the cold chain, and the child is followed up after 60 days.
  • Environmental surveillance of sewage for poliovirus.
  • High routine immunisation coverage through Mission Indradhanush.

Conclusion Poliomyelitis is a faeco-orally spread viral infection that can cause asymmetrical flaccid paralysis. Care of the paralysed child centres on rest, avoiding injections, correct positioning, respiratory care and rehabilitation. Although India is polio-free, high OPV and fIPV coverage, AFP and environmental surveillance must continue until global eradication.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: Explain HIV infection in children, with special reference to prevention of parent-to-child transmission.
answer_html:
Introduction Most children with HIV acquire the infection from their mothers during pregnancy, delivery or breastfeeding (parent-to-child transmission). Without intervention, about one-third of exposed babies become infected; with effective prevention the risk falls to below 2–5%. Other routes – unsafe blood, unsafe injections and sexual abuse – are less common; adolescents may acquire HIV sexually or through drug use.

Clinical features in children

  • Infected infants progress quickly; without treatment many die before the age of 2 years.
  • Failure to thrive, persistent diarrhoea, recurrent or severe infections (pneumonia, otitis media, sepsis).
  • Persistent oral thrush after 6 weeks of age, Pneumocystis pneumonia (especially at 3–6 months), tuberculosis.
  • Generalised lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, parotid swelling, chronic skin conditions.
  • Developmental delay and encephalopathy.

Diagnosis

  • Below 18 months – maternal antibodies are present in the baby, so a virological test (HIV DNA PCR on a dried blood spot) is used – early infant diagnosis (EID) at 6 weeks, repeated at 6 months, 12 months and 6 weeks after stopping breastfeeding.
  • At 18 months and above – antibody tests (three rapid tests) confirm the status.

Prevention of parent-to-child transmission (PPTCT)

  1. Universal HIV testing of all pregnant women at the first antenatal visit (along with syphilis and hepatitis B – the goal of elimination of vertical transmission).
  2. Lifelong ART for every HIV-positive pregnant and breastfeeding woman ("test and treat"), aiming at an undetectable viral load.
  3. Safe delivery practices – institutional delivery, avoiding unnecessary episiotomy, artificial rupture of membranes and instrumental delivery.
  4. Infant ARV prophylaxis – nevirapine syrup for 6 weeks (extended for high-risk infants as per national guidelines).
  5. Infant feeding – exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months while the mother is on ART (avoid mixed feeding), then complementary feeding.
  6. Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis from 6 weeks of age until HIV infection is excluded.
  7. EID and linkage of positive infants to ART centres.

Treatment of children with HIV

  • ART for every child diagnosed with HIV, at the earliest, through NACO ART centres – dolutegravir-based regimens (including paediatric dispersible tablets) according to age and weight.
  • Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis, treatment of opportunistic infections, TB screening and preventive treatment.
  • Nutrition and growth monitoring; routine immunisation (live vaccines may be withheld in severely immunosuppressed children as advised).

Role of the nurse

  • Pre- and post-test counselling of pregnant women; ensuring ART adherence; safe delivery with standard precautions.
  • Teach parents to give infant nevirapine and cotrimoxazole correctly and to attend EID visits.
  • Adherence support for children – correct measurement of syrups, linking doses with daily routines, pill swallowing training.
  • Age-appropriate disclosure of HIV status to the child over time; adolescent support.
  • Fighting stigma, maintaining confidentiality, linking families with support groups and social welfare schemes.

Conclusion Paediatric HIV is mostly acquired from the mother and presents with failure to thrive, recurrent infections and developmental delay. Universal antenatal testing, lifelong maternal ART, infant prophylaxis, safe feeding and early infant diagnosis can nearly eliminate transmission, while early ART, adherence support and family-centred nursing care allow infected children to grow and live normally.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: Explain dengue fever in children, with special reference to warning signs and fluid management.
answer_html:
Introduction Dengue is an acute viral illness caused by dengue virus serotypes 1–4, transmitted by the day-biting Aedes aegypti mosquito, which breeds in clean stagnant water in containers, coolers, tyres and pots. Children, especially infants and those with a second infection, are at risk of severe dengue with plasma leakage and shock. Incubation period is 4–7 days.

Phases of dengue

  1. Febrile phase (2–7 days) – sudden high fever, headache, pain behind the eyes, body and joint pains, flushed face, vomiting, rash, positive tourniquet test, mild bleeding (petechiae, gum bleeding).
  2. Critical phase (around the time fever falls, day 3–7, lasting 24–48 hours) – plasma leakage with rising haematocrit and falling platelets, pleural effusion and ascites; may progress to shock – cold clammy extremities, restlessness, rapid weak pulse, narrow pulse pressure (20 mmHg or less), delayed capillary refill, low urine output; bleeding.
  3. Recovery phase – leaked fluid is reabsorbed; appetite returns; bradycardia; convalescent rash with itching; risk of fluid overload if IV fluids are continued.

Warning signs (need admission)

  • Abdominal pain or tenderness, persistent vomiting.
  • Clinical fluid accumulation (pleural effusion, ascites).
  • Mucosal bleeding.
  • Lethargy or restlessness.
  • Liver enlargement more than 2 cm.
  • Rising haematocrit with a rapid fall in platelet count.

Diagnosis – NS1 antigen (first 5 days), IgM ELISA (after day 5); complete blood count with platelets and haematocrit, liver enzymes; ultrasound for fluid accumulation.

Fluid management

  • Without warning signs (can drink well) – home care with oral fluids (ORS, water, coconut water, soups, juices), paracetamol only for fever, rest; daily review during the critical days.
  • With warning signs – admit; IV isotonic crystalloid (normal saline or Ringer's lactate) starting at about 5–7 ml/kg/hour for 1–2 hours, then gradually reduced (3–5, then 2–3 ml/kg/hour) according to pulse, BP, urine output and haematocrit.
  • Dengue shock – crystalloid bolus of 10–20 ml/kg (over 15–60 minutes depending on severity), repeated as needed; colloids if shock persists; blood transfusion if haematocrit falls with continuing shock (hidden bleeding); PICU care.
  • Platelet transfusion is not given routinely – only for significant bleeding or very low counts with bleeding risk.
  • Reduce and stop IV fluids in the recovery phase to avoid fluid overload.
  • Avoid aspirin, ibuprofen and other NSAIDs, IM injections and steroids.

Nursing management

  • Monitor pulse, BP, pulse pressure, capillary refill, respiration, temperature and level of consciousness hourly in the critical phase.
  • Follow haematocrit and platelet counts as ordered; strict intake and output; urine output of at least 0.5–1 ml/kg/hour.
  • Accurate IV fluid calculation by weight with an infusion pump; watch for fluid overload (puffy face, breathlessness, crackles, enlarging liver).
  • Observe for bleeding (gums, nose, stool, urine); soft toothbrush; avoid invasive procedures.
  • Tepid sponging and paracetamol; light diet and fluids; rest.
  • Nurse the child under a mosquito net to prevent spread; health education on source reduction – empty and dry water containers weekly ("dry day"), cover water storage, larvicides in large containers, full-sleeved clothing, repellents and nets; notify cases to the health authorities.

Conclusion Dengue in children can progress from a simple febrile illness to plasma leakage and shock around the time the fever subsides. Recognising warning signs, careful weight-based IV fluid therapy guided by vital signs and haematocrit, avoiding NSAIDs and fluid overload, close nursing monitoring and community mosquito control are the keys to preventing deaths.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: Explain the common exanthematous (fever with rash) illnesses of childhood and how they are differentiated.
answer_html:
Introduction Exanthematous illnesses are infections in which fever is accompanied by a skin rash. Most are viral and self-limiting, but some (meningococcaemia, Kawasaki disease, dengue) need urgent treatment. Correct identification also decides isolation and protection of contacts.

Differentiation of common exanthems

Illness (cause) Key features Rash
Measles (measles virus) High fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis; Koplik's spots Dusky red maculopapular, starts behind ears and hairline on day 4, spreads downwards; brown staining
Rubella (rubella virus) Mild fever; tender post-auricular and suboccipital lymph nodes Pink, discrete maculopapular, starts on face, fades in 3 days; danger to the foetus if a pregnant woman is infected
Chickenpox (varicella-zoster virus) Mild fever, itching Crops of papules → vesicles ("dewdrops on a rose petal") → crusts, all stages together; central (trunk) distribution; mucous membranes involved
Roseola infantum / exanthem subitum (HHV-6) Infants 6–24 months; high fever for 3–5 days, then the rash appears as the fever falls; febrile seizures Rose-pink maculopapular rash on trunk
Erythema infectiosum / fifth disease (parvovirus B19) Mild illness "Slapped cheek" red face, then lacy rash on limbs
Hand, foot and mouth disease (Coxsackie A16, enterovirus 71) Fever, sore mouth, poor feeding Vesicles in the mouth, palms, soles and buttocks
Scarlet fever (group A streptococcus) Sore throat, strawberry tongue, flushed face with circumoral pallor Fine sandpaper-like rash, more in skin folds (Pastia's lines), peeling later
Kawasaki disease (cause unknown, vasculitis) Fever for 5 days or more, red eyes without discharge, red cracked lips and strawberry tongue, swollen red hands and feet, neck lymph node Polymorphous rash; risk of coronary artery aneurysm – needs IVIG and aspirin
Dengue High fever, body pains, retro-orbital pain Flushing, petechiae; convalescent "islands of white in a sea of red"
Meningococcaemia (N. meningitidis) Rapidly ill child, shock, meningitis Purpuric, non-blanching rash – a medical emergency

Nursing approach to a child with fever and rash

  • Isolate the child until the diagnosis is clear (airborne precautions if measles or chickenpox is possible); keep away from pregnant women and immunocompromised patients.
  • Assess for danger signs – a non-blanching rash (does not fade under pressure of a glass – "glass test"), drowsiness, shock, breathing difficulty, convulsions, dehydration – and arrange emergency care.
  • Take a history of immunisation, contacts and the order of appearance of fever and rash.
  • Symptomatic care – paracetamol (not aspirin), fluids, calamine for itching, short nails, mouth care, eye care.
  • Notify notifiable diseases; advise on exclusion from school and protection of contacts (for example, vaccine for measles contacts).

Conclusion Fever with rash in children has many causes – measles, rubella, chickenpox, roseola, fifth disease, hand-foot-mouth disease, scarlet fever, Kawasaki disease, dengue and meningococcaemia. The pattern of fever, associated features and type and spread of the rash help to differentiate them, while the nurse isolates the child, looks for danger signs such as a non-blanching rash and provides supportive care.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: What are Koplik's spots?
answer_html:
Koplik's spots are small (1–2 mm), bluish-white or greyish spots on a red base, like grains of salt, seen on the buccal mucosa opposite the lower molar teeth.

  • They appear in the prodromal stage of measles, 1–2 days before the rash, and fade within 2–3 days after the rash appears.
  • They are pathognomonic (diagnostic) of measles.
  • Significance – they allow early diagnosis, so the child can be isolated and given vitamin A before the rash appears, and contacts can be protected.
  • They are best seen with a good light and a tongue depressor.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: Write the dose schedule of vitamin A therapy in measles.
answer_html:
Vitamin A is given to every child with measles because measles depletes vitamin A, and supplementation reduces complications (pneumonia, diarrhoea, blindness) and deaths.

Age Dose (each day, for 2 days)
Below 6 months 50,000 IU
6–11 months 1,00,000 IU
12 months and above 2,00,000 IU
  • Two doses are given on two consecutive days (day 1 and day 2).
  • A third dose is given 2–4 weeks later if the child has eye signs of vitamin A deficiency (Bitot's spots, corneal xerosis, ulcer) or severe malnutrition.
  • It is given orally; the nurse records the doses and teaches eye care and a vitamin A-rich diet.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Orthopaedic, Eye, Ear and Skin Disorders and Communicable Diseases in Children
question: What is multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C)?
answer_html:
Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) is a severe post-infectious inflammatory condition that develops 2–6 weeks after infection with SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19), often after a mild or unnoticed infection.

  • Features – persistent fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, red eyes, red cracked lips, swollen hands and feet (resembling Kawasaki disease), and involvement of two or more organ systems – especially the heart (myocarditis, shock, coronary artery dilatation).
  • Investigations – raised inflammatory markers (CRP, ferritin, D-dimer), evidence of recent COVID-19 (antibodies), echocardiography.
  • Treatment – IV immunoglobulin and steroids, low-dose aspirin, supportive care and PICU care for shock; cardiac follow-up.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Behavioural and Social Problems in Children
question: (a) Define behavioural problems in children and explain their causes. (4 marks) (b) Describe the common behavioural problems of childhood and the principles of their management. (8 marks) (c) Explain the role of the nurse in the prevention of behavioural problems. (3 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition and causes (4 marks)

Definition Behavioural problems are patterns of behaviour in a child that are unusual for the child's age, persistent, and cause distress or difficulty to the child, family or school. Many such behaviours (for example, thumb sucking in a toddler) are normal at one age and become a problem only when they persist beyond the expected age, are frequent or severe, or interfere with health, learning and relationships.

Causes – usually several factors act together:

  1. Child factors – temperament ("difficult child"), developmental delay, intellectual disability, ADHD, hearing or vision problems, chronic illness, hospitalisation, hunger and fatigue.
  2. Family factors – faulty parenting (over-protection, over-strictness, inconsistent discipline, rejection, excessive indulgence), marital discord, domestic violence, separation or death of a parent, arrival of a new sibling, sibling rivalry, comparison with others, parental mental illness or substance use, lack of time and attention.
  3. School factors – academic pressure, unsuitable teaching methods, bullying, punishment, change of school.
  4. Social and environmental factors – poverty, overcrowding, migration, exposure to violence, excessive screen time, peer influence, neighbourhood crime.
  5. Emotional stress – anxiety, insecurity, jealousy, need for attention; the behaviour often serves to relieve tension or to gain attention.

(b) Common behavioural problems and principles of management (8 marks)

1. Habit disorders (tension-relieving habits)

  • Thumb sucking – normal in infancy; a problem if it persists beyond 4–5 years (dental malocclusion). Ignore it in young children, keep hands busy, praise periods without sucking; never punish.
  • Nail biting (onychophagia) – a sign of tension in school-age children; reduce stress, keep nails short and clean, distract, praise.
  • Head banging, body rocking, hair pulling – usually at bedtime or when tired or bored; ensure safety and look for under-stimulation or developmental problems.

2. Elimination disorders

  • Enuresis – repeated voiding of urine into the bed or clothes after 5 years of age; managed with reassurance, no punishment, star charts, bladder training and enuresis alarms.
  • Encopresis – passage of stool in inappropriate places after 4 years, usually due to chronic constipation with overflow; managed with treatment of constipation, regular toilet sitting and positive reinforcement.

3. Emotional and attention-seeking behaviours

  • Temper tantrums – outbursts of crying, kicking and screaming in toddlers (1–3 years) when frustrated; stay calm, keep the child safe, ignore the tantrum and do not give in, praise calm behaviour.
  • Breath-holding spells – the child cries, holds the breath in expiration, becomes blue or pale and may lose consciousness briefly (6 months–6 years); harmless; reassure parents and treat iron deficiency.
  • Sibling rivalry and jealousy – regression or aggression after a new baby; prepare the child, give individual attention, avoid comparisons.

4. Antisocial behaviours

  • Stealing – a young child below 5–6 years does not understand ownership; in older children it may express deprivation, peer pressure or need for attention; explain, help return the object, avoid labelling, look for the cause.
  • Lying – imaginative lies in young children are normal; persistent lying to avoid punishment calls for less harsh discipline and good example by parents.
  • Aggressiveness – hitting, biting and destroying things; teach alternative ways to express anger, use time-out, avoid physical punishment (which teaches aggression), limit exposure to violence.
  • Juvenile delinquency – a child who commits an act that is an offence under law; dealt with under the Juvenile Justice Act through rehabilitation rather than punishment.

5. School-related problems – school phobia (school refusal), learning difficulties, truancy and poor performance; need early identification and cooperation between parents, teachers and health professionals.

6. Feeding and sleep problems – food refusal, picky eating, pica (eating mud, chalk or paint – look for iron deficiency, worms and lead poisoning), nightmares, night terrors and sleepwalking.

Principles of management

  1. Assessment – detailed history from parents and teachers, observation of the child, physical examination to exclude organic causes (for example, UTI or diabetes in enuresis, constipation in encopresis), and assessment of family relationships.
  2. Reassurance and explanation – most problems are common and temporary; remove guilt and blame.
  3. Remove or reduce the cause – family counselling, reducing school stress, ending bullying, giving love and attention.
  4. Behaviour modification techniques
    • Positive reinforcement – praise, attention or rewards immediately after desired behaviour.
    • Planned ignoring (extinction) – withdrawing attention from attention-seeking behaviour that is not dangerous.
    • Time-out – removing the child to a quiet place for a few minutes (about one minute per year of age).
    • Token economy and star charts – rewards for agreed targets (dry nights, toilet use).
    • Modelling – parents demonstrate the behaviour they expect.
  5. Consistency – both parents and all caregivers follow the same rules; clear, simple limits.
  6. Avoid punishment, shaming, threats and labelling – they increase anxiety and worsen the problem.
  7. Specific treatment – enuresis alarms, laxatives for constipation, psychotherapy, family therapy and, rarely, medicines.
  8. Referral to a child guidance clinic or child psychiatrist when the problem is severe, persistent or associated with other disorders.

(c) Role of the nurse in prevention (3 marks)

  • Anticipatory guidance to parents at each well-baby and immunisation visit about normal behaviour at different ages (for example, tantrums in toddlers, thumb sucking in infants), so that they do not over-react.
  • Promote positive parenting – warmth, quality time, play, consistent discipline without physical punishment, praise for good behaviour, and avoiding comparisons.
  • Prepare children for new siblings, hospitalisation and school entry.
  • Early identification of children at risk – developmental delay, family conflict, abuse, chronic illness – and early referral.
  • School health – life-skills education, anti-bullying measures, teacher orientation, counselling services.
  • Parent education groups through anganwadis, schools and community meetings.

Nightmares and night terrors – a common parental concern | Feature | Nightmares | Night terrors | |---|---|---| | Sleep stage | REM sleep, later part of the night | Deep non-REM sleep, first few hours of sleep | | Child's state | Wakes fully, frightened, seeks comfort | Screams, sits up, eyes open, but is not awake and cannot be comforted | | Memory next morning | Remembers the dream | No memory of the episode | | Management | Comfort, reassurance, avoid frightening stories and screens at bedtime | Do not wake the child; keep safe; regular sleep schedule; usually outgrown |

When to refer to a specialist (red flags)

  • The problem is severe, persistent or getting worse despite good management at home.
  • It interferes with schooling, friendships or family life.
  • It is associated with developmental delay, regression, self-injury, cruelty to animals, fire setting or threats of harm.
  • There are features of depression, anxiety, ADHD, autism or suspected abuse.
  • Parents are unable to cope or are themselves distressed.

Nursing importance Behaviour problems are among the commonest concerns of parents. Nurses who understand normal development, reassure parents, teach positive parenting and behaviour modification techniques, and refer severe cases early, prevent many children from developing lasting emotional and social difficulties.

Conclusion Behavioural problems in children arise from an interaction of child, family, school and social factors, and include habit disorders, elimination disorders, tantrums, breath-holding, stealing, lying, aggression and school-related problems. Management is based on assessment, reassurance, removal of causes, behaviour modification with positive reinforcement and consistency, and avoidance of punishment, with the nurse playing a key preventive role through parent education.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Behavioural and Social Problems in Children
question: (a) Define child abuse and neglect and explain their types. (4 marks) (b) Explain the risk factors and the warning signs (indicators) of child abuse. (4 marks) (c) Describe the role of the nurse in the prevention, identification, management and reporting of child abuse, including the legal provisions in India. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Sites of accidental and non-accidental injuries in children

answer_html:
(a) Definition and types (4 marks)

Definition According to WHO, child abuse or maltreatment is all forms of physical and emotional ill-treatment, sexual abuse, neglect or negligent treatment, and commercial or other exploitation, resulting in actual or potential harm to the child's health, survival, development or dignity in the context of a relationship of responsibility, trust or power. Child neglect is the failure of parents or caregivers to provide for the child's basic needs – food, clothing, shelter, health care, education, supervision and emotional care – when they are able to do so.

Types

  1. Physical abuse – deliberate injury: hitting, slapping, kicking, burning, scalding, biting, shaking, poisoning.
    • Battered child syndrome (described by Kempe, 1962) – repeated injuries of different ages.
    • Abusive head trauma (shaken baby syndrome) – violent shaking of an infant causing subdural haemorrhage, retinal haemorrhages and brain damage.
  2. Emotional (psychological) abuse – persistent rejection, threatening, terrorising, humiliating, constant criticism, comparison, isolating the child, exposure to domestic violence.
  3. Sexual abuse – involving a child in sexual activity he or she does not understand or cannot consent to, including touching, penetration, exposure to pornography and exploitation; the abuser is most often a known person.
  4. Neglect – physical (inadequate food, hygiene, clothing), medical (not seeking treatment or immunisation), educational, emotional, and lack of supervision leading to repeated accidents.
  5. Exploitation – child labour, child trafficking, child marriage, begging, commercial sexual exploitation.
  6. Fabricated or induced illness (Munchausen syndrome by proxy) – a caregiver invents or produces symptoms in the child.

(b) Risk factors and warning signs (4 marks)

Risk factors

  • Child – infants and preterm babies, children with disabilities or chronic illness, unwanted children, girls in some settings, "difficult" temperament.
  • Parents/caregivers – young or single parents, history of abuse in their own childhood, mental illness, alcohol or drug use, unrealistic expectations, poor parenting knowledge, stepparents in some situations.
  • Family and society – poverty, unemployment, domestic violence, social isolation, overcrowding, acceptance of harsh physical punishment, children in institutions, street children, conflict and disaster situations.

Physical indicators

  • Injuries not explained by the history, or a history that keeps changing; delay in seeking care.
  • Bruises in unusual sites – ears, cheeks, neck, upper arms, back, buttocks, inner thighs; bruises in a non-mobile infant; bruises of different colours (different ages).
  • Patterned marks – hand prints, belt or cord loop marks, bite marks, cigarette burns, immersion scalds with sharp "glove and stocking" margins.
  • Fractures – multiple fractures of different ages, metaphyseal "corner" fractures, posterior rib fractures, fractures in non-walking infants.
  • Head injury in an infant with subdural haemorrhage and retinal haemorrhages.
  • Sexual abuse – genital or anal injury, bleeding or discharge, sexually transmitted infection, pregnancy in a young adolescent, pain on walking or sitting.
  • Neglect – failure to thrive, poor hygiene, untreated illnesses, missed immunisations, repeated accidents.

Behavioural indicators

  • Fearfulness, frozen watchfulness, flinching at sudden movement, fear of going home or of a particular person.
  • Withdrawal, depression, aggressive or self-harming behaviour, regression (bedwetting), sleep disturbances.
  • Age-inappropriate sexual knowledge or behaviour.
  • Poor school performance, frequent absence, running away, substance use.

(c) Role of the nurse and legal provisions (7 marks)

1. Prevention

  • Positive parenting education – realistic expectations of child development, non-violent discipline, managing crying babies (never shake a baby), anger management.
  • Support high-risk families through home visits by ANMs and ASHAs, anganwadis and social welfare services; early bonding and breastfeeding.
  • Body safety education for children – "good touch and bad touch", the right to say no, telling a trusted adult; life-skills education in schools.
  • Community awareness about child rights, child marriage, child labour and helplines.

2. Identification

  • Maintain a high index of suspicion when the history does not fit the injury or the developmental stage.
  • Take a careful, non-judgemental history from the caregiver and, separately and gently, from the child, using open questions and the child's own words; do not ask leading questions.
  • Perform or assist with a complete head-to-toe examination with the child's consent and in the presence of a female attendant where needed.

3. Management and care of the child

  • Treat injuries first; ensure safety – admit the child if necessary for protection.
  • Investigations as ordered – skeletal survey, CT head, fundus examination, bleeding profile, forensic samples in sexual abuse (with consent and proper chain of custody).
  • Provide emotional support, a calm environment, one consistent caregiver, play therapy; never blame the child.
  • Psychological counselling and follow-up for the child and the non-offending family members.

4. Documentation

  • Record the history in the exact words used, date and time, persons present, a detailed description of injuries (site, size, shape, colour) with body diagrams and photographs as per protocol, and actions taken. Accurate records are essential for legal proceedings.

5. Reporting and legal provisions in India

  • Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 – mandatory reporting of any sexual offence against a child (below 18 years) to the Special Juvenile Police Unit or local police (Section 19); failure to report is punishable (Section 21); medical examination of the child by a doctor (a woman doctor for girls) in the presence of a trusted adult; free first aid and treatment.
  • Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 – cruelty to a child by a person in charge is a punishable offence (Section 75); children in need of care and protection are produced before the Child Welfare Committee (CWC); corporal punishment is prohibited in schools under the Right to Education Act.
  • Child helpline 1098 – now run through State/UT WCD control rooms under Mission Vatsalya and integrated with the Emergency Response Support System (ERSS-112); District Child Protection Units coordinate rescue and rehabilitation.
  • Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 and Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act protect against exploitation.
  • Follow the hospital's child-protection policy; inform the doctor in charge, social worker and authorities; maintain confidentiality.

6. Rehabilitation and follow-up – coordination with CWC, DCPU, police, counsellors and schools; foster care or child care institutions if home is unsafe; follow-up of growth, development and emotional health.

Nursing importance Nurses are often the first professionals to see an abused child in the emergency room, ward or community. Recognising suspicious patterns, documenting carefully, reporting as required by law and providing compassionate care can save a child from repeated abuse and long-term harm.

Conclusion Child abuse includes physical, emotional and sexual abuse, neglect and exploitation, and is linked to child, parental and social risk factors. Unexplained or patterned injuries and fearful or regressive behaviour are warning signs. The nurse prevents abuse through parent and child education, identifies and documents it carefully, ensures treatment and safety, and reports it under the POCSO and Juvenile Justice Acts through the police, CWC and child helpline 1098/112.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Behavioural and Social Problems in Children
question: (a) Explain the meaning of mentally, physically and socially challenged children with examples. (3 marks) (b) Describe the management of challenged children and the role of the nurse in their care and in supporting their families. (7 marks) (c) Explain the welfare services available for challenged children in India. (5 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Meaning with examples (3 marks) Challenged children (children with special needs) are children who, because of a physical, mental or social condition, face barriers to normal growth, development, learning and participation, and need special care, services and support.

  1. Mentally challenged children – children with intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, specific learning disability, mental illness, and multiple disabilities (for example, cerebral palsy with intellectual disability).
  2. Physically challenged children – locomotor disability (cerebral palsy, polio, spina bifida, muscular dystrophy, amputation, club foot), visual impairment (blindness, low vision), hearing and speech impairment, chronic illnesses such as thalassaemia and haemophilia.
  3. Socially challenged children – children who are disadvantaged by their social situation: orphans and abandoned children, street children, child labourers, children of migrant workers, sex workers or prisoners, child victims of trafficking, abuse or disasters, children in conflict with law, and children affected by HIV.

(b) Management and role of the nurse (7 marks)

Principles of management

  • Early identification and early intervention – the first 1,000 days and early childhood are critical; under RBSK, mobile health teams screen children for 4 Ds (defects at birth, diseases, deficiencies and developmental delays including disability) and refer them to District Early Intervention Centres (DEIC) for therapy.
  • Multidisciplinary team – paediatrician, nurse, physiotherapist, occupational therapist, speech therapist, psychologist, special educator, social worker and orthopaedic or other specialists.
  • Habilitation and rehabilitation – medical treatment, therapy, assistive devices, special and inclusive education, vocational training, social integration.
  • Family-centred and community-based care, with the child living at home wherever possible.

Role of the nurse in the care of challenged children

  1. Screening and early detection – newborn examination, developmental screening at immunisation visits, red reflex and hearing screening, growth monitoring; prompt referral.
  2. Assessment – the child's abilities (not only disabilities), needs for daily living, nutrition, safety and family resources.
  3. Physical care – nutrition (special feeding techniques for children with swallowing problems), hygiene, toilet training, skin care and pressure-area care, prevention of contractures by positioning and exercises, seizure care, prevention of infections and injuries.
  4. Promoting development and independence – stimulation through play, teaching self-care skills step by step (feeding, dressing, toileting) using task analysis and positive reinforcement; use of aids (spectacles, hearing aids, calipers, wheelchairs, communication boards).
  5. Education – encourage enrolment in inclusive schools or special schools; liaise with teachers and special educators.
  6. Health supervision – immunisation, dental care, vision and hearing checks, management of associated conditions.
  7. Safety and protection – children with disabilities are at higher risk of abuse and neglect; watch for warning signs.

Supporting the family

  • Help the parents through shock, denial, guilt and grief; listen, give honest information and hope; avoid blame.
  • Train parents to carry out home therapy and care; teach them to recognise complications.
  • Encourage involvement of both parents and siblings; prevent over-protection and rejection.
  • Link the family with parent support groups, NGOs, respite care and government schemes; help them obtain the disability certificate and UDID card.
  • Genetic counselling where relevant; counselling for planning future pregnancies.
  • For socially challenged children – coordinate with the Child Welfare Committee, District Child Protection Unit, child care institutions, foster families and adoption agencies; ensure health care, nutrition, education and emotional support.

(c) Welfare services for challenged children in India (5 marks)

1. Legal provisions

  • Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016 – recognises 21 types of disabilities; free education for every child with benchmark disability (40% or more) from 6 to 18 years in a neighbourhood or special school; inclusive education; reservation in higher education (5%) and government jobs (4%); accessibility in public places and transport.
  • National Trust Act, 1999 – for autism, cerebral palsy, intellectual disability and multiple disabilities; provides legal guardianship and schemes.
  • Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 – care, protection, adoption and rehabilitation of children in need of care and protection.

2. Health services

  • RBSK screening and DEICs with free therapy and surgery for birth defects (club foot, cleft lip, CHD, cataract).
  • Unique Disability ID (UDID) card – a single document for all benefits.
  • ADIP scheme – free or subsidised aids and appliances (wheelchairs, tricycles, calipers, hearing aids, braille kits, cochlear implants for young children).
  • Niramaya health insurance (National Trust) for children with autism, CP, intellectual and multiple disabilities.
  • District Disability Rehabilitation Centres (DDRCs) and national institutes – for intellectual disabilities (NIEPID, Secunderabad), locomotor disabilities (Kolkata), hearing (Mumbai), visual (Dehradun) and multiple disabilities (Chennai).

3. Educational services

  • Samagra Shiksha – inclusive education for children with special needs: identification camps, aids and appliances, resource teachers, braille and large-print books, transport and escort allowances, home-based education for severely disabled children.
  • Scholarships (pre-matric, post-matric and top-class) for students with disabilities; special schools and vocational training centres.
  • National Trust schemes such as Disha (early intervention), Vikaas (day care), Samarth (respite care) and Sahyogi (caregiver training).

4. Social welfare and financial support

  • Disability pensions and allowances by States; concessions in rail and bus travel; Accessible India Campaign (Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan).
  • For socially challenged children – Mission Vatsalya (sponsorship, foster care, after-care, child care institutions, open shelters, child helpline 1098), adoption through the Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA), PM CARES for Children scheme for children orphaned by COVID-19, National Child Labour Project schools, bridge schools and residential schools, and Integrated Child Development Services (anganwadis).

Common problems faced by families of challenged children

  • Emotional – grief, guilt, blame, anxiety about the future, depression in mothers, marital strain.
  • Social – stigma, superstitions (disability seen as punishment), isolation from relatives and community, difficulty in finding schools that will admit the child.
  • Financial – cost of repeated hospital visits, therapy, aids and travel; loss of income when a parent gives up work to care for the child.
  • Physical – exhaustion from lifting, feeding and round-the-clock care; lack of respite.
  • Siblings – feel neglected or burdened; may be teased.

The nurse as an advocate

  • Speaks for the rights of the child to health care, education and participation, as guaranteed by the RPwD Act.
  • Helps families navigate certification, UDID registration and scheme applications.
  • Promotes inclusive attitudes in schools, anganwadis and the community, using the child's abilities rather than the disability as the focus ("person-first" language – "a child with cerebral palsy", not "a spastic child").

Nursing importance With early identification, regular therapy and family support, most challenged children can achieve much greater independence. The nurse is the link between the child, the family and the many services available, and helps families obtain the benefits to which the child is entitled.

Conclusion Challenged children include children with mental, physical and social disadvantages. Their care is based on early identification and intervention, multidisciplinary habilitation, inclusive education and family-centred support, with the nurse playing roles in screening, physical care, teaching, advocacy and referral. India provides support through the RPwD Act, RBSK and DEICs, UDID and ADIP, National Trust schemes, Samagra Shiksha and Mission Vatsalya.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Behavioural and Social Problems in Children
question: Explain the child guidance clinic – its objectives, team and functions.
answer_html:
Definition A child guidance clinic is a specialised service for the assessment, treatment and prevention of behavioural, emotional, developmental and learning problems of children and adolescents, working closely with parents and schools. The first child guidance clinic in India was started in 1937 at the Sir Dorabji Tata Graduate School of Social Work, Bombay (now TISS); today such clinics function in medical colleges, mental health institutions, general hospitals and NGOs.

Objectives

  • Early identification and treatment of behaviour and emotional problems.
  • To help children achieve healthy personality development and adjustment at home, school and in society.
  • To guide and counsel parents and teachers in understanding and managing children.
  • Prevention of mental illness and delinquency through mental health promotion.
  • Training and research in child mental health.

The team

  • Child psychiatrist / paediatrician – medical assessment, diagnosis and treatment.
  • Clinical psychologist – psychological testing (IQ, personality, learning), behaviour therapy, psychotherapy.
  • Psychiatric social worker – family assessment, home visits, linkage with community resources.
  • Psychiatric or paediatric nurse – intake, observation, health education, counselling, follow-up.
  • Special educator, speech therapist, occupational therapist as required.

Common problems seen – enuresis and encopresis, temper tantrums, aggression, stealing, lying, school refusal, learning difficulties, ADHD, autism, intellectual disability, anxiety and depression, conduct problems, substance use, effects of abuse and family conflict.

Functions

  1. Intake and assessment – detailed history from parents and teachers, observation, physical examination, psychological testing and family assessment.
  2. Treatment – behaviour modification, play therapy, individual and group psychotherapy, family therapy, medication where needed, remedial education.
  3. Parent guidance – positive parenting, consistent discipline, home management programmes.
  4. School liaison – advice to teachers, classroom adjustments, special education referral.
  5. Referral and follow-up – to paediatric, neurology, speech or special services; regular follow-up.
  6. Preventive and educational work – talks to parents, teachers and community groups on child mental health.

Role of the nurse – first contact and rapport with the child and family; observation of behaviour in the waiting area and during play; health and developmental assessment; counselling and teaching of parents; organising group sessions; home visits and follow-up; maintaining records.

Conclusion A child guidance clinic is a multidisciplinary service that assesses and treats children's behavioural, emotional and learning problems and guides parents and teachers. The nurse is an important member of the team in assessment, counselling, health education and follow-up.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Behavioural and Social Problems in Children
question: Explain nocturnal enuresis in children and its management.
answer_html:
Definition Enuresis is the repeated involuntary (or intentional) passage of urine into the bed or clothes by a child aged 5 years or more, occurring at least twice a week for 3 months or causing significant distress (DSM-5). Nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting) occurs during sleep and is the commonest form. About 15% of 5-year-olds wet the bed, and it resolves spontaneously in about 15% of affected children each year.

Types

  • Primary – the child has never been dry for 6 months (80%); usually a maturational delay.
  • Secondary – wetting after a dry period of at least 6 months; often due to stress or an organic cause.
  • Monosymptomatic (only night wetting) and non-monosymptomatic (with daytime symptoms – urgency, frequency, daytime wetting).

Causes

  • Nocturnal polyuria – inadequate night-time rise of antidiuretic hormone.
  • Small functional bladder capacity or overactive bladder.
  • Difficulty in waking from deep sleep in response to a full bladder.
  • Genetic – strong family history (risk is high if one or both parents wet the bed as children).
  • Organic causes – urinary tract infection, constipation, diabetes mellitus or insipidus, spinal abnormalities, sleep apnoea due to enlarged adenoids, threadworms.
  • Psychological stress – birth of a sibling, school change, family conflict, abuse (secondary enuresis).

Assessment – history (pattern, daytime symptoms, fluid intake, bowel habits, family history, stress), a bladder diary, examination of the abdomen, spine and genitals, urine routine and culture, urine sugar.

Management

  1. Reassurance and explanation – bedwetting is common, not the child's fault and usually outgrown; never punish, shame or tease the child.
  2. Motivational therapy – a star chart for dry nights; involve the child in changing wet sheets without blame.
  3. Fluid and toilet habits – adequate fluids during the day, reduce fluids 1–2 hours before bed, avoid tea, coffee and fizzy drinks in the evening; pass urine before sleeping; regular daytime voiding; treat constipation.
  4. Enuresis alarm (first-line for motivated children above 6–7 years) – a moisture sensor in the underwear rings at the first drops of urine and wakes the child, who goes to the toilet; used every night for 2–3 months; has the best long-term success.
  5. Desmopressin (synthetic ADH) at bedtime – reduces night urine; useful for short-term dryness (camps) or when the alarm is not suitable; fluids must be restricted from 1 hour before to 8 hours after the dose to prevent water intoxication (hyponatraemia).
  6. Imipramine – rarely used now because of cardiac toxicity in overdose.
  7. Treat underlying causes – UTI, constipation, diabetes; counselling for stress in secondary enuresis.

Role of the nurse – take a non-judgemental history, teach parents and child about the condition and the plan, demonstrate the alarm, maintain the chart, check urine tests, follow up and support the family's patience; protect the child's self-esteem (sleepovers, school camps).

Conclusion Nocturnal enuresis is common in children over 5 years and is usually due to maturational delay, nocturnal polyuria, small bladder capacity and deep sleep, with a strong family tendency. After excluding organic causes, reassurance, motivational charts, good fluid and toilet habits, enuresis alarms and desmopressin cure most children, while punishment only worsens the problem.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Behavioural and Social Problems in Children
question: Explain school phobia (school refusal) and its management.
answer_html:
Definition School phobia (school refusal) is a persistent reluctance or refusal to go to school, or to stay there for the whole day, due to emotional distress (anxiety or fear), in a child who otherwise wishes to do well and whose parents know where the child is. It is different from truancy, in which the child stays away from school without the parents' knowledge, often with antisocial behaviour.

  • It occurs at school entry (5–7 years), at change of school (11–12 years) and in early adolescence.

Causes

  • Separation anxiety – especially in young children who fear leaving the mother (after illness, birth of a sibling, parental illness or family conflict).
  • Fear related to school – bullying, a strict or harsh teacher, fear of failure or examinations, learning difficulties, ridicule by classmates, toilet problems, travel fears.
  • Social anxiety, depression or other emotional disorders in older children.
  • Over-protective parents, parental anxiety, family problems, secondary gain (staying at home is comfortable and rewarded).

Clinical features

  • Physical complaints on school mornings – headache, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, fatigue – that disappear once the child is allowed to stay home, and are absent on weekends and holidays.
  • Crying, clinging, pleading or tantrums when it is time to leave; refusal to get out of bed or leave the house.
  • Anxiety about school, sleep disturbances, irritability; academic decline.

Management

  1. Exclude physical illness with a careful but not excessive examination; avoid repeated investigations that reinforce the illness behaviour.
  2. Early return to school is the key – the longer the child stays away, the harder the return becomes.
    • Graded return (for example, attending for an hour, then half a day, then the full day) if necessary.
    • Firm, kind and consistent parents; the child is escorted to school by a calm adult.
  3. Find and remove the cause – stop bullying, adjust academic expectations, assess for learning difficulties, address family problems.
  4. Cognitive behaviour therapy – relaxation, gradual exposure, coping statements, problem-solving and social skills training.
  5. Parent counselling – avoid over-protection; do not make home more rewarding than school on school days (no television or games during school hours); praise attendance.
  6. School liaison – a supportive teacher or counsellor, a "safe person" and place in school, a buddy, flexibility in the early days.
  7. Treat associated anxiety or depression; medication (SSRIs) only in severe cases under a psychiatrist.

Role of the nurse – identify the pattern of symptoms in the school health clinic or OPD, reassure, counsel parents, coordinate with teachers and the school counsellor, and refer to a child guidance clinic when needed.

Conclusion School refusal is an emotional problem in which anxiety (separation, fear of school situations or social anxiety) leads to persistent refusal to attend school, often with morning physical complaints. Early, supported return to school, removal of the cause, CBT, firm parenting and close cooperation between home, school and health workers are the essentials of management.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Behavioural and Social Problems in Children
question: Explain depression in children and adolescents and its management.
answer_html:
Definition Depression in children and adolescents is a mood disorder in which persistent sadness or irritability and loss of interest or pleasure last for at least two weeks and interfere with the child's functioning at home, school and with friends. It is often missed because children may not express sadness in words.

Risk factors

  • Family history of depression, parental mental illness or substance use.
  • Loss and stress – death or separation of parents, family conflict, migration, academic pressure and examination failure.
  • Bullying (including cyberbullying), abuse and neglect, chronic illness or disability, learning difficulties.
  • Low self-esteem, social isolation, excessive screen use; adolescence and puberty-related changes.

Clinical features

  • Young children – irritability, crying, clinging, temper outbursts, frequent physical complaints (stomach-ache, headache), loss of interest in play, regression, poor appetite and weight gain failure, sleep problems.
  • School-age children and adolescents – persistent sadness or irritability, loss of interest (anhedonia), withdrawal from friends, decline in school performance, fatigue, changes in sleep and appetite, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, poor concentration, boredom, substance use, risky behaviour, self-harm and suicidal thoughts.

Assessment – interview of the child and parents separately, information from school, screening tools (for example, child depression rating scales), assessment of suicide risk, physical examination (to exclude hypothyroidism, anaemia and other illness).

Management

  1. Psychotherapy (first-line) – cognitive behaviour therapy (recognising and changing negative thoughts, activity scheduling, problem solving), interpersonal therapy, play therapy for young children, family therapy.
  2. Medication for moderate to severe depression – fluoxetine is the preferred SSRI in children and adolescents, prescribed by a psychiatrist with close monitoring for increased suicidal thoughts, especially in the first weeks.
  3. Treat contributing problems – stop bullying, address abuse, support learning difficulties, reduce academic pressure.
  4. Lifestyle – regular sleep, physical activity, outdoor play, balanced diet, limits on screen time, maintaining friendships.
  5. Hospitalisation if there is serious suicide risk.

Nursing care

  • Establish trust; listen without judgement; encourage the child to express feelings through talk, drawing or play.
  • Safety – ask directly about suicidal thoughts, remove access to means (medicines, pesticides, sharp objects), close observation when at risk.
  • Encourage small, achievable activities and praise success; maintain routines of sleep, meals and hygiene.
  • Teach parents to recognise warning signs, communicate supportively, avoid criticism and comparison, supervise medicines and keep follow-up appointments.
  • Liaise with the school counsellor; inform families of Tele-MANAS (14416), the national tele-mental health helpline.

Conclusion Depression in children often appears as irritability, physical complaints, withdrawal and falling school performance rather than sadness. Early recognition, psychotherapy (especially CBT), careful use of fluoxetine when needed, safety measures against self-harm, and family and school support, with active nursing involvement, lead to recovery in most children.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Behavioural and Social Problems in Children
question: Explain substance abuse among children and adolescents and the role of the nurse in prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction Substance abuse is the harmful use of tobacco, alcohol, inhalants, cannabis or other drugs that damages health and development. In India, experimentation often begins in early adolescence, and inhalants (solvents such as correction fluid, glue, petrol and paint thinners) are used more by children than by adults, especially by street and working children.

Commonly used substances

  • Tobacco – cigarettes, bidis, gutkha, khaini, e-cigarettes (banned in India); a gateway to other substances.
  • Inhalants – "whitener", glue, petrol, aerosol sprays; cause euphoria, dizziness, slurred speech; risk of sudden death, brain, liver and kidney damage.
  • Alcohol, cannabis (ganja, bhang, charas), prescription drugs (cough syrups containing codeine, sedatives) and, less commonly, opioids and stimulants.

Causes and risk factors

  • Peer pressure, curiosity, desire to look adult, influence of media.
  • Family factors – parental substance use, family conflict, lack of supervision, abuse and neglect.
  • Stress, academic failure, depression, ADHD, conduct problems, low self-esteem.
  • Easy availability, poverty, homelessness, child labour.

Warning signs

  • Change in behaviour – irritability, secrecy, lying, stealing money, new friends, withdrawal from family.
  • Falling school performance, absenteeism.
  • Physical signs – red eyes, smell of tobacco, alcohol or chemicals on breath or clothes, rash or sores around the nose and mouth (inhalants), stained fingers, weight loss, sleep changes.
  • Finding empty tubes, cloth soaked in solvent, cigarette packets or bottles.

Effects – addiction, accidents, violence, school drop-out, risky sexual behaviour, HIV and hepatitis, delinquency, depression and suicide; tobacco-related cancers later.

Role of the nurse in prevention

  1. Primary prevention
    • Life-skills education in schools – decision making, refusal skills ("saying no"), coping with stress, self-esteem, critical thinking about advertisements.
    • Parent education – being role models, open communication, supervision, knowing their children's friends, safe storage of medicines and alcohol.
    • Support the tobacco-free educational institution guidelines; enforcement of COTPA – no sale of tobacco to persons under 18 years or within 100 yards of educational institutions.
    • Community awareness under the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan; healthy recreation – sports, arts, youth clubs.
  2. Secondary prevention
    • Early identification through school health and adolescent health clinics (RKSK – Adolescent Friendly Health Clinics); screening with simple questions; brief counselling.
    • Referral to child guidance clinics and de-addiction or counselling services; tobacco quitline.
  3. Tertiary prevention
    • Support during treatment and rehabilitation, family therapy, return to school, relapse prevention and aftercare.
    • Throughout, the nurse maintains a non-judgemental, confidential approach.

Conclusion Substance use among children and adolescents – especially tobacco and inhalants – is linked to peer pressure, family problems, stress and availability. Nurses prevent it through life-skills education, parent guidance, support for tobacco-control laws and community programmes, and through early identification, counselling and referral of children who have started using substances.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Behavioural and Social Problems in Children
question: How is thumb sucking in children managed?
answer_html:
Thumb sucking is a common, normal self-soothing habit in infants and toddlers; most children stop on their own by 3–4 years. It becomes a problem if it persists beyond 4–5 years, when the permanent teeth erupt, because it may cause protrusion of upper teeth (malocclusion), speech problems and teasing. Management

  • Ignore it in young children; do not scold, shame or forcibly remove the thumb.
  • Find and reduce causes – boredom, tiredness, anxiety, hunger.
  • Keep the hands busy with toys and activities; offer comfort in other ways (cuddling, a soft toy).
  • Praise and reward periods without thumb sucking (star chart); gentle reminders.
  • Bandages or bitter nail paint only as a reminder if the child wishes to stop; dental appliances in persistent cases; refer to a dentist.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Behavioural and Social Problems in Children
question: What is nail biting? How is it managed?
answer_html:
Nail biting (onychophagia) is a tension-relieving habit, commonest in school-age children and adolescents, often occurring when the child is anxious, bored or concentrating (watching television, studying, before examinations). It may cause damaged nails, infection around the nails (paronychia), dental problems and worm infestation. Management

  • Look for and reduce the sources of stress – school pressure, family conflict, bullying.
  • Do not punish or nag; the child is often unaware of the habit.
  • Keep nails short and clean; provide something to do with the hands (stress ball, drawing, games).
  • Praise periods without nail biting; make the child a partner in stopping.
  • Bitter nail varnish as a reminder in older children who want to stop; relaxation techniques; refer if the habit is severe or associated with anxiety disorders.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Behavioural and Social Problems in Children
question: What are temper tantrums? How should parents handle them?
answer_html:
Temper tantrums are sudden outbursts of anger and frustration – crying, screaming, kicking, throwing things, lying on the floor or holding the breath – commonest between 1 and 3 years, when the child wants independence but cannot express needs in words. They are worse when the child is tired, hungry or unwell. Handling by parents

  • Stay calm; do not shout, hit or argue with the child.
  • Ensure safety – move the child away from dangerous objects.
  • Ignore the tantrum (planned ignoring) and do not give in to the demand, otherwise the child learns that tantrums work.
  • Use time-out for older toddlers; talk about feelings after the child is calm.
  • Prevent – regular meals and naps, warn before changes, offer simple choices, distract early.
  • Praise calm behaviour and be consistent; seek help if tantrums are very frequent, prolonged, cause injury or continue beyond 5 years.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Behavioural and Social Problems in Children
question: What are breath-holding spells?
answer_html:
Breath-holding spells are involuntary episodes in which a young child stops breathing after crying or a sudden fright or pain, between 6 months and 6 years (peak 1–2 years).

  • Cyanotic type (commonest) – after vigorous crying from anger or frustration, the child holds the breath in expiration, turns blue, may become limp and lose consciousness for a few seconds, sometimes with a few jerks, then recovers spontaneously.
  • Pallid type – after a sudden fright or minor injury, the child turns pale and limp (due to slowing of the heart).
  • They are harmless and do not cause brain damage or epilepsy; most children outgrow them by 5–6 years.
  • Management – reassure parents, lay the child on the side during an attack, stay calm and avoid giving in to the child's demands afterwards; treat iron-deficiency anaemia (iron reduces the spells); ECG in pallid spells if advised.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Behavioural and Social Problems in Children
question: What is encopresis?
answer_html:
Encopresis is the repeated passage of faeces in inappropriate places (clothes, floor) by a child aged 4 years or more, at least once a month for 3 months, not due to a physical illness.

  • Retentive encopresis (commonest, about 80–90%) – due to chronic constipation: the child withholds stool (painful defecation, fear of school toilets, coercive toilet training), the rectum becomes stretched and loses sensation, and liquid stool leaks around the hard mass (overflow soiling).
  • Non-retentive encopresis is linked with emotional stress or behaviour problems.
  • Management – explain that the child cannot control the leakage; disimpaction and regular laxatives (polyethylene glycol) for months; toilet sitting for 5–10 minutes after meals; high-fibre diet and fluids; star charts and praise; no punishment; counselling for emotional causes.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Behavioural and Social Problems in Children
question: How should stealing in children be managed?
answer_html:
Stealing is taking something that belongs to another without permission. Children below 5–6 years do not fully understand ownership, so taking things is not true stealing. In older children it may result from deprivation of love or material needs, jealousy, peer pressure, desire for attention, revenge or a poor example at home; persistent stealing with other antisocial acts may indicate conduct disorder. Management

  • Stay calm; explain that the act is wrong and help the child return or pay for the article – without public humiliation.
  • Avoid labelling the child a "thief" and avoid harsh punishment.
  • Find the cause – give attention and affection, reasonable pocket money, supervise friends.
  • Parents set a good example of honesty; praise honest behaviour.
  • Refer to a child guidance clinic if stealing is repeated or associated with other problems.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Behavioural and Social Problems in Children
question: What is a "child in conflict with law" under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015?
answer_html:
Under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, a "child in conflict with law" is a child below 18 years of age who is alleged or found to have committed an offence.

  • Such children are dealt with by the Juvenile Justice Board (JJB) – a magistrate with two social workers (at least one woman) – and not by regular criminal courts.
  • They are kept in observation homes during inquiry, not in police lock-ups or jails; the focus is on reformation, rehabilitation and social reintegration (counselling, education, vocational training, community service).
  • A child of 16–18 years accused of a heinous offence (punishable with 7 years or more) may, after a preliminary assessment by the JJB, be tried as an adult by the Children's Court.
  • Children who need protection (orphaned, abandoned, abused) are "children in need of care and protection" and are produced before the Child Welfare Committee.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Behavioural and Social Problems in Children
question: What is childhood-onset schizophrenia?
answer_html:
Childhood-onset (very early-onset) schizophrenia is schizophrenia beginning before 13 years of age. It is rare (much less common than adolescent or adult schizophrenia).

  • Onset is usually insidious, often preceded by developmental delays, social withdrawal and odd behaviour.
  • Features – auditory hallucinations, less organised delusions, disorganised speech and behaviour, flat affect, social withdrawal, decline in school performance and self-care.
  • It must be differentiated from autism, intellectual disability, mood disorders and organic causes.
  • Management – antipsychotics (for example, risperidone or aripiprazole) under a child psychiatrist, psychosocial interventions, special education and family psychoeducation; the course is often chronic, so long-term follow-up is needed.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Behavioural and Social Problems in Children
question: What is conversion reaction (functional neurological symptom disorder) in children?
answer_html:
A conversion reaction (functional neurological symptom disorder) is the appearance of neurological symptoms – such as weakness or paralysis of a limb, inability to walk, loss of voice (aphonia), blindness, abnormal movements or non-epileptic "fits" – without an underlying physical disease, in response to psychological stress.

  • It is commoner in adolescent girls; triggers include examinations, family conflict, loss, bullying and abuse.
  • Symptoms are not consciously produced; the child may show little concern, and symptoms may bring secondary gain (attention, escape from stress).
  • Management – rule out organic disease; reassure that the body is healthy and recovery is expected; avoid dramatic attention to symptoms; physiotherapy for gradual recovery of function; psychotherapy and family counselling to address the stress; screen for abuse.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Behavioural and Social Problems in Children
question: List the features of post-traumatic stress disorder in young children.
answer_html:
Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) can follow a frightening event such as abuse, an accident, violence, disaster or the death of a loved one. In young children the features differ from those in adults:

  • Re-living through play – repetitive play or drawings that re-enact the event.
  • Frightening dreams without clear content; night terrors, sleep problems.
  • Regression – loss of acquired skills such as toilet training (bedwetting), speech, or return to thumb sucking.
  • Clinging and separation anxiety; fear of new situations; avoidance of places or people linked to the event.
  • Hyperarousal – irritability, temper outbursts, startling easily, poor concentration.
  • Physical complaints such as headache and stomach-ache.
  • Management – safety and routine, psychological first aid, caregiver support and trauma-focused cognitive behaviour therapy or play therapy.

subject: Child Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Behavioural and Social Problems in Children
question: What is fabricated or induced illness (Munchausen syndrome by proxy)?
answer_html:
Fabricated or induced illness (FII), earlier called Munchausen syndrome by proxy, is a form of child abuse in which a parent or caregiver (usually the mother) invents, exaggerates or deliberately produces symptoms of illness in a child to gain attention or sympathy from health professionals.

  • Methods – false reports of symptoms (fits, apnoea), tampering with samples (adding blood or sugar to urine), poisoning (salt, laxatives, sedatives, insulin), suffocation, withholding food or medicines.
  • Warning signs – symptoms that occur only in the presence of the caregiver, unexplained, recurrent illnesses not matching any disease, failure of usual treatment, many hospital visits and investigations, a caregiver who seems unusually eager for procedures.
  • Management – careful documentation, close observation, discussion with the senior team and child-protection referral; the child's safety comes first.
